events.title: SpaceX up 10% in premarket after earnings beat and Musk hints at Tesla tie-up
events.summary: SpaceX soared in premarket trading after reporting strong revenue growth and beating estimates. The company pinned the results on its growing AI business, and recurring revenue from its satellite business. Billionaire owner Elon Musk also floated a potential merger with his electric-vehicle firm Tesla. SpaceX jumped in premarket trading on Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX- Tesla merger. The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest IPO ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion. Meanwhile, its operating income from operations came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier. On the earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday. SpaceX shares rose 10.2% before the markets opened on Wednesday. Meanwhile, Tesla shares were up 2.5% in premarket trading. It forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, per LSEG. "We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnson said in the earnings release. Johnson pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink , and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure. The company has dived into AI this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note. "Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added. They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates." — Lora Kolodny contributed to this report

events.title: James Robinson on What It Looks Like When a State is Failing
events.summary: The third and last episode from our Chicago live show is with James Robinson, a professor at the University of Chicago and a recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics (which he shared with Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson). His most famous work is 2012's Why Nations Fail, and in that book he and his co-author Acemoglu document the institutional factors — whether it is reliably run elections or open markets that help facilitate innovation — that determine why some states thrive and others don't. So we ask Robinson the big question: What would have to happen for the US to be considered a failed state? (Source: Bloomberg)

events.title: Data centre gas plant could be mothballed after two years, court told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Court hears gas power plant for Moss Vale data centre could be mothballed An artist's impression of one of three data centres planned for the Moss Vale site. ( Supplied: Cloud Carrier ) Nakar Property is appealing in court to build a $23 million gas power plant and battery storage system in the Southern Highlands. Its lawyers say the gas plant will be eventually replaced with cheaper energy supplied via the grid. Cross-examination of expert witnesses will continue for the hearing's third day on Thursday. A gas-fired power station proposed for the NSW Southern Highlands could be mothballed once the grid can meet the energy demands of an onsite data centre, a court has heard. The NSW Land and Environment Court is considering an appeal by developers Nakar Property, after Wingecarribee Shire Council refused its development application for a 16-megawatt power station and battery energy storage system in Moss Vale. The station is one of three planned to power a data centre campus on site proposed by Sydney company Cloud Carrier. Barrister James Smith, acting for Nakar Property, told the court the power plant was needed to provide constant power for customers using the centre. "[Cloud Carrier's] investment in computers is circa a $1 billion; the fundamental requirement is firm supply," Mr Smith said. "It's akin to enrolling your child in school without any teachers; Cloud Carrier can't sell any product unless there is firm supply." The proposed gas-fired power plant would be used to run Cloud Carrier's data centre campus. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) The second day of hearings before Commissioner Nicola Targett came after the court travelled to Moss Vale to inspect the site of the $23 million project on Tuesday. In his opening submissions, Mr Smith said developers would stop using gas power as soon as a reliable supply of energy from the grid could be secured. "The cost savings per year via connecting to the grid is approximately $14 million per year," he said. "There is clear financial incentive to use the grid when that power becomes available. The issue is there is not sufficient supply." Referencing expert reports, Mr Smith said the power plant was projected to emit less greenhouse emissions than if it were powered by the grid until approximately 2029. Addressing Commissioner Targett, barrister Michael Staunton, for Wingecarribee Shire Council, said that power supplied by the grid had been touted as a "panacea" to the project, but not investigated thoroughly. "All of that work and investigation should have been done, and you'll find when you get to the documents, it hasn't been," Mr Staunton said. After an adjournment, Wingecarribee Shire Council tendered draft conditions of consent in the middle of the hearing. These included a new requirement that canopy trees be planted across approximately 40 per cent of the development site. Expert air-quality, electrical and engineering consultants appeared as witnesses for cross-examination about reports they had prepared for the project. Mr Staunton argued during cross-examination that the project would not have the secure power needed to fill the full capacity of servers in the proposed data centre for two years, when an upgrade of a nearby power substation operated by Endeavour Energy would be completed. "You've got no firm supply for two years," Mr Staunton said. "That time could be spent negotiating with Endeavour Energy while you wait for the permanent connection." The matter will return to court on Thursday for a third day of hearings.

events.title: Surging fuel prices push UK inflation rate to 3.5% ahead of Budget
events.summary: Published 21 October 2026, 07:08 BST The pace of UK price rises accelerated ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices. The rate of inflation rose to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, its quickest pace since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies. The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, adding to pressure on Healey as he gears up for the Budget. Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre. Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures. ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year. The wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have pushed up fuel prices. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure. As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said. With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide." He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field . The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space". But the figures came as the ONS said the government borrowed £25bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs. The Conservatives said higher inflation and borrowing showed Labour had "lost control of the economy". Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith called for Healey to use his Budget to "tackle the deficit, and reduce the red tape and net zero costs that are driving up the cost of living for families". He added that the Conservatives would cut taxes, the costs of benefits and "wasteful" spending to "make our country prosperous again". Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the borrowing figures "painted a dismal picture" ahead of Healey's Budget. She said the amount borrowed in September was higher than analyst expectations as well as spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)'s forecast. "This reinforces our view that the Chancellor will deliver a cautious Budget on 28 October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year," she said. events.title: A $345,000 writing job at Anthropic says a lot about what humans still bring to the table
events.summary: Anthropic is advertising the role of an executive communications writer for $295,000 to $345,000 a year. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Anthropic is hiring an executive communications writer for up to $345,000. A comms pro told Business Insider that "When speed becomes cheap, judgment carries a premium." 3 writing experts gave Business Insider tips for young workers on practicing critical thinking. Anthropic's AI chatbot can draft a speech in seconds, but the company is now hiring a human writer — for $295,000 to $345,000 a year. Anthropic isn't looking for just anyone with a way with words. It wants someone with at least 8 years of experience who can quickly grasp technical concepts, help executives sharpen their thinking, and remain composed when news breaks. While some LinkedIn users reacted skeptically to the idea that the new hire's work would be used to  train AI , with an Oregon-based author commenting that this is the job one would take if the "writer wanted to build their own gallows," communication pros say the Anthropic job offers clues about the enduring value of human creatives. Three professional writers and comms experts told Business Insider that young writers need to understand that the work starts long before the typing does, and that being good with words is only part of the job. “When speed becomes cheap, judgment carries a premium," Ann Handley, the chief content officer at MarketingProfs and author of “Everybody Writes,” told Business Insider. "I think we're seeing that value extended to the role of the writer.” What AI could not achieve The opening for an "Executive Communications Writer" comes as Anthropic’s own research shows how AI is reshaping its workforce . According to the company's report, junior workers accounted for 9% of hires in technical departments in June, down from 27% in early 2025. In May, Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao said that AI already writes 90% of the company's code, which shifted hiring needs in all office roles toward oversight, judgment, and strategy, away from the actual execution. Rao also added that the company may actually expand hiring because "there's no shortage of work to do." Handley said that successful corporate communicators need to become strategists for the company's leaders, rather than simply polish their language. "Good writers have always been strategic, in the sense that they have always made choices about what goes on the page, and what does not," Handley said. "The successful candidate isn't merely shaping language, but shaping thought leadership and how the team is presenting to the world," Handley added. "That means knowing which ideas are worth owning, which are worth exploring, and which are just plain dumb." Joseph Braue, the executive editor of Content Marketing Partners, told Business Insider that a large part of the job as a corporate writer is to challenge unsupported claims, avoid overpromising, and resist pressure to publish weak material. “The decisions I’ve regretted the most were times I didn’t push back enough on corporate or customer executives,” Braue said, adding that while many writers do collaborate with AI , they must control the narrative and ensure accuracy. Measure your impact The compensation for Anthropic's communication role is high compared to similar openings, and professional writers said that there are ways a new hire in such a role could prove they are worth the expense. By comparison, Amazon Web Services has a job opening for an Executive Communications Manager based in Seattle, offering between $126,700 and $171,400 in annual pay. Josh Bernoff, an author on business strategy and former executive with 20 years of experience,   told Business Insider that a bigger pile of content isn’t proof of a writer’s value in a company, and that to get promoted, writers need to collect evidence of the impact of their writing. “If your job is to create market research reports, then you're only effective if people read those reports and say, 'here are the changes we're going to make on this product,'" Bernoff added. "Your job is to move people and think about how to do it before you start writing." Braue, who leads a content strategy team, said that writers looking to prove their value need to understand business language and check whether internal partners and key sales leaders are using their content. “Learn basic marketing analytics. Understand attribution, conversion, and how a pipeline works," Braue said. "Writers who speak revenue get promoted." Build evidence that you can think For young graduates, the pros recommend practicing original thinking while learning to use AI deliberately, even if you don't intend to be a writer. Bernoff said he would urge all early-career workers to take writing classes and to practice using AI for research and efficiency while composing the words themselves. Bernoff, who conducts an annual survey on how writers use AI, said he found last year that writers commonly used AI as a thesaurus or search engine, but fewer than 10% used it to create content intended to be published as is. "If you're in a position to move your fellow students or people reading a school newspaper or your professors, then you're going to be taking the first step that's necessary to be able to move people in a corporate environment," Bernoff said. Handley said she recommends that early career professionals start a newsletter and publish at least every two weeks, even with a small audience. “Maybe you'll learn to interview people or ask better questions or notice things others don't," Handley said. "In doing so, you'll build a body of work that shows a potential employer that, sure, you can write, but most importantly, you can think, and you can engage on the page.” Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Total UK government debt hits £3tn for first time while inflation jumps to highest in nearly a year – business live
events.summary: 1h ago Adura CEO: Jackdaw 'equivalent to Norwegian gas in terms of environmental performance' 1h ago UK borrowing hits £24.5bn in September as John Healey prepares for budget 2h ago Green party leader calls Jackdaw approval 'climate vandalism' 2h ago UK chancellor: Energy wealth fund to 'spark new wave of clean power' 2h ago Introduction: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% on rising motor fuels cost; UK approves Jackdaw gas field Carla Denyer , MP for Bristol and the former co-leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, said: Jackdaw will not bring down bills or protect jobs. This is an irresponsible decision from a government that seems to care more about the profits of fossil fuel companies than the money in your pocket or the safety of our planet. There is no future in fossil fuels. Pretending otherwise fails workers, billpayers, and the next generation who deserve to inherit a planet safe from climate catastrophe. It is now more important than ever that politicians, campaigners, scientists, and lawyers continue to work together to stop any more climate vandalism at the hands of this government. We must implore them to say no to Rosebank and to halt any plans to allow new oil and gas extraction through tie-backs to existing production facilities. What the government should be doing is making large-scale investments in cheap and reliable renewables to safeguard our energy security. They must also offer a package of support to future-proof jobs in the energy sector so that workers in oil and gas can transition to good-quality green jobs, alongside a nationwide home insulation programme and making polluters pay. Industry groups in north-east Scotland have said the decision on the Jackdaw gas field is “hugely welcome”, but the pending decision on the Rosebank oil field is “every bit as vital”. The Scottish government has called for the Treasury’s income from oil and gas to be placed in a “future generations fund”. The approval came after months of speculation about the Jackdaw offshore development, which is in the North Sea 150 miles to the east of Aberdeen. Groups representing the offshore industry had urged the UK government to approve the new development, stressing the economic and energy security benefits. However, environmental groups are dismayed by the move. Russell Borthwick , chief executive of Aberdeen + Grampian Chamber of Commerce, said: This is a hugely welcome decision, and exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for. Jackdaw is 99.9% complete and, with approval now secured, gas from this field will be flowing into homes up and down the country within weeks. This is a direct, tangible boost to the UK’s energy security at a time when it matters most. Every molecule of gas we produce in the North Sea, under some of the world’s highest environmental standards, is a molecule we don’t have to import on a tanker from overseas. But Jackdaw cannot be the end of the story. Rosebank is every bit as vital to our energy security and every bit as ready to deliver for the UK supply chain anchored here in the north east of Scotland. Government must now move with the same urgency and pragmatism and get Rosebank over the line without further delay. The Scottish government’s energy minister Stephen Gethins said the economic benefits of the Jackdaw field must be felt in Scotland. Perhaps the most significant failure of the past half-century of Westminster energy policy has been the failure to establish a futures fund. The UK has been almost the only country to discover oil and gas but not deliver a long-term benefit from a finite resource. That must change today. It is crucial that all further income from oil and gas resources taken by the UK Treasury is placed in a future generations fund. That would deliver a long-term benefit from a limited resource.” I am sure that the prime minister will agree that it is absolutely critical that if any new production goes ahead, then the economic benefits should be felt in Scotland and should be used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to plug more short-term spending gaps by the Treasury. The UK government must also replace the Energy Profits Levy with a fair system that protects jobs, energy security and investment in our energy sector. Angela Hepworth, chief executive of Scottish Renewables, said global events have brought the need for domestic energy into “sharper focus”. Today’s decision must now be matched by a renewed drive to deliver our long-standing clean energy ambitions. The UK needs a pragmatic approach to its energy future that secures investment, jobs and energy supplies in a volatile world. As the global shift towards electrification continues, the case for homegrown clean energy is stronger than ever. The approval of Jackdaw is an “important step” for the North Sea, according to Shell . The UK energy giant jointly owns Jackdaw operator Adura , which is headquartered in Aberdeen, together with Norway’s Equinor .

events.title: Oil prices climb as traders assess Middle East developments
events.summary: Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as escalating supply risks in the Middle East keep investors on edge. Attacks on tanker near the Hormuz Strait and on Saudi Arabian facilities by Iran-backed Houthis have Oil prices climbed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment. Brent crude futures gained 0.86% to $109.73 a barrel as of 3:33 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.78% to $98.58 a barrel. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized. "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their official Sepah News website . Adding to regional worries, Yemen's Houthi militants claimed responsibility on Monday for strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha. The escalating tensions have also sent global oil shipping costs soaring, adding another layer of pressure to energy markets. The global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel, compared with just $3 a year earlier, according to a Goldman Sachs report published Tuesday. While rates have eased slightly in recent days, they remain roughly seven times higher than a year ago. Goldman estimated that war-risk premiums associated with crossing the Strait of Hormuz accounted for about $7 of the $20 year-on-year increase in average crude freight rates, while ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf contributed another $4. The investment bank warned that elevated shipping costs could widen price differences between crude grades, squeeze refiners' profit margins and ultimately push up refined fuel prices. "High freight costs have weighed particularly heavily on Asian refineries' net margins, threatening their refined product output, which could then raise global refined product prices," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.

events.title: UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
events.summary: Decision was widely expected after lobbying by Shell but will dismay environmental campaigners What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely expected move that will nonetheless dismay environmental campaigners and a number of Labour MPs. While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project, which is being decided on separately, have sought environmental approval for existing licences. The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. The decision on Jackdaw had been expected last month but was delayed , seemingly to take it beyond the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October, where Labour was defending a seat against a Green challenge and ultimately won . The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said after approving the scheme. Andy Burnham has said drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter”. “At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” the prime minister said. “We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” When asked to clarify how many jobs the gasfield would create Fahnbulleh said: “It will create 27 jobs. “It will secure 273 jobs. But, look, that was not the primary consideration.” Announcing the decision, Fahnbulleh, said: “Following careful consideration of all relevant factors I have agreed that the regulator can grant consent for gas to be produced at Jackdaw, which will begin to supply the UK with gas from this winter thanks to the highly skilled and vital North Sea workers. “This decision will support the country’s energy security with homegrown gas this winter and help minimise the UK’s use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear. “The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050.” Fahnbulleh also said the government would launch a new energy wealth fund with a £2bn downpayment to reinvest oil and gas revenues into the climate transition. It hopes this fund will demonstrate that approving new gas fields is not at odds with Britain’s climate commitments. Environmental campaigners have called for Jackdaw and Rosebank to be abandoned, while Donald Trump has urged Burnham to open them. Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.” She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.” The oil and gas industry says the fields will provide 10% of the UK’s output at their peak. But campaigners say they will cause so much environmental damage as to obliterate any economic benefit. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, an independent joint venture half owned by Equinor and half by Shell . Both have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled that the companies needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce. The companies have been lobbying hard for the green light. Adura commissioned a report this week that said rejecting the two projects would cost the UK economy nearly £10.8bn over the next decade. The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling. That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and about half of 18- to 24-year-olds.

events.title: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
events.summary: U.K. inflation jumped to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% the previous month. Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%. Markets are pricing in two rate hikes from the Bank of England by the end of the year. U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. September's print marked a continuation of the U.K.'s upward trend for inflation, which came in at 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July. The September reading was the highest annual inflation figure in almost a year. The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that the motor fuel inflation rate had hit its highest level since August 2022, when fuel costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Britain is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks, such as the U.S.-Iran war and the subsequent struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz. U.K. motor fuel prices surged 29.8% in the year to September, ONS data showed on Wednesday. The British pound was flat against both the euro and the U.S. dollar following the data release, and yields on U.K. government bonds were also little changed. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note Wednesday morning that recent growth in headline inflation had "undone the progress we saw in the spring." "Bank of England policymakers will be looking beyond the headline figure," he said. "Services inflation, in particular, has accelerated in recent months which will create concern that we are starting to see second round inflationary effects beyond energy prices. While we face a different set of challenges compared to 2021, the prolonged conflict is weighing on the U.K. economy and making the case for a rate hike stronger." Markets are pricing in a 98% chance that the Bank of England raises its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 4% next month, according to LSEG data, with the majority of traders also pricing in a further hike of the same size at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December. Wednesday's expected rise in inflation also complicates the fiscal picture for the U.K. government and its finance minister. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to unveil his first fiscal shakeup next week during the U.K.'s hotly anticipated Autumn Budget. He is tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules, which aim to rein in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs. But separate data published Wednesday showed the U.K.'s national debt was estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion ($4 trillion) in September for the first time. The cost of servicing those debts has risen drastically over the past year, and the British economy is struggling to grow . Healey said in a statement following Wednesday's data release that he would be "maintaining our fiscal discipline" in the budget next week, while working to "drive for growth [and give] businesses and families some breathing space." Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said in a note Wednesday morning that rising inflation is turning the Autumn Budget into "a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor." He said surging prices were "increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options." "With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," he said. "Policymakers will also be looking to the Chancellor to avoid adding fuel to the inflation fire by delivering a credible, fiscally disciplined Budget."

events.title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it

Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months. OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so. An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks. "In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech. The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks. OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

events.title: Singapore to update restructuring and insolvency framework to better serve economy, businesses
events.summary: Law Minister Edwin Tong speaking at the Singapore Insolvency Conference on Oct 21. The IRDA will be amended to make judicial management a clear rescue process. Applicants must show how it can save a business and why it is better than liquidation. Cross-class cramdown rules will be made easier to use. Voting thresholds will be refined, and shareholders may be bound in some cases, with safeguards to protect fairness. Singapore will adopt two more UNCITRAL model laws on group insolvency and insolvency-related judgments. This will improve cross-border cooperation and support its role as a restructuring hub. SINGAPORE – Forty years after judicial management was introduced in Singapore, the process has not always fulfilled its purpose of rescuing beleaguered but viable businesses and preserving their value. “Too often, it has become a precursor to liquidation, adding time and costs without necessarily achieving meaningful rehabilitation,” said Minister for Law Edwin Tong on Oct 21. “This is unacceptable,” he added, giving the keynote address at the Singapore Insolvency Conference organised by the Insolvency Practitioners Association of Singapore. His ministry will amend the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (IRDA) to make it clear that judicial management is a rehabilitative process, with the first reading of the Bill in Parliament slated for later in 2026 or early 2027. In May, the Ministry of Law broadly accepted reform recommendations made in 2025 by the Committee to Enhance Singapore’s Corporate Restructuring and Insolvency Regime, after a public consultation. Tong stressed that premature liquidation can destroy value and that financial distress does not necessarily mean a business is no longer viable. “The company may well have a very sound underlying business and good assets, but an unsustainable debt burden or temporary liquidity difficulties. And in such a situation, premature liquidation or prolonged administration can destroy them,” said Tong, who is also the Second Minister for Home Affairs. “In a mature economy like Singapore’s, business cycles, ups and downs will be inevitable. They will be recurring, and industries will go through periods of growth and decline. We need a stronger restructuring framework to allow businesses to recover and to absorb the shocks of that ebb and flow.” Under judicial management, control of a financially distressed company is temporarily placed under an independent, court-appointed judicial manager with the aim of keeping the company afloat, or to work out a debt restructuring plan. The company is protected against lawsuits by creditors during this period. The business typically shifts to liquidation and winding up if the creditors reject the proposed rescue plan by the judicial manager. As part of the amendments to the IRDA, applicants for judicial management must be able to explain how the process is expected to rehabilitate the company or its business, and the tangible benefits compared to winding up the company. A company, its directors or a creditor can apply to the court for a judicial management order. Should judicial management fail to rehabilitate the company and it proceeds to liquidation, the circumstances leading to this must be explained. The judicial manager will also typically not be allowed to transition into the company’s liquidator role. “Not every rescue will succeed, even when there were good prospects at the outset for a successful restructuring,” Tong said. “But it is really about making sure that the judicial management is pursued for the right reasons, with clear objectives and, importantly, in this case, accountability for the outcomes that are sought.” The second recommendation is to make cross-class cramdown to be more accessible and user-friendly. Cross-class cramdown allows the court to approve a restructuring or bankruptcy plan even if it is not accepted by the majority of the voting creditors or shareholders. Such plans are typically structured to ensure a better overall outcome for stakeholders compared to other alternatives. In Singapore, a restructuring plan must be approved by at least one group of creditors who would be worse off or whose rights would be affected by the plan and who would receive some payment if the company were wound up. At least 75% of the creditors in this group must vote to support the plan. The plan must also be approved by a majority in terms of the number of creditors voting on the plan , and those voting in favour must hold at least 75% of the total value of claims held by all creditors covered by the plan. At the conference, Tong noted that the cross-class cramdown mechanism has seen limited use since its introduction in 2017. In its report, the committee noted that the “overall numerosity and value cramdown conditions jointly constitute a high threshold, which deters the putting together of a plan that involves a cross-class cramdown”.

The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket's international platform. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.” “Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.” Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract. Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities. Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird. Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization. A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James. A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved. events.title: AI's spending boom faces a 'gut check': Who can actually make money?
events.summary: Elice's bruising IPO debut and next-day recovery highlights growing investor scrutiny over whether AI infrastructure spending can deliver sustainable profits. Rising borrowing costs are exposing debt-heavy neocloud providers to financing risks. Analysts expect a widening divide between AI companies generating sustainable returns and those reliant on external financing. The artificial intelligence boom may be entering a more unforgiving phase, as investors increasingly question whether the billions poured into data centers will translate into sustainable profits. A bruising stock market debut by South Korean AI infrastructure provider Elice has become the latest warning sign that investors may be more closely scrutinizing ambitious expansion plans and paths to profitability. "This is a gut check moment in the tech trade," said Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives. "Investors are trying to better discern between the winners and losers and if there are any weak links in the tech AI food chain." "Patience is wearing thin and scrutiny will be elevated especially for those taking on a major debt load like some of the neoclouds," he added. The weak debut underscores a broader shift in sentiment toward the AI trade, where rising borrowing costs and concerns over debt-fueled expansion may force investors to distinguish between companies generating cash from the boom and those spending heavily in anticipation of future demand. "The AI trade has moved from a phase where the size of the capex announcement was itself viewed positively to one where investors are asking who can actually earn an adequate return on that capital," said Billy Leung of Global X ETFs. "The market is distinguishing between companies that need capital to survive the build-out and companies that are being paid as the build-out continues." The most vulnerable companies are neocloud providers expanding faster than their ability to generate cash, particularly those heavily dependent on external financing, according to Leung. CoreWeave, one of the largest neocloud providers, is "the poster child of this whole thing," according to John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research. "This is broad market stress, not just speculation," he said, pointing to widening credit spreads. Companies borrowing heavily to build computing capacity could face a squeeze if financing costs rise faster than revenue, particularly where construction expenses and depreciation mount before facilities reach full utilization. The shift is particularly significant for Asia, where technology markets are heavily exposed to the semiconductor and memory-chip industries that have powered the global AI investment frenzy. "U.S. semiconductor and AI plays are overbuilt. And in South Korea, even more overbuilt," Blank said. South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics have been among the biggest beneficiaries of soaring demand for advanced memory chips, but their shares have come under pressure as investors reassess the sustainability of AI spending. "Asia is simply much more directly geared to the hardware and memory side of the AI trade, so when investors question AI capex and financing, Korea and other North Asian technology markets feel it disproportionately," Leung said. He added that rising earnings estimates across South Korea and Taiwan suggest the recent selloff reflects deteriorating sentiment and shrinking valuations rather than a sudden collapse in demand. The change reflects a growing divide between companies with the financial firepower to sustain aggressive AI investments and those relying heavily on borrowing to fund expansion. HSBC Chief Executive Officer Georges Elhedery warned that investors and lenders must become more discerning about which data-center projects deserve financing. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements," he said. "You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."

events.title: The right to enforce civil rights is under attack in the US
events.summary: The Trump administration and conservative courts are restricting the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to challenge rights violations. Lecturer in Government at Harvard University and lecturer in Social Sciences at Boston University. This autumn, the Supreme Court will consider a question with potentially far-reaching consequences for civil rights in the United States: Who gets to enforce them? On November 30, the justices will hear a case over whether employees of federally funded universities can sue under Title IX over alleged workplace sex discrimination. The Trump administration has urged the court to rule that they cannot, arguing that Congress never gave university employees a private right to bring such claims. The dispute is the latest front in a broader legal push to restrict the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to take rights violations to court themselves. In June, the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to a federal appeals court ruling that barred Arkansas United, an immigrant advocacy organisation, from suing to enforce protections for voters who need assistance at the polls. Across a growing number of cases, Republican-led states and the Trump administration are advancing the same basic principle: Unless Congress has clearly authorised private citizens to sue, enforcement should largely be left to the government. That may sound like an arcane legal argument, but its implications are anything but. If individuals and civil rights groups cannot go to court when laws protecting them are violated, the power to decide which rights are actually enforced increasingly rests with the very government that may be violating, ignoring or choosing not to enforce them. A private right of action allows individuals, or groups acting on their behalf, to file lawsuits to enforce rights protected by law. These lawsuits can seek compliance with the law or compensation for past violations. Private rights of action are not automatic under US federal and state law. Congress and state legislatures sometimes explicitly authorise private lawsuits. Where they have not, courts have had to determine whether a law implicitly allows individuals or groups to sue, or whether enforcement rests solely with government authorities. In practice, private litigation has been an essential part of enforcing rights throughout much of US history. As University of Virginia School of Law Professor George Rutherglen writes in a 2015 law review article ( PDF ): “The long history of civil rights, dating back to Reconstruction, makes them quintessentially private rights, whose exercise and enforcement should depend primarily on the initiative of the individuals who bear those rights. Public enforcement no doubt remains necessary, and it has an equally long and distinguished pedigree in civil rights law, but it cannot entirely displace individual control over individual rights.” Proponents of private rights of action, such as AARP, consider them an effective tool for vulnerable individuals and groups to protect their rights when government agencies are unwilling or unable to act. Critics, such as the US Chamber of Commerce Institute for Legal Reform, however, argue that private lawsuits can encourage frivolous litigation . These critics, often from the political right, have attempted to restrict private litigation through legal arguments against private causes of action. An example is the 2001 Alexander v Sandoval decision, in which a Supreme Court majority led by Justice Antonin Scalia ruled that Title VI did not provide a private right of action to enforce regulations prohibiting policies or practices with a disparate impact on protected groups – discrimination that can occur without clear evidence of intent. The legal push against private rights of action has intensified in recent years. Republican-led states have increasingly challenged the doctrine of implied private rights of action, arguing that courts should reject private suits to enforce various types of rights. The Trump administration has also adopted this stance. When the court decided a 2021 voting rights case, Justice Neil Gorsuch submitted a one-paragraph concurrence, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, questioning whether “the Voting Rights Act of 1965 furnishes an implied cause of action,” despite that issue not being raised in the case itself. The conservative push to restrict private rights of action has extended to a variety of areas. In June, the Supreme Court ruled against Falun Gong practitioners who accused Cisco Systems of helping the Chinese government develop surveillance technology used to facilitate their persecution, concluding that they could not pursue those aiding-and-abetting claims under the federal laws they had invoked. One of the most consequential implications of restricting private rights of action is the threat to voting rights.

events.title: UK approves long-awaited Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
events.summary: Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea ​gasfield , ending years ​of legal and political wrangling that had ⁠pitted the Labour government's climate commitments against its push ⁠to bolster energy security. Energy Minister Miatta ​Fahnbulleh said the project will start to supply gas to British homes and businesses from as ⁠early as the end of this month. At the same time, she said a new Energy Wealth Fund would be established by the government with a £2 billion downpayment to reinvest oil and ⁠gas revenue into the climate transition. Ms Fahnbulleh said Jackdaw was expected to increase ​domestic gas ⁠production by about 6 per cent at ‌its peak and support the country's gas supply over its lifespan of up to ​11 years, boosting energy security and protecting hundreds of jobs. “At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” Adura, the joint venture between energy giants Shell and Norway's Equinor that operates the project, has said Jackdaw will produce gas equivalent to up to 40,000 barrels of oil a day at peak output. Environmental groups could mount a fresh legal challenge to the approval. The issue ​has become a rallying point for climate activists, who say approving new fossil fuel projects undermines Labour's green pledges and ignores warnings from a summer of record-breaking heat across Europe. The fate of Jackdaw had been in ​limbo for years and has forced Mr Burnham to take sides in a battle over the future of the North Sea while risking alienating voters. The relatively small gas project has become a symbol of a bitter political fight over Britain’s energy transition. Approving Jackdaw risked a backlash from some on the left of the Labour Party and the Greens. Rejecting drilling in the field would have fuelled criticism from Reform UK, the Conservatives and the oil industry that climate policies are costing Britain jobs and investment. The previous Conservative government approved the project ‌in 2022, but climate activists challenged ⁠the decision in court alongside approval for ​the Rosebank oil and gasfield. A 2025 ruling barred operators from ​extracting oil ‌or gas until they received fresh government consent that takes into account emissions from the burning ⁠of the fields' hydrocarbons. The decision has taken on added significance for Mr Burnham since ⁠he took office in July. In its 2024 general election manifesto, the Labour Party pledged to block new drilling in the North Sea, but officials say decisions on Jackdaw and Rosebank – the largest undeveloped oil and gas reservoir in British waters – fall outside that commitment because they involve licences approved years ago under the previous government. “Jackdaw has been made into this big issue because it’s become a symbol of the wider North Sea debate,” said Jess Ralston, head of energy at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, an independent non-profit. “But even if the government approves it and Rosebank, the North Sea debate isn’t going to get any less flammable.” Even once drilling gets under way, few believe the UK could ever compete again with major oil and gas regions. Its stretch of the North Sea is 90 per cent depleted for commercial resources, according to consultant Wood Mackenzie. The international companies that pioneered drilling there 60 years ago have retreated.

events.title: The Bezos Earth Fund has given away $2.4 billion. Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos’ latest $100M bet is saving species on the edge of extinction
events.summary: Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos are putting $100 million behind the idea that the world’s most endangered animals and plants can still be pulled back from extinction. The Bezos Earth Fund is one of nine founding members of the new Species Recovery Alliance , a $500 million commitment announced Oct. 16 at the Leaders’ Summit of COP17 , the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia, by Cristián Samper, the fund’s managing director and leader of nature solutions. The Earth Fund is contributing $100 million of that total, a spokesperson told Fortune . “We know how to bring species back from the brink,” Samper said in a statement to Fortune . “What too many conservation teams lack is reliable funding to keep that work going. Rebuilding a population can take years, and a break in support can put hard-won progress at risk.” The other founding members are Leonardo DiCaprio’s Re:wild, Rainforest Trust, the Colossal Foundation, the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund, Fondation Segré, the Franklinia Foundation, the Ayers Wild Cat Conservation Trust, and WildLives Earth.  Members won’t pool their money into a single fund. Instead, each will direct its own grants while coordinating with the others. The money will go to conservation groups and local partners working on species the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies as endangered, critically endangered, or extinct in the wild.  Depending on the species, that could mean breeding animals in captivity and releasing them, restoring habitat, managing disease, or controlling invasive species. Members will measure their progress using the IUCN’s Red List and its Green Status of Species, the fund said. The alliance is targeting a long list. More than 49,500 species are threatened with extinction, according to the IUCN Red List . The alliance will fund work on species in the three highest-risk categories (endangered, critically endangered, and extinct in the wild), which together include more than 31,000 species. The alliance builds on the Phoenix Species Project , which the Earth Fund launched in August with Re:wild, the conservation group co-founded by DiCaprio. Each organization committed $100 million to Phoenix, for a total of $200 million. The project aims to recover 100 critically endangered and extinct-in-the-wild species across 30 countries, including Madagascar’s golden-crowned sifaka and Australia’s elusive night parrot. “Kids fall in love with animals before anyone tells them those animals are disappearing. Ask any seven-year-old about their favorite creature. It’s something wild,” Sánchez Bezos said in a statement at the time. “Something most adults have never heard of. What do we tell them when the night parrot or the golden-crowned sifaka isn’t there anymore to fall in love with? This project is our answer.” Filling a government gap The new pledge comes as governments fall far behind their own nature-funding targets. At the 2022 biodiversity summit in Montreal, countries pledged to raise $200 billion a year for biodiversity by 2030. Countries raised between $75 billion and $92 billion a year from 2023 through 2025, which was less than half of that goal, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data cited by the Associated Press . A UN progress report released ahead of the summit found fewer than half of countries’ biodiversity targets are on target. “We’re not moving fast enough,” Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, told the AP . Alongside the private alliance, 17 governments led by Colombia and Armenia launched a separate initiative, the Coalition of Action to Recover Endangered Species (CARES). Samper called it “an encouraging expression of ambition,” but “the next step is to ensure that ambition is backed by the resources needed to deliver.” “Philanthropy can help accelerate recovery, and sustained public funding is essential to achieving it at scale,” he continued. The $10 billion clock Bezos, the Amazon founder worth $372 billion , launched the Earth Fund in 2020 with a $10 billion pledge to fight climate change and protect nature by 2030, which is the largest individual philanthropic commitment to climate and nature ever. Sánchez Bezos, the fund’s vice chair since its early days, has become a more visible face of the couple’s giving . The fund has granted $2.4 billion to date, the spokesperson told Fortune . That leaves more than $7 billion to distribute in about four years. Fund officials told Bloomberg in May they remain committed to the target.  The pace of giving has been steady in recent months. The fund has announced $34 million for sustainable fabrics , $26 million for wildfire detection, $100 million to turn vacant urban land into parks in eight U.S. cities, and more than $25 million in Pacific Ocean grants in September. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Fiber alignment is the main bottleneck to optical engine testing, which would be alleviated significantly by multi-site probe cards. Optical connectors must be optimized for the best optical properties yet be mechanically robust to withstand assembly and use. Simultaneous loopback on both optical and electrical sides could simplify testing. Experts At The Table : The industry is forging a path from single-site to multi-site testing while system architectures and connector types continue to evolve. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne ; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America ; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group ; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click here . Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal. SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today? Armstrong: I would hope some insertions will go away over time, but right now there are more things being added than being subtracted. It’s a hard one. In terms of testing one die, that depends on the die. If an 8 kW GPU is your main ASIC, and you have multiple connectors around multiple sides of the part from a tester resource standpoint, and the amount of power a tester can deliver and take out of the part, it’s pretty challenging to get beyond one die. But if you look down the NPO-versus-CPO path, NPO is typically a single connector device. You’re going to have to be able to go to multi-site to scale that to high volume. Insertions two and three are the fertile ground for multi-site. Those are longer more complex test insertions. PIC wafer testing tends to be single-site today. From my experience, there is some hope on the horizon to bring it up a little bit higher with some capabilities in the probe card area, notably from Technoprobe. Griffin: I agree with Dave. Most production solutions today are single-site, and when you talk about the optical engine, the main bottleneck is fiber alignment. Many companies are working on multi-site solutions, and I hope they succeed and take off because that only helps the whole industry ramp faster. But we’ve got a little bit longer to go there. SE: For these alignment ports, can you repeatedly test at that site? Griffin: Ideally, you’re able to repeatedly test almost infinitely because you should never be contacting the device with the optical probe or the fiber array unit (FAU). When you’re bringing up a new test solution, you do sometimes crash FAUs on first systems. In reality, the bigger concern is contamination on the FAU, so cleaning is needed. On the connector side, at the module level or for optical engines with receptacles attached, the optical connector lifecycle is where we need more effort, because the device-side connector is designed to be attached once and, hopefully, never disconnected. And every new connector generation changes both the connector recipe and the automation recipe. Leventhal: In a sense, this is nothing new. For instance, with BGAs, if you socket at the device too many times, then you start worrying about damaging the balls on the BGA. It’s a similar problem and the industry will gravitate toward connector designs that are more robust. Matt made a really important point about how your test side connector needs to be some sort of a hardened connector that doesn’t wear out easily after 20 to 50 insertions. It needs to last for tens of thousands or 100,000 insertions. So you’ve got to go to a hardened metal, and then you’ve got a hardened metal going against the receptacle on the device, which is not going to be that hardened metal. If you’re not careful, you could damage that connector sooner than the spec lifetime. So as the industry evolves to the winning connector designs, robustness on the device side is going to be a really important part of that. SE: What are the challenges with making simultaneous electrical and optical connections? Armstrong: It’s just a question of time. Yamaguchi: Beyond DC and optical probing, the harder part of simultaneous electrical and optical connection is characterizing electro-optic devices in RF. Modulator and photodetector performance is ultimately validated through S-parameters, so you need optical and high-frequency RF contact at the same time. Probe cards can only fit a limited number of RF lines, and their bandwidth is also limited, while today’s devices are characterized beyond 200 GHz. At wafer and die insertions, simultaneous connection is really an RF probing challenge. Leventhal: Warpage is going to create additional challenges on top of just trying to solve the problem in an ideal case. You need to be able to align in multiple axes. And the BGA has a crazy amount of pins that you have to make reliable contact with, so that problem is getting more challenging. Adding to that is being able to do the right level of alignment, either coming from the top or coming from the side. It’s significantly challenging. I agree with Dave, it’s a question of time in multiple senses. Each insertion takes time, although there are ways of minimizing that by integrating certain operations together. But also, it’s going to take time for all of this to mature to the point that it’s going to be easier to test at scale. Griffin: At its core, there’s an optical and an electrical interface to the device at every insertion, and sometimes those interfaces are on the top side of the device, sometimes the bottom side, and sometimes both. And then when you talk about module level, they’re on two to four sides of the package across some number of optical engines. So if you look at optical alignment on its own, it’s not that big of a challenge. But when you start combining it with all the different, I’ll say, flavors of architecture that we’re seeing, and trying to design a scalable test system that can handle as many of those flavors as possible for your customers, that’s really where some of the fun challenges are. Armstrong: I also chair the IPSR test roadmap for photonics, and in our latest report we highlight a test methodology for AC testing. AC testing, bit error rate testing, will be one of the bigger time sinks. If we had good DFT, we could just do loopback on the optical side and loopback on the electrical side at the same time. And technically, there’s no reason you couldn’t combine those two tests. But today, most people are saying, “Okay, I’ll do loopback on one side or the other side, and a bit error rate test of some nature on the other side, so that becomes a very expensive setup that doubles the effective test time. events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Fab workflow connects GDS layout import, 3D process simulation, GPU-accelerated FDTD, design of experiments, with AI-based surrogate modeling. Photonic integrated circuit (PIC) performance is increasingly bounded by fabrication realities such as sidewall angle, critical-dimension bias, thickness variation, and line-edge roughness, which idealized, as-drawn FDTD simulations fail to capture. Here, we show a Fab Technology Co-Optimization (FTCO) workflow that connects GDS layout import, three-dimensional process simulation, GPU-accelerated FDTD, design of experiments (DOE), with AI-based surrogate modeling. We show that when manufacturing variations are included in the modeling that the simulation results align well with experimentally reported results. A directional-coupler DOE with 25 unique combinations of 4 different process variations requiring a 65-million-cell 3D FDTD model and completes in under 10 hours on a single NVIDIA A100-equipped workstation is showcased. The generated digital twin provides intuitive and real-time access to the process-to-performance relationship for non-simulation experts: A game-changer in the industry. Achieving the requisite target yield as early as possible during silicon ramp is a lead indicator of product success. Delays in reaching yield entitlement can impact time-to-market, increase manufacturing costs, and reduce overall product competitiveness—particularly at advanced nodes where complexity and cost continue to rise. As a result, incorporating a solution that can rapidly identify and resolve systematic yield limiters has become essential to enabling efficient ramp to high-volume production. Such a solution requires analytics-driven volume diagnostic and failure analysis capabilities to reverse engineer test failures captured on automatic test equipment (ATE). These capabilities identify the precise failing location within the chip, rank failure candidates based on yield impact, and provide the highest-priority candidates to the failure analysis lab for final root-cause confirmation. Corrective action can then be performed on either the design or the silicon process to correct and improve the yield of your chip and ultimately enable you to go to high volume production and into the market ahead of the competition. events.title: ‘Tap dancing through a minefield’: Elon Musk’s $3.5 trillion Tesla-SpaceX merger talks expose his power—and scant accountability
events.summary: Elon Musk said Tuesday that independent directors at Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to explore combining the two companies—a deal that, at current market values, would create a roughly $3.5 trillion giant. Musk said he can’t take part in the talks because he is a “conflicted party.” “This is definitely the kind of question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield,” Musk said on SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call , adding that it would be “overstating it” to call a merger a certainty. The talks put a fresh spotlight on a question that has followed Musk since SpaceX’s June IPO made him the world’s first trillionaire, at least on paper: When one person holds this much wealth and controls this many companies, who holds him accountable? A trillion-dollar fortune, on paper SpaceX priced its shares at $135 and began trading under the ticker SPCX on June 12. The stock closed its first day at $161.11 , up nearly 20%, and the company’s market value topped $2 trillion during the session. According to SpaceX’s IPO filing, Musk held about 4.8 billion shares plus 350 million options exercisable at $8.39 each—enough to push his net worth past $1 trillion at the offering price, CBS News reported . That status has proved fragile. Musk has since called himself a “former trillionaire,” and his fortune has hovered around the line. Forbes said he regained trillionaire status on Oct. 9 , then pegged his net worth at $977.2 billion on Oct. 13 after SpaceX shares slid. Much of that wealth is also tied up in stock he can’t sell for a year under the IPO lockup. Even so, the scale is hard to overstate. Only 19 countries have a GDP above $1 trillion, according to World Bank data cited by CBS. Nabil Ahmed, Oxfam America’s senior director of economic justice, said Musk’s fortune represents a “new Gilded Age” of wealth inequality. “Elon Musk’s rise to trillionaire status marks a new pinnacle of oligarchy,” he said. A company built for one person’s control The sharpest accountability questions center on how SpaceX is governed. The company went public with a multi-class share structure in which Class B shares carry 10 votes apiece. Musk owns about 45% of SpaceX but controls roughly 82% of its voting power, Fortune reported . As Fortune detailed ahead of the IPO , only Class B holders can remove Musk as CEO, chairman, or director. SpaceX uses the “controlled company” exemption to skip a majority-independent board and independent nominating and compensation committees. The company reincorporated from Delaware to Texas in 2024, and its charter pushes shareholder claims into mandatory arbitration and limits derivative suits to investors holding at least 3% of the stock—a stake worth tens of billions of dollars. In a May 13 letter, CalPERS and the New York City and New York State comptrollers warned that the structure “would constitute the most management-favorable governance structure ever brought to the U.S. markets at this scale.” Musk’s potential upside is also outsize. SpaceX’s board set aside 1 billion super-voting shares for him that vest only if the company hits market-cap milestones of up to $7.5 trillion and establishes “a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants.” Deals between Musk’s own companies Transactions among Musk’s businesses are another pressure point. In November 2025, Tesla shareholders weighed a nonbinding proposal for the carmaker to invest in xAI, Musk’s AI startup. About 1.06 billion shares voted for it and 916.3 million against, with more than 473 million abstaining. Because Tesla’s bylaws count abstentions as votes against, the measure failed , Bloomberg reported. In January, Tesla disclosed a $2 billion investment in xAI anyway. “We’re just doing what shareholders asked us to do, pretty much,” Musk said. Days later, SpaceX acquired xAI in a deal that valued the combined company at $1.25 trillion. Tesla also did more than $573 million in business with Musk-controlled companies in fiscal 2025, including $430.1 million in Megapack battery sales to xAI and $143.3 million in Cybertruck sales to SpaceX, according to an analysis of Tesla’s SEC filings by Transparency Lab . Tesla’s audit committee deemed the deals to be at arm’s length, and the analysis does not allege illegal conduct. Regulators and courts have had limited reach Musk’s run-ins with regulators show how difficult he can be to rein in. In 2018, he tweeted: “Nothing stopping Tesla team at our car plant from voting union… But why pay union dues & give up stock options for nothing?” The National Labor Relations Board ruled the post was an illegal threat and ordered it deleted, and a Fifth Circuit panel upheld that decision in 2023. The full court reheard the case in January 2024 , and in October 2024 ruled 9-8 that the NLRB had no power to order the tweet removed, citing the First Amendment. The Securities and Exchange Commission sued Musk in January 2025, alleging he waited too long to disclose his Twitter stake and cost other shareholders more than $150 million. He settled for a $1.5 million penalty without admitting wrongdoing. U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan approved the deal in July despite “serious misgivings,” noting the court is “not a rubber stamp” but can reject only settlements that are clearly unreasonable. Safety questions at Starbase Worker safety at SpaceX’s Starbase site in South Texas has also drawn scrutiny. A TechCrunch analysis of OSHA data found Starbase recorded 4.27 injuries per 100 workers in 2024—almost six times the average for comparable space-vehicle manufacturers and nearly triple the 1.6 rate for aerospace manufacturing overall. Rival sites run by United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin reported rates near 1.1. NASA is paying SpaceX more than $4 billion for two crewed Starship landings on the moon. But under its contracts, a high injury rate alone isn’t an automatic trigger for action and doesn’t meet the definition of a “major breach of safety,” which covers events such as a fatality or a willful or repeat OSHA violation, TechCrunch reported. In January, OSHA cited SpaceX for seven “serious” violations tied to a June 2025 crane collapse at Starbase, with penalties totaling $115,850; SpaceX is contesting them. Then, on May 15, a worker died at the site. OSHA opened an investigation and said it could take months to complete. Who else shares in the upside Musk isn’t the only one getting richer. About 4,400 SpaceX employees stood to become millionaires once the stock began trading, the New York Times reported, and Fortune profiled workers from top executives to welders whose equity is now worth seven figures or more. The proposed Tesla tie-up may be the clearest test yet of whether outside shareholders still have a meaningful say. Musk said a combination would require approval from a majority of all outstanding Tesla shares—“quite a high hurdle,” in his words. Tesla’s annual proxy, filed Monday, includes no merger proposal.
