events.title: Powerful new AI models are powering a growing wave of cyber attacks, experts say
events.summary: Starting on Sept. 25, a hacker set loose an army of AI agents that attempted to break into over 1,200 websites over the next few weeks—autonomously, with no additional work required of the human hacker after sending them off on their task. The agents successfully breached about 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere , home appliance ​company SharkNinja, and engine manufacturer Cummins, according to Reuters, which first reported the incident, discovered by cybersecurity researchers. While the hacker didn’t need to execute the attack themselves, they had to foot the bill for the AI tools. It cost about $5,000 worth of tokens from a combination of DeepSeek and Anthropic’s Claude Code models, researchers told Reuters. That’s roughly $50 per successful breach. Autonomous attacks powered by AI agents are becoming more common, Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) told Fortune . This is primarily happening because the tools have “gotten meaningfully better” over the past year or so, she said. Specifically, AI companies have improved their models’ coding skills, which has led to “dramatic increase in their ability to do cybersecurity-relevant tasks like analyze large volumes of code,” she said. Also, they have become more agentic, meaning they can use other software to complete tasks, as opposed to merely outputting text.  “These AI systems are now both more capable of hacking and are able to act more autonomously,” Ji said.  Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) can run all day and night without stopping, at a “fraction of the cost of human attackers,” Varun Chandrasekaran, Assistant Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois’ Grainger College of Engineering, told Fortune . This “fundamentally changes the economics of exploitation,” he said, citing the attackers who spent only $50 per successful reach.  Debate grows over the value and risks of open weight AI Open-weight models, or those that are publicly downloadable and customizable, can also offer powerful, low-cost tools for agentic hacks, Ji said. Attackers are “not restricted to the most capable ‘closed’ models and can use similarly-capable open models that are potentially more difficult to set up, but less expensive,” she said.  The wide availability of low-cost, powerful open models is one reason Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that open models in particular pose a risk of widespread and potentially devastating cyber attacks. It is one reason that Amodei and others have said that there may need to be government restrictions placed on the distribution and use of open models. However, others disagree and say open models benefit defenders more than attackers. For example, when the AI company Hugging Face discovered it was being autonomously attacked by an agent in July, it first tried to use a closed model to defend itself, but the model refused the request due to its security guardrails. Hugging Face then switched to an open model, GLM 5.2 made by China-based Z.ai , which it used to help fend off the attack. More autonomous cyber attacks The same thing happened during another agentic attack this week that targeted OpenCode, an AI-powered coding platform. A hacker unleashed an autonomous AI model on OpenCode that was “non-stop trying to attack our systems for the past 48 hours,” OpenCode founder Dax Raad posted on X on Oct. 18. The attackers broke into certain OpenCode user accounts, affecting 1.4% of its users, according to the company. It spent their money, with some people losing as much as $1,700, Dealroom reported .  The company fought back with its own AI agents, which it kept running “24/7,” according to Raad. OpenCode had been running its defense with an OpenAI model, which started to refuse its requests in the middle of the attack. This was “a bit frustrating,” Raad said. But the company was able to continue after asking OpenAI to admit it to the company’s Daybreak Blue, an application-only program that allows verified cybersecurity professionals to use its most advanced tools. After some mild online backlash to OpenAI’s models initially refusing OpenCode’s requests, OpenAI executive Dean Ball said this was required to prevent bad actors from using its models for “sustained autonomous cyberattacks.” In what appears to be a first, OpenAI refunded OpenCode users who lost money in the attack, OpenAI’s Head of Core Products Thibault Sottiaux said on X. In a third agentic attack this month—the most severe one—bad actors hacked into several South Korean banks. The attackers were likely based in China, according to Reuters, and used a combination of a Chinese state-developed AI tool called Artex, built on open models, as well as Anthropic Claude Code. They stole data from an estimated 68,000 people, The Wall Street Journal reported . South Korean officials urged banks to harden their defenses. “Cybersecurity attacks powered by AI agents have been increasing in South Korea, and I expect they will grow in number worldwide in the future,” Mun Chong-hyun, who heads Genians Security Center, a Seoul cybersecurity analytics firm, told The Journal . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Political campaigns have poured $137 million on AI-made ads ahead of a crucial midterm—after spending virtually nothing last election cycle
events.summary: Just two years ago, ahead of the 2024 presidential election, the use of AI in political ads was nearly unheard of. Today, it’s a nine-figure budget line. A new report from the Wesleyan University-based research group Wesleyan Media Project found more than $137 million in spending on 220 campaign videos made at least partly with AI through Oct. 11, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. By comparison, the group detected less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in 2024 campaigns. “It is a large number, definitely, especially when you consider we went from about zero in spending on AI ads in the last election cycle,” Travis Ridout, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project and professor of political science at Washington State University, told Fortune. “That’s what’s really striking.” The magnitude of funding being poured into AI ads is not just evidence of how consequential this election cycle is, but also how pervasive artificial intelligence has become in content creation. The use of AI can range from a replacement for stock footage like a handshake to the likeness of a candidate. But the broad use of AI without much restriction or regulation has raised concern among both candidates and researchers about the spread of misinformation from the ads. More than 70% of AI campaign videos did not contain a disclaimer or disclosure that they were generated by or contain AI, the report found. AI ads have taken the forefront of some of the U.S.’s most contentious and expensive campaigns, including the Texas Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton. One Paxton campaign ad depicted an AI-generated Talarico writing in a Bible with a crayon and delivering a fabricated monologue on God and gender. Talarico responded by saying he has tried to ban AI deepfakes through legislation “because they are misleading.” “They are lying about a candidate in this race,” Talarico said. As the new technology pervades the campaign trail ahead of a crucial midterm election, Ridout warned the consequences of AI ads go beyond just individual elections and have the potential to shape the very psychology of elections more broadly. Candidates may spend more of their time combatting misinformation as opposed to sharing their platform, Ridout said. Despite voters recognizing these ads as AI, they may still be influenced by the misinformation they contain. Others may become skeptical of candidates’ credibility “For voters, there’s a temptation to say, ‘I don’t know what to believe anymore, and so I’m not going to believe anything,’” Ridout said. “That makes voting on the basis of facts quite difficult.” Voters’ changing perceptions of AI According to the report, Republicans are the primary drivers of AI-generated ads: Republican campaigns or political action committees accounted for 81% of the ads and 88% of the spending. Ridout attributes this to the party’s more favorable view of the technology. He said that despite AI video capabilities being around for a couple of years, political campaigns are slow to adopt new technologies out of an abundance of caution over campaign ethics and how campaign tactics would be perceived by their respective parties’ bases. Because Republican leaders like President Donald Trump have been outspoken about their support for the AI infrastructure buildout, Republican voters are more likely to respond neutrally or favorably to AI-generated ads, Ridout explained. But attitudes towards AI, even among Republicans, are changing, and that has the potential to shift attitudes around AI campaign ads more broadly. One Gallup poll found 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local area, including opposition from 75% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans. In one rural community in Pennsylvania, data center protests were a nonpartisan issue according to protesters. “It’s invigorating, in the sense that you’re meeting people who might not be like-minded on a lot of things, but it feels for so many people like this a righteous cause,” one Sugarloaf Township, Pennsylvania, protester told Fortune . “We can maybe disagree on the political finer points of things, but we can find this very real camaraderie in the midst of everything.” The proliferation of AI isn’t all negative for some candidates. Ridout argued AI ads eliminate the need to film B-roll or film on-location, making it easier for candidates with tighter budgets to put out campaign videos and gain exposure they wouldn’t have gotten otherwise. Some ads defy clear-cut logic or voter attitudes around AI, an indication of the integration of this technology into advertisements still being in its infancy. Ridout recalled an AI-generated ad from Pennsylvania Republican candidate for governor Stacy Garrity depicting Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro proudly espousing his support for AI data centers—an apparent paradox of using AI to criticize a candidate for supporting it. The ad discloses its AI origins, opening with the line “This ad was created with AI, thanks to big, beautiful data centers.” “Everyone’s still trying to figure this out right now,” Ridout said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change
events.summary: Humanity is losing more ground in its fight against climate change WASHINGTON -- Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says. If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday's update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year's projections by the same science team. “This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas. “In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report. The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries' climate fighting plans. He wasn't part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound. The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year's projection. Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact . The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees. The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.” Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen. “The report's message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn't part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.” Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century. events.title: Dario Amodei spent 2,000 words laying out to a critic on X why Anthropic must persist in the AI ‘race to the top’
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei engaged in a lengthy exchange with a critic on X. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Dario Amodei responded to a critic on X who said Anthropic wasn't delivering on its safety commitments. He said Anthropic would be best placed to make AI safe by staying at the top of the game. The critic, Nathan Calvin from Encode AI, said Anthropic was trying to win a race to superintelligence. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei disputed a criticism that the company was putting AI safety in the back seat in its "race to the top." On Tuesday, the executive wrote a nearly 2,000-word response to a critical X post which said Anthropic was trying to win a race to superintelligence and deprioritizing AI safety . The original Monday X post was by Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer of Encode AI, an AI-safety advocacy nonprofit. Calvin listed nine actions by Anthropic over the past year that he said undermined its safety commitments, including signing deals for more than $500 billion in compute and increasingly relying on Claude to develop its AI models. His post was lengthy, too, at over 1,500 words. Amodei said in his response that while he was a "fan of the investigative work" Calvin had done for AI safety, he disagreed with many of Calvin's criticisms. Amodei said his position was that Anthropic can do more to keep the AI industry safe if it stays at the frontier. "Our strategy has always been what I've called the 'race to the top' — by showing how it's possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry," Amodei wrote. He then wrote out his own nine-item list of actions that were "very costly" to Anthropic commercially, but had "strong safety benefits." This included releasing its powerful Mythos model only to a select group of cybersecurity partners and restricting the sale of its AI services to Chinese state-controlled companies. However, Amodei acknowledged Anthropic could have handled some of the issues Calvin raised better. These included a draft bill Anthropic circulated to Congress this month — obtained exclusively by Politico — that critics said would make it harder for the federal government to block dangerous AI models. "We'll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it," he wrote. Amodei and Calvin's exchange comes at a time when model safety has become one of the most pressing issues in the AI sphere. In September, AI researchers predicted an "AI apocalypse," in which the increasingly capable and rogue technology could kill all of humanity in the next decade. In response to the concerns, AI chiefs like Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk all agreed to " pace the frontier ," referring to slowing down AI development to ensure there were enough checks and balances in place. Meanwhile, Anthropic is on the brink of its hotly anticipated IPO, expected to list at a $2 trillion valuation in November. Last week, it reported a third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion. events.title: What a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would mean
events.summary: Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create ​one ​of the most valuable companies in the ​world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company ⁠SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as ⁠Mr Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing , satellite communications and computing infrastructure, ​including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: Why merge the companies? A merger would create a ⁠single company at the centre of Mr Musk's long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. “I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained ⁠from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centres), connectivity,” Mr Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing ​the companies ⁠together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Mr Musk's projects ‌already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering ​talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Mr Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence. What does it mean for investors? Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in cars, robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together? Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future ​data-centre projects. Mr Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing ‌the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and ⁠Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Mr Musk ​hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship production, ​while SpaceX technologies ‌have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could also co-ordinate efforts to secure strategic ⁠supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite ⁠hardware. What are the key risks? The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and Nasa. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors ​would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

events.title: 'MAKE DEALS': Trump says data centers should pay communities a 'dividend' to win support
events.summary: President Donald Trump urged data center companies to strike financial deals in a Truth Social post. Data center development has become a political flashpoint as communities raise concerns about electricity, water and land use ahead of the November midterm elections. U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday urged data center companies to "MAKE DEALS" with local communities to ensure their support for the costly facilities. Trump said that to make them more popular, data center operators should pay the community, "and/or individuals within the community, a 'dividend.'" "I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.," the president said in a post on Truth Social. Data centers have become a hot-button issue ahead of the midterm elections in November. Public opposition to the buildout of the facilities and their environmental impact has been growing, with multiple states considering moratoriums. Data center stocks have also come under pressure this week amid growing concerns about the financial health of the sector. As the AI infrastructure buildout grows more costly, companies are increasingly turning to debt markets to finance deals. When it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery advised discernment over an all-in approach. "One has to be selective," Elhedery told CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging." Much of the concern centers around water usage , power consumption , electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. Access to power is a major constraint on the sector, as power grids in the U.S. and Europe become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers. Trump, a long-time supporter of data centers, said Wednesday that he has been watching them "very closely" and has now come to a "very strong conclusion." "New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data enters are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease," Trump said. events.title: Plans for commercial helium production on Yorke Peninsula
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Commercial helium production planned for the Yorke Peninsula Neil McDonald (left) during a proof-of-concept exercise with extracted helium. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) Gold Hydrogen has announced plans for commercial helium production at its Yorke Peninsula site. It will be the first time helium is produced in Australia since 2023. The plant is expected to be up and running within 18 months. Australia's only commercial helium production is expected to begin on the Yorke Peninsula within 18 months, aiming to address a global shortage of the rare and vital gas. Three months after it first extracted the gas at its Ramsay 1 site just outside Port Vincent, Gold Hydrogen has announced plans to turn the project commercial. It would be the first helium production in Australia in three years. While additional testing and approvals are required before a commercial plant can begin, managing director Neil McDonald said he was feeling positive. "Based on the robust numbers, not of just having the world's best helium purities ever reported, but all our geology and all the economics, we're very confident." The drilling process involves an almost 900-metre-deep hole in the ground. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) As part of commercialisation, a modular helium plant "the size of two tennis courts" will be constructed on the company's 75,000-square-kilometre Yorke Peninsula tenement, creating additional jobs. "As we progress with working out the feasibility ... we'll be able to then isolate what type of specialty jobs and ongoing normal jobs would be available," Mr McDonald said. "But it will be reasonably significant for the size of York Peninsula." Helium has not been produced in Australia since Santos's Darwin LNG plant exhausted its supply in 2023 , and at the time there was little concern about supply constraints. But a global shortage has developed after about a third of the world's helium supply was taken out by Iranian missile strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan gas plant in March. Mr McDonald said he believed there was enough helium at the Yorke Peninsula site for "tens of years" of domestic and international supply. Gold Hydrogen's Ramsay 1 site, just outside Port Vincent, has produced helium gas. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) There is an estimated 41 billion cubic feet (BCF) of the gas in total at just one of the company's seven permits. "To give that context, the world consumes approximately 5BCF of helium per year," Mr McDonald said. Mr McDonald said local and international markets were interested. "Our initial plan is to scale up and make sure that we can supply initially the domestic market and get as much supply into the domestic market as we can," he said. "But like all commodities ... quite often Australia produces a lot more than they can ever consume." events.title: Man United’s Carrick doesn’t ‘need reassurance’ despite team’s horror start
events.summary: Manchester United manager’s troubles grow as seven players are out injured before a Champions League trip to Como. Manchester United manager Michael Carrick says he needs no reassurances from the club’s hierarchy as he knows winning games is the only way to silence speculation over his future. Before a Champions League trip to Italian side Como on Wednesday, United have won just two of their 10 games in all competitions this season. The Red Devils are off to their worst start to an English top-flight campaign in 40 years, having been knocked out of the League Cup by Brighton last month and comfortably beaten by Atletico Madrid last week in the Champions League. Carrick was appointed manager on a permanent basis in May only after an impressive spell as interim boss in the second half of last season. But he has quickly become just the latest manager under pressure at Old Trafford at a club that has fallen from grace since Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013. “I know we’ve got to win football games for everything to flow and everything to fit into place. That’s the great thing about it; we can do something about it,” Carrick told his pre-match news conference in Italy. “I don’t need any reassurance. It’s pretty clear. “I know the role, I know the responsibilities. I don’t need anyone else to kind of tell me that or tell me when it’s going well or when it needs to be better. I know that myself.” Carrick’s hopes of turning things around have not been aided by a growing injury list. Lisandro Martinez started Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds, despite his stinging criticism of the club’s lack of transfer activity following the defeat at Atletico, but had to be replaced at half time. The Argentinian international will miss the trip to Como, as will Luke Shaw, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Ayden Heaven.

events.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
events.summary: Published 21 October 2026, 05:13 BST Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together . Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (£1.1tn) and SpaceX at $2tn (£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models . Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. Published 12 June However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said. The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month. "I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.

events.title: Samsung, SK Hynix upgrading China plants to make more advanced chips: Sources
events.summary: Both companies are now required to seek US licences annually if they want to install US-made equipment such as etching machines in China. Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading China plants to make more advanced NAND chips. They want to meet AI demand and compete with China’s YMTC, but US export controls make the work difficult. Samsung’s Xian site may switch to 286-layer V9 NAND, with output targets of 5,000 wafers a month in December 2026 and 40,000 by December 2027. Samsung says the plan follows US rules and does not add capacity. SK Hynix aims to make 240-layer-plus NAND at Dalian and may seek approval for 300-plus-layer research. YMTC has grown fast, reaching 38.5% of China’s NAND market in the second quarter, while Samsung and SK Hynix have lost share. SEOUL/BEIJING/NEW YORK – Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are upgrading their China factories to produce more advanced memory chips, four people familiar with the plans said, aiming to fend off competition from a fast-growing Chinese rival and meet huge AI demand. How much to invest in their Chinese operations has become a tricky question for the South Korean semiconductor giants ever since the US began imposing export controls on some chip-making equipment in 2022 amid an effort to slow China’s technological progress. The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security also said in 2025 it did not intend to grant licences to upgrade technology and expand capacity at the foreign chipmakers’ factories in China. The regulatory headaches have limited their ability to refit their factories and contributed to loss of market share to Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). Executives at the South Korean chipmakers have publicly warned that geopolitical tensions are undermining their Chinese operations. Samsung and SK Hynix confirmed in statements to Reuters that upgrades were underway and were being done in close consultation with Washington, but did not disclose details of production plans that are being reported here for the first time. Reuters could not, however, determine to what extent US authorities have granted export licences for equipment that Samsung and SK Hynix need for their planned upgrades. According to the sources, the two companies are working to manufacture flash NAND memory chips with more than 200 layers at their Chinese plants, which would bring them in line with what is being produced in South Korea. NAND, a type of memory chip that retains data without power, is widely used in smartphones, PCs and solid-state drives for AI data centres. More layers per chip means more storage density and lower costs. Samsung sets signs on 286-layer chips Samsung’s plant in Xian in north-western China, which accounts for about 40% of the company’s global NAND output, currently makes chips that have about 200 layers, according to two of the people. As part of a project known internally as “Monami” – from the French for “my friend” – Samsung is converting the facility to make 286-layer V9 NAND chips, aiming for monthly output of 5,000 wafers in December 2026 and then a jump to 40,000 wafers by December 2027, one of the people said. Samsung said its upgrade was in compliance with US export regulations, adding: “The upgrade is aimed at meeting growing demand from global customers, including those in the US. The company is not expanding production capacity or constructing new manufacturing facilities.” SK Hynix is looking to switch to producing NAND products with 240 layers or more at its Dalian facilities in north-eastern China, three people familiar with the matter said. It currently makes products with 192 layers there, one person said. SK Hynix acquired the Dalian site when it bought Intel’s NAND operations in 2021 and it remains the sole NAND chip manufacturing site for that business, which is now named Solidigm and is preparing for a US initial public offering. One of the sources said the company is authorised to make chips with up to 240 layers at Dalian and may seek permission from Washington to conduct research and development on 300-plus-layer chips there that would help it lay the groundwork for potential production in the US. The company is in discussions with the Trump administration over plans to build a new NAND factory in the United States. The US government’s Bureau of Industry and Security did not directly address Reuters questions on the status of approvals for the South Korean chipmakers. It referred Reuters to its 2025 statement that the bureau intended to grant licence applications for them to operate their existing factories in China, but not expand capacity or upgrade technology. As Samsung and SK Hynix have wrestled with the question of how much to invest in their Chinese plants, YMTC has made great strides. It commanded 38.5% of China’s NAND market in the second quarter, up from 28% for all of 2025 and overtaking Samsung, according to research firm Omdia.

events.title: Who owns India’s textile traditions in age of AI-enabled mass production?
events.summary: Technological tools meant to preserve a craft are now able to digitally reproduce it without involving the craftsperson. Bitupan Deka was out shopping for a “gamusa” (traditional scarf) with his mother in India’s northeastern state of Meghalaya when he noticed something unusual. “Every shop selling the scarf had the same handful of patterns repeated over and over,” he told Al Jazeera over the telephone from Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya. list 1 of 4 How US tariffs are unraveling India’s textile industry list 2 of 4 Photos: Weavers of India’s famous Banarasi sari are struggling list 3 of 4 Fast fashion and the dark side of textile recycling in India list 4 of 4 AI tool helps stranded protesters find their way home in the Indian capital “When I asked around, I found that weavers in Sualkuchi [district in neighbouring Assam state] are paid a one-time fee of roughly 2,000 rupees [$21] for each design they develop, instead of royalties. Cutting down the number of designs they produce was a cost-saving practice followed by the manufacturers.” This discovery prompted Deka, an assistant professor of computer technology at Shillong’s MIT University, to create a system that can produce infinite new designs for such fabrics. “My work isn’t meant to replace the traditional designers. I hope, instead, that it will become a tool in their hands to create new and modern motifs more easily, so the consumers can have variety,” Deka said. Once the patent, which is being applied for under the research and development department of his university, comes through, Deka plans to monetise the system by making it a commercial designing service that the textile industry can avail. In India’s varied textile traditions, patterns and motifs carry the memory of a place and the mythology of its people – sometimes even the history of migrations. The designs are imagined by weavers from things that exist around them, and then painted with locally available colours, mostly using carved clay and wooden frames. These weavers do not simply reproduce a pattern; they inherit it. Their hands hesitate where their grandmother’s did, and they know why a particular flower must face left. A computer has no such inheritance or hesitation. It learns by analysing pictures and repeating them in endless variations. And yet, as Deka’s system shows, the computer can now draw and weave the same flower. The Rekh Sanganeri Dataset is a similar system developed for hand-block printed Sanganeri textiles from the western Indian state of Rajasthan. It includes high-resolution images of printed patterns, annotated down to ink bleed and slight misalignment – the imperfections that are the hallmark of the handmade work. Its developer, Reddy Sai Nivas C, says it should be used as a resource for research and art, not as a substitute for artisans. But the disclaimer is the paradox: Tools built to preserve a craft are making its visual language easier to digitally reproduce without involving the craftsperson. Dinesh Chhipa comes from one of the oldest Chhipa families, an artisan and merchant caste renowned for dyeing and block printing. He is a Bagru designer – a block printing technique from Bagru town in the western state of Rajasthan – and a textile businessman. “Traditional craft is slow to produce. Even if someone offered us a fortune, we wouldn’t be able to produce these pieces in mass numbers, so I don’t fault those using digital technology and AI to fill the gap,” he told Al Jazeera. “But don’t borrow craft and regional names like Bagru and Jaipuri [named after the capital city of Rajasthan]. These designs and motifs were born out of a culture and necessities of the communities they come from.” Who owns culture when it turns into plain data? India has been digitising its textile memory for years – from the Botanical Survey of India’s historical collections to the Bharatiya Vastra Shilpa Kosh, a national portal built by the state-run National Institute of Fashion Technology and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC). Without documentation, the fragile traditions and knowledge could disappear. But digitisation also allows the same archive to be used by an AI system seeking to reproduce these crafts at scale. At the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February this year, Indian software company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) showcased Bridgital Loom, an AI system that converts textile designs into loom-ready instructions. LED lights on the loom guide a weaver through the thread sequences of intricate Banarasi and Kanchipuram patterns – named after the cities where these iconic arts grew. TCS says the technology helps weavers execute complex designs faster and with fewer errors, and is meant to be a bridge between the artisans and technology. A pilot project that uses the loom is already under way at Kanchipuram, a town in southern Tamil Nadu state.

events.title: Foden shines as Man City rout Athens 5-1 despite Haaland, Semenyo injuries
events.summary: Phil Foden scored a hat-trick as Manchester City bounced back from last week’s loss to PSG despite off-field troubles. Enzo Maresca believes Phil Foden has provided evidence that his prolonged slump might finally be over by scoring a hat-trick in Manchester City’s 5-1 rout of AEK Athens in the Champions League. After struggling badly over the last two seasons, England playmaker Foden could be on the brink of a long-awaited renaissance after his sublime display at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday. It has been a trying period for the 26-year-old, who has admitted suffering from mental health issues. Foden fell out of favour with former City boss Pep Guardiola and had not scored for 10 months prior to his goal in Saturday’s Premier League win against Ipswich. This season has been another turbulent experience for Foden, who was sent off in City’s win at Manchester United and has been forced to battle for a place in Maresca’s starting lineup. Taking advantage of injuries that left Erling Haaland on the bench against AEK and sidelined Antoine Semenyo for eight weeks, Foden starred on the left wing before switching to the “false nine” role as the focal point of City’s attack. “It is good news for me because you know he is doing well and this is what we want for many reasons,” City boss Maresca said. “First of all, because he is a top player and we know that. Happy for him, but also happy for the team that we have one more weapon that we can use.” Foden’s hat-trick will surely have caught England manager Thomas Tuchel’s eye as he prepares to pick his squad for the Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain in November. Long heralded as one of England’s brightest talents, Foden was left out of his country’s World Cup squad earlier this year in a damning sign of his fall from grace. Having ended his run without a goal in the Champions League since November 2025, Foden now has to produce nights like this on a regular basis to earn the trust of Maresca and Tuchel.

events.title: Singapore sets aside $45m to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI solutions
events.summary: Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang speaks at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific event at the Suntec Singapore Convention & Exhibition Centre on Oct 21. Singapore has set aside more than $45 million over three years to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI. The Catalytic AI Solutions initiative will offer ready-to-deploy tools for design, scheduling and predictive maintenance. Enterprise Singapore will co-fund adoption of AI solutions for eligible SMEs, and is working to extend the initiative to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors. SINGAPORE - More than $45 million has been set aside over the next three years to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the advanced manufacturing industry deploy artificial intelligence solutions. This was one of the initiatives under Singapore’s national AI strategy that was announced by Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang on Oct 21. Gan said the Catalytic AI Solutions initiative will make the technology more accessible to SMEs, and support them in overcoming common barriers when adopting AI. “We want AI to be accessible not just to large manufacturers, but also to our SMEs,” she said at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific (ITAP) event at the Suntec Singapore Convention & Exhibition Centre. “Through this initiative, manufacturers can access ready-to-deploy AI solutions to improve productivity, optimise efficiency and strengthen their competitiveness,” she added. Under the initiative, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) will work with trade associations and chambers and qualified vendors to offer a suite of solutions to SMEs, with some firms having already confirmed their interest. The solutions will enable tasks such as the optimisation of product and component design, and the enhancement of production scheduling and predictive maintenance. EnterpriseSG’s assistant managing director for manufacturing Wong Zeng Yi said: “AI is creating new possibilities for manufacturers to improve productivity, quality and responsiveness, while opening new revenue opportunities through faster innovation. “We want to help more manufacturers embed AI into their core operations, so they can realise these gains at scale.” Eligible SMEs will have their adoption of AI solutions co-funded by EnterpriseSG, which plans to extend the initiative to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors. Another initiative announced at ITAP was a manufacturing jobs portal developed by the Singapore Manufacturing Federation. Gan encouraged prospective employers and jobseekers to sign up for the Manufacturing and Talent Connection Hub, which is expected to be operational later this year. The manufacturing industry accounts for around 20% of Singapore’s gross domestic product, and employs about 12% of its workforce. Industrial transformation has never been more important, Gan said, as manufacturers are operating in a more complex environment, with tight labour markets, intensifying competition for investments, and supply chains which are being reshaped by geopolitics. Companies must also become more sustainable while remaining competitive, she added. Gan said: “Advanced technologies such as robotics, digital twins, and AI can help our manufacturers raise productivity, strengthen competitiveness, and bring about skilled roles for our workforce. “If we move decisively, Singapore can strengthen our position as a critical global node for advanced manufacturing, where companies develop new technologies and engineering capabilities, deploy them at scale, and contribute to global manufacturing.” A set of national AI missions, namely in advanced manufacturing, connectivity, finance and healthcare, was announced by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong earlier at Budget 2026. This came alongside the creation of a National AI Council, chaired by PM Wong, to help Singapore harness AI as a strategic advantage. The advanced manufacturing mission aims to reimagine the industry to grow its output and productivity. This involves advancing product and process innovation, anchoring best-in-class factories in Singapore, and building a base of industrial AI companies that develop AI solutions locally and export them to the rest of the world. Gan said the AI Centre of Excellence for Manufacturing, jointly established by A*STAR and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in September 2024 , has been an important enabler of this mission. Companies including drinks producer Coca-Cola and tech manufacturer Philips, had signed on to collaborate with the centre at its launch. In all, Gan said the centre has collaborated with 30 manufacturers in sectors including aerospace, semiconductor, pharmaceuticals and energy, ranging from local firm Sunningdale Tech to the multinational Rockwell Automation. It has also completed 23 projects which deployed AI solutions to companies.

events.title: Gaza children face worsening food shortages as prices rise and aid is cut
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Families say they are struggling to provide nutritious meals for their children as commercial supplies are disrupted. Gaza City, Gaza Strip – It has been months since Huda Abu Leila had to resort to serving only tea and bread to her five daughters for breakfast. But this week, that’s what the 30-year-old has had to do, after Israel restricted the entry of goods into Gaza earlier this month. After living through three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza , and the accompanying blockade that often leaves markets partly empty and goods unaffordable, Huda is used to struggling to provide her children – aged between 18 months and 10 years – with a balanced and nutritious diet. list 1 of 3 ‘Not getting involved’: US vice president declines to endorse Netanyahu list 2 of 3 Three months of PM Andy Burnham: Can he sustain the ‘hope vibe’? list 3 of 3 Israeli attacks kill at least four Palestinians in Gaza But the current situation, with shortages of commercial goods, rising food prices, and cuts to humanitarian assistance, has made it ever harder for her to put enough food on the table. “We were affected immediately. We couldn’t find eggs or milk, and we don’t have the money to stock up on food,” Huda said. She lives with her daughters in a tent in western Gaza City. Her husband was injured during the war and can no longer work, while she earns a little money by baking bread for other people. Some days, the family eats canned beans with duqqa – a local spice blend – or za’atar. On days when food is not as readily available, like this week, they dip bread in tea. What worries her most is how the worsening situation will affect her children’s health, particularly as she is already struggling to provide them with enough nutritious food. Israel halted commercial shipments into Gaza on October 14, disrupting supplies of food and other essential goods as families already struggling with high prices faced further shortages. The suspension came amid a dispute over a demand for merchants to pay 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck to bring goods into the enclave. On October 19, Israel announced that commercial shipments would gradually resume. The Israeli military body responsible for coordinating aid and commercial access to Gaza, COGAT, said merchants had reported that Hamas had withdrawn the demand. Hamas described the payment as a voluntary contribution to a fund supporting people affected by the war. The disruption comes as humanitarian assistance is also reduced. On October 19, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza. The programme reduced the number of people it supports from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October. It has also halved food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, alongside a smaller bag of wheat flour. The number of hot meals WFP provides daily has been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000. WFP said about 1.4 million people in Gaza, approximately two-thirds of the population, were facing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. Famine was declared in Gaza City in August 2025. The UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said in December of the same year that it had receded after the beginning of the Gaza ceasefire two months earlier. Families struggle to provide nutritious meals For Huda, the crisis means she can no longer afford many of the foods her daughters need for a balanced and nutritious diet. Eggs have become too expensive. A shopkeeper recently quoted her 60 shekels ($19.40) for a tray. She also said some shops appeared to be holding back stock. Fresh vegetables have also become difficult to afford. When she goes to the market, which she usually does about once a week, she buys only small quantities. “Onions cost about 10 shekels [$3.25] per kilogramme, while tomatoes cost between 10 and 15 shekels per kilogramme [$3.25 and $4.85],” she said. The vast majority of Gaza’s population is unemployed as a result of Israel’s war and its restrictions on allowing the territory to rebuild its infrastructure and economy. The lack of food is starting to have an impact on Huda’s children. She says that they are struggling to concentrate, and often become dizzy and exhausted. The health of her eldest daughter, Salma, has become so poor that she is receiving follow-up care at al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza, where a doctor advised Huda to improve her daughter’s diet. “We have been through so much hardship over the past three years,” she said. “I worry that my daughters will get sick if I cannot provide them with enough nutritious food.” For Raeda Soboh, 40, the struggle to feed her nine-member family means her children have gone months without some of the foods they need to stay healthy.

events.title: How might Andy Burnham tackle Thames Water debacle?
events.summary: A look at some of the options after PM is urged to consider radical alternatives to deal with stricken company Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. Here are some ideas the prime minister is being urged to consider. Burnham must introduce emergency legislation immediately to protect the supply of water for the public, said Richard Murphy, tax accountant and the brains behind Corbynomics. A new state-owned company, with a management team in waiting and all the necessary steps ready to take over the existing company’s systems, has to be put in place now. “A prime minister who cannot deliver water to maybe a quarter of the UK’s population would not be someone to be trusted with anything else. Andy Burnham has no choice but to address this matter, now,” said Murphy. The 1971 nationalisation of the Rolls-Royce aeronautical engineering company, to protect the national interest after it collapsed into receivership, could be used as a blue print. A similar national emergency exists now to protect the supply of water, Murphy said. Murphy said that, in essence, Thames Water was financially insolvent, with real doubt about whether it could survive into 2027. It was failing in its regulatory obligations, including to maintain clean water supplies and keep rivers and beaches clean. Emergency legislation should ensure that the nationalisation is of the assets and undertakings of Thames Water, and not of the company itself. All financial liabilities of Thames Water would be left for the old company to settle. The government should not acquire them. The new company needed to be structured within days, said Murphy. “There is no time to wait.” Public control – probably via the courts Burnham must be prepared to go to court to take Thames Water back into public control, said Ewen McGaughey, professor of law at University College London. Moody’s has estimated a one-off cost of £14.5bn in 2019 to bring water into public ownership. But privatisation, said McGaughey, would cost up to £22bn extra for bill payers from 2025 to 2030, or £176 a household a year, in returns on capital to shareholders and banks, as set by Ofwat’s price review. McGaughey believes that this year public ownership of failed water companies will cost closer to £0, using the special administration procedure within the 1991 Water Industry Act. The higher the repair bills, the less that creditors or shareholders deserve under UK law, international law and our investment treaties, he said. He advises Burnham to prepare to go to court – creditors will probably sue – but they have no reasonable prospect of success. McGaughey says privatised water and the regulators have failed so badly that England pays among the highest bills in Europe, while nearly every river is illegally polluted, taps run dry and a trillion litres of water is leaked each year. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The government should bring our accounting practice up to international and European standards, by separating public corporation borrowing from the national debt, so that the borrowing of a publicly owned company does not contribute to national debt. Continuing the theme of using the special administrative powers of the 1991 legislation, Cat Hobbs of We Own It wants Thames Water’s licence taken away immediately. Hobbs has written to the government and water regulator, Ofwat, calling for bill rises to be blocked and for Thames Water to be brought into public hands. “It is absurd that Thames Water is now asking its creditors for a further £2.4bn to stay afloat – this saga has dragged out since July 2024 when the company was first in breach of its licence conditions,” said Hobbs. Under the 1991 act, companies can have their licences removed if they are insolvent or if they fail to fulfil their statutory duties to provide water, protect the environment and properly manage wastewater. Hobbs told Burnham his government should be using this power and facing down threats from the water industry and the prospect of a legal challenge from special administration under the 1991 act. Public ownership of water would deliver savings of £3bn to £5bn a year over time from cheaper financing costs – no shareholder dividends, less expensive debt. Taking water into public ownership would reduce the cost of living burden as well as freeing up money for infrastructure. The government should make it possible for new publicly owned water companies to borrow to invest on their own account – rather than adding to the national debt – as is standard practice elsewhere in Europe. Hobbs pointed out that when Network Rail’s debt of £31bn was transferred to the public sector, bond yields fell from 3% a year to 2.2% a year.

events.title: ‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers?
events.summary: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery W hen Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels. However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law. From Wednesday, drivers in England who do not have off-street parking will no longer need to get planning permission to put in a pavement gully outside their home. The gullies sit flush within the pavement and allow an EV charging cable to reach a parked vehicle without creating a trip hazard. By charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can slash the cost by up to 90% . But some of the 9.3 million households without off-street parking will be left frustrated as more than 20 local authorities will still not allow the installation of gullies after the law changes. Williams’s council is Ealing, which does not allow them for cost and safety reasons. She charges her car at a public charger, at much greater cost than if she could do it at home. “It’s really frustrating,” Williams says. “When we decided to buy an electric car … the reason we wanted to buy one was for the environmental impact. “You either have to have enough money to have a house with a driveway, or you have to be able to afford the additional cost of charging at a public charger.” Motorists are not allowed to string EV charging cables across the pavement from their home to the road, but many councils allow cross-pavement charging if you use a gully. To use one, a charging cable is run from the home through the gully and then plugged into the car. This previously meant getting planning permission from the local authority. Removing that step will save drivers between £300 and £500. However, anyone who lives in a conservation area will still have to apply. Caroline Pidgeon, a Liberal Democrat peer, campaigned for the change in the law. She says one in three households in England do not have a driveway. Approval for the gullies has taken up to 15 months in some areas, she says. “Simpler rules will make it easier for people to switch to an electric car,” she adds. The government has given £25m in funding to councils in England for pavement gullies for people with on-street parking, but the money is being distributed in different ways, depending on the local authority. How much you pay for installation varies widely around the country. If you want to apply for a gully to be installed, you should check with your council to see whether it allows them and, if it does, it should direct you on how to apply. Kerbo Charge, a company that installs gullies, operates a postcode checker you can use to see whether you can get one in your area and sign up for an alert if that changes. Ben Whitaker of Kerbo Charge says the average fee for the work is about £1,200 (including VAT) without a grant. “Some [councils] are using it [the funding] to provide half-price channels to early adopters, others are making it totally free while funds last – but, after that, residents will have to pay full price,” he says. “For example, Surrey is £499 for the channel and installation, South Gloucestershire is £250,” he adds. “Sadly, there is quite a variety of approaches and prices.” To illustrate the difference in prices between local authorities, Redbridge council in London says the grant will cover up to £1,200 of installation costs. But applicants must pay £815 in fees and for a bond, as well as any additional installation costs. On top of the cost of installing the gullies, some councils charge an additional annual fee for maintenance. For example, Redbridge charges an “ongoing annual licence fee” of £185. Enfield, also in London, charges £107 a year . Shayne Rees of Gul-e, a company that has installed 400 gullies, says it takes between one and two hours to put the unit in place. “It’s a really heavy-duty steel channel that can take a truck driving over it, and once we put it in the ground, that will be there for decades and decades without any maintenance,” he adds. It emerged in May that more than 20 local authorities appear to be holding out against having the gullies installed, among them Kent, Leicester and Worcestershire. Most of the holdouts are in London, including Waltham Forest and Hackney. The reasons given often concern safety and maintenance, and because of issues over who will be liable if there is an injury.

events.title: Childcare chain collapses amid wave of closures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Childcare chain's collapse into administration highlights private credit risks A former national children's commissioner says a lot of private providers are divesting childcare centres or pulling out of the sector altogether. Childcare chain Shared Beginnings has hit financial strife, becoming the latest early education provider to run into trouble amid a wave of closures in the sector. The childcare service, owned by private lender Finexia Financial Group, operates centres in Queensland, Victoria and the ACT. Finexia wrote to staff, informing them the centres had been operating "at a loss". The collapse highlights the risks of the private credit sector, with Finexia taking on ownership of the centres in the 2025 financial year after the previous owner, Genius Education, defaulted on substantial loans owed to Finexia. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has recently said it was closely scrutinising private lending , which has typically been a much more lightly regulated sector than the banking industry, and was concerned "the first significant cracks" were appearing. The impact on childcare places and jobs at Shared Beginnings remains unclear as the administrators continue to operate the centres. The firm said the decision came after exhausting all other options. Neil Sheather says all options to save Shared Beginnings have been exhausted. ( Supplied: Linkedin ) Finexia managing director Neil Sheather said placing Shared Beginnings into administration was not taken lightly, but was necessary. "Ultimately, the administrators are in control of Shared Beginnings." In a letter to staff, Mr Sheather said the administration would affect all seven of its centres, including Sinnamon Park and Kenmore in Queensland, Reservoir, Mont Albert and Beaumaris in Victoria, and Bonython and Conder in the ACT. All Shared Beginnings centres remain open under the control of administrators. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) In a separate letter to parents, Mr Sheather assured families that all centres remained open, and care would continue as normal. Bill Karageozis and Nick Keramos of DVT McLeods have been appointed administrators to find suitable buyers. The federal minister for education has been contacted for comment. A September report by the Early Learning and Care Council Australia has found the rate of early childhood education and care (ECEC) service closures has continued to increase. The report said 152 long daycare services had closed since 2024, with a further 276 services (both long day care and preschool/kindergarten) identified as at risk of closing in the next 12 months. Anne Hollonds AO says the childcare sector is undergoing a significant adjustment. ( Supplied: Australian Human Rights Commission ) Former national children's commissioner Anne Hollonds AO said the childcare sector was undergoing a significant adjustment, driven by increased regulatory costs and a number of prominent crises. For-profit centres dominate the long daycare sector. Most of the growth in recent years has been in private for-profit providers, with a recent report from the Mitchell Institute finding they made up 74 per cent of long daycare places. Ms Hollonds said the sector would be better if it were shared 50-50 between non-profit and for-profit organisations. "We really need to focus on the safety and well-being of children as the priority," she said, adding that she had no problem with for-profit providers as long as their operation was up to scratch. A recent report finds for-profit centres drive substantial instability in the long day care sector. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) The Mitchell Institute also found substantial instability or "churn" in the long daycare sector was driven by for-profit centres. "Since 2013, about one-third [32 per cent] of long day care services open in 2025 had changed approved provider," the report said. "The rate is higher in for-profit centres where 40 per cent have changed provider, compared to 11 per cent of all other centres." Have you been impacted by the closure of childcare centres or private lending? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me . The seven Shared Beginnings centres arose from the ashes of Genius Early Learning, which operated more than 30 early childhood centres across the country and collapsed under massive debt in March 2025 . Finexia said it had since "provided significant financial and operational support, including rebranding, marketing, staffing support and substantial funding to cover working capital shortfalls".

events.title: Elon Musk confirms talks to merge Tesla and SpaceX
events.summary: Elon Musk is the top executive of both Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday. While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move. "The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained." With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history. The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google. That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn. Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX? Published 1 hour ago SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year. Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned. The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together. Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more. Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger. He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX. Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield". He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve". While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics. SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut. events.title: Anthropic posts $80bn loss in first half of 2026: WSJ
events.summary: The loss is up $13 billion more than last year, driven by accounting charges, the report said. Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company known for creating the chatbot Claude, recorded a net loss of more than $80bn in the first half of 2026, according to the Wall Street Journal, as the market anticipates its looming initial public offering (IPO). The corporation also indicated it could spend up to $750bn in coming years to acquire more computing capacity, including potential deals currently under discussion, the Journal said on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 Why are eight US states suing OpenAI? list 2 of 3 AI tool helps stranded protesters find their way home in the Indian capital list 3 of 3 Ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting device has Saudi backing: Prosecutor The main driver for the loss was the $72bn in accounting charges related to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financial instruments Anthropic issued to raise funding, the report said. The loss figure was up from $13bn a year earlier, according to a draft prospectus, a legal document corporations submit to financial regulators, for its IPO. The figures show the hefty costs of the AI race, even as investors look more closely at whether the money companies are pouring into chips and data centres will pay off. Anthropic also shared a list of potential risk factors, including uncertainty over how to prevent its products from doing harm, whether through sophisticated cyberattacks or blackmail by uncontrolled models. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment, and the report on the non-public information could not be immediately verified. Reuters first reported in September that Anthropic posted a net loss of $42bn in 2025, as part of a series of exclusives from its IPO prospectus. The company has benefited from the popularity of Claude Code, its coding assistant that developers use to write software and build apps. But some current and prospective investors who attended Anthropic’s investor day in San Francisco, California, last week are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter told Reuters. The investors who attended the event discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, three of the people said, a significant step down from the roughly $2 trillion valuation previously expected for the November share sale. Anthropic’s revenue jumped to $16.3bn in the six-month period that ended June 30, up from $1.1bn a year ago, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost $9bn, the Journal reported. Anthropic reported last week that AI could be months away from learning to self-replicate on everyday home devices.
