events.title: Fortescue senior executive sacked after sexual harassment probe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals sacked after sexual harassment, bullying probe A senior Fortescue executive has been sacked for alleged ( Supplied: Fortescue Metals Group ) A senior executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals Group has been sacked following an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment and bullying at the iron ore miner. The executive, who was not named by Fortescue in its short statement about the matter, "breached Fortescue’s policies, as well as our values", it said. Fortescue had engaged law firm MinterEllison to examine a series of allegations about the employee's conduct. "Sexual harassment, bullying, and other behaviour that makes people feel unsafe has no place at Fortescue," the company said. Mining magnate Dr Andrew Forrest is the founder of Fortescue. ( ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates ) It said it would provide "ongoing support" to those who took part in the investigation. In August, Reuters reported Fortescue had allowed the executive to continue working at the firm while the MinterEllison investigation was underway. The company's energy chief Gus Pichot said at the time the company was "quite confident we are following the proper process" in allowing it. It comes after a group of female Fortescue employees launched a class action in the Federal Court against the company in June, alleging rape, sexual assault and stalking at remote FMG mine sites in WA's Pilbara. The allegations included drink spiking, promotions offered in exchange for sexual favours and a widespread culture of sexual harassment and denigration. Andrew 'Twiggy' Forrest warns Fortescue staff after sexual harassment class action In an email sent to all staff, Mr Forrest said: "Anyone who thinks this behaviour has a place at Fortescue is in the wrong company." The sacking comes despite a 2023 deal with WorkSafe WA in which Fortescue agreed to spend $1.4 million on addressing inappropriate workplace behaviour after allegedly failing to supply documents about dozens of sexual harassment allegations to the work safety regulator. FMG is not the first mining company to face claims of unsafe work practices and a toxic culture. Hundreds of women have come forward in the two years since BHP and Rio Tinto were taken to federal court over similar allegations . A 2022 report into the sexual harassment of women in the mining industry by a parliamentary committee found nearly three quarters of women in mining had experienced sexual harassment at work in the past five years, and that it was generally accepted in workplaces. The scathing report found mining companies failed to recognise the problem or act on it, and while the government accepted its recommendations, not all have been enacted. Some of these included changes to equal opportunities laws, which the WA government yesterday announced it would introduce , four years on from the landmark report.

events.title: World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says
events.summary: Action needed to avoid disastrous overshoot of climate targets, according to organisation’s environment body The world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. Although the “window has closed” on holding temperature rises to 1.5C , in line with scientific advice, limiting the “overshoot” of that target is still possible, according to the UN Environment Programme (Unep). But countries are failing to translate their long-term targets on reducing emissions into short-term actions, a report on the “emissions gap” between climate goals and policies has found. Global carbon output appears to have stalled: the emission levels in 2025 were broadly similar to those of the previous year. But Unep analysts were wary of calling it a peak or plateau, given the vast uncertainties of geopolitics and an increased reliance on fossil fuels, despite strong growth in renewable energy . Cutting greenhouse gases by 18% by 2030, and by 45% by 2045, would yield a good chance of limiting temperature rises to 1.7C above preindustrial levels. This would still allow events such as the record heatwaves of the last few months to become frequent and common, but could help prevent them from getting drastically worse. Governments were warned for years that time was running out, said Inger Andersen, the executive director of Unep. “[We used to say] there’s still an opportunity if we make this herculean effort [to stay within the 1.5C limit],” she said. “It’s now clear the herculean effort was not made. We procrastinated, and now we are saying this window has closed.” Nevertheless, she urged countries to keep the 1.5C goal – the centrepiece of the Paris climate agreement. “We can make the overshoot as brief and as short as possible. It’s not time to throw in the towel and give up. This is about how to find our way back, as shortly and quickly as possible.” Under Donald Trump, the US – the world’s second biggest emitter, after China – has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement and is threatening to reverse its longstanding trend of falling greenhouse gas emissions. Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, said: “All governments have a job to do, but in particular it is time for major fossil fuel producers such as the US and Saudi Arabia, which produce 20-25% of fossil fuels globally, to stop playing politics and face the scientific reality. Right now they are looking at the fire, denying it exists and pouring more petrol on it, while their own citizens increasingly face searing heat, wildfires and other impacts.” Other countries appear to have been affected by US intransigence – pledges made last year on greenhouse gases were noticeably weak, according to UNEP analysis. At the Cop30 climate summit in Brazil last November , governments were supposed to make fresh commitments under the Paris agreement to cut emissions. But the commitments made were nowhere near strong enough. Even if all of those updated pledges were fulfilled, temperatures would still rise to 2.6C above preindustrial levels, according to Unep’s projections, endangering life across swathes of the globe. Policy has also not kept up with pledges: on current policies around the world, temperatures would rise to 2.8C. Every five years of greenhouse gas emissions at current levels pushes up forecasts of global heating by 0.1C. Scientists also fear that the greater the margin by which we exceed 1.5C, the greater the likelihood of triggering tipping points in the climate system . Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, said: “The tragedy is that we have the solutions within our grasp. Solar and wind power are growing far faster than anyone expected, yet governments are still failing to move away from fossil fuels quickly enough. The technology is racing ahead while political leadership is dragging its feet.” The shortfall in countries’ commitments is supposed to be corrected under a Paris agreement mechanism called the “global stocktake”, an assessment of emissions targets next scheduled for 2028. But that has also been thrown into doubt: this week, the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change failed to set a timetable to publish its latest report before the global stocktake, which would prevent governments from assessing their progress against the latest science. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and one of the world’s leading climate scientists, said rows over the timing of IPCC reports must not be allowed to stall government action. “If all current national commitments are implemented, global emissions are projected to reach approximately 50 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually by 2035, when they should be below 35 gigatonnes. The science is already clear.

events.title: The way we consume energy is changing. Abu Dhabi’s integrated system has already embraced that change
events.summary: Across the global energy sector, a quiet but significant shift is underway. The debate around energy usage is intensifying because the pressures on it are becoming more real: grid queues, water resource pressures, increased industrial electrification and the need for reliable power at every hour of the day to match changing demand patterns. Recent strategy resets among global energy majors BP , Shell and ExxonMobil illustrate a greater focus on delivering reliable supply and ensuring that infrastructure can meet fast-growing power demand.  The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global electricity demand to grow at an average annual rate of 3.6% between 2026 and 2030 . That represents an acceleration of around 50% from the average pace of growth over the past decade. Global data center electricity consumption is already spiking , driven in particular by the rapid expansion of AI-focused facilities. That trend shows no signs of slowing down.   The IEA estimates that data center electricity demand rose 17% in 2025, with AI-focused facilities seeing demand skyrocket by around 50%. AI may be digital in use, but it is deeply physical in its requirements. It needs land, energy grids, clean power, water, cooling and flexible supply.  That is why the question facing governments and the energy industry is changing. As AI and other sources of electricity demand grow rapidly, the question is no longer which source of energy will grow fastest or which project will attract the most attention. The more practical question is how do we build the right energy mix in order to provide reliable, affordable and progressively lower-carbon power under increasing pressure? A solar farm or desalination plant does not, in itself, create a national advantage. It becomes an advantage when it is integrated into a diversified and synchronized ecosystem.  Here in Abu Dhabi, we have been building that ecosystem for more than five decades. We have developed an energy and water architecture in which the right energy mix delivers secure, sustainable and affordable energy, working in harmony with grid planning, water desalination and reuse, and underpinned by progressive regulation and long-horizon capital. Our approach is not to choose between energy security and sustainability, but to remove that false trade-off through system design, built on four elements. H.E. Dr. Abdulla Humaid Saif Al Jarwan is the Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Department of Energy (DoE) and a member of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council The first of these is responsible hydrocarbon production. Oil and gas will remain important to global energy security for years to come, especially in sectors where alternatives need time to scale. The question for producers is therefore becoming more focused: how can these resources be produced and used more efficiently?   The performance of hydrocarbons must be considered as part of a wider system that is simultaneously scaling clean electricity input and improving efficiency across the value chain.  Murban crude, produced by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), has a carbon intensity less than half the global industry average . Meanwhile, the use of clean grid power through ADNOC’s partnership with Emirates Water and Electricity Company (EWEC) is helping to further reduce its emissions profile.  The second element is delivering clean, reliable power at scale, especially for fast-growing economies. Solar can scale quickly where the resource is strong. Nuclear can provide continuous low-carbon electricity. Gas can support flexibility as demand grows.   The challenge is integrating these resources into a power system that can consistently meet the needs of households, industry and critical infrastructure every hour of the day. Abu Dhabi’s experience shows how long-term planning can deliver a diverse, resilient energy mix. EWEC has met more than 80% of the emirate’s total power demand using renewable and clean energy from solar and nuclear sources. The Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant provides a large-scale clean baseload, while Masdar’s global renewable energy portfolio has reached 65GW and is set to increase to 100GW by 2030. Together, these assets show how clean power can become a core part of a balanced and secure energy mix.  The third element is water. A data center needs electricity, but it also needs water for cooling. A desalination plant provides water, while also creating energy demand. Treating these as separate challenges increases cost and complexity over time.  In arid regions, it is also one of the clearest tests of whether resilience has been designed into the system from the outset.   For Abu Dhabi, water security is part of the same economic platform as energy security. We have built resilience through diversified desalination, energy demand management and long-term infrastructure planning. This is increasingly important as water scarcity places pressure on communities and infrastructure, even in traditionally water-secure regions, leading to restrictions and, in some cases, constraints on power generation. Our experience shows the value of planning for these pressures before they constrain growth.  As the United Nations convenes its Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December this year, co-hosted by the UAE and Senegal, it will be a timely opportunity to reinforce the connection between water security and energy infrastructure, technology and long-term investment.  The fourth element is capital with a long-term horizon. Energy systems require investment cycles measured in decades. Generation and storage, grids, and digital infrastructure all depend on capital that can look beyond short-term market conditions. They also require forward-looking regulation, agile planning and commercial foresight to move together successfully.  This is becoming especially important as the AI economy expands. AI infrastructure will compete on the speed and reliability of the power and water systems behind it. The UAE-US AI Campus , with a planned 1 GW cluster in Abu Dhabi , shows how energy, water, and digital infrastructure are becoming part of the same competitiveness equation.  Abu Dhabi’s Energy and Water Resilience Framework strengthens how we anticipate risk across infrastructure, governance, technology and operations, so that essential systems can continue to perform as conditions change. Such resilience is not separate from competitiveness. It is part of what gives economies the confidence and capacity to keep growing through disruption.  Today, governments and investors are increasingly looking at how infrastructure can keep pace with demand in the decades to come.   In that sense, Abu Dhabi’s model is relevant beyond the UAE. events.title: U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plant
events.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. is looking to work with Reliance Industries for refining Western energy supplies. Rubio is visiting Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which is the world's "largest and most complex single-site refinery" with crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Rubio underscored Reliance's ability to refine heavy crude and referred to India as a "refining superpower" when asked about the role the country can play in meeting the world's energy demand. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will discuss refining Western energy supplies with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries when he visits the company's plant in Jamnagar, Gujarat — the world's largest single-site refinery. The U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance for refining energy from the "Western Hemisphere," Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18, which is owned by Reliance. "I think that's helpful to India, but it's also helpful to us," he added. Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which Rubio will visit on Wednesday, has a crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Reliance has also emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside of the U.S., as of end-September. The company's "extraordinary" refining capacity could help India diversify its energy supplies, Rubio said, hinting at possibly greater offtake of Venezuelan crude. "We think there's an opportunity for them [Reliance Industries] to continue to help India diversify its supply chain, its supply of energy," Rubio said, adding that Venezuela was ramping up energy production, and that "India has had a long history of being able to refine some of that." U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing India to buy more Venezuelan oil to replace Russian barrels, and while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer. Beyond oil purchases, Reliance has been deepening ties with the U.S. this year, with Trump announcing in March that America will build its first new oil refinery in 50 years, helped by investment from Ambani's Reliance. While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS A HISTORIC $300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY." Reliance has never made an announcement about the refinery investment, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC, adding that it creates an air of uncertainty around the deal. Rubio would seek to "clinch" that deal or take it a little further, Chaudhuri said. Rubio told Network 18 that Reliance had "invested in increasing the refining capacity within the United States." His visit to Jamnagar also comes at a time when diesel prices have surged in the U.S., with midterm elections looming. Diesel prices, which affect American truckers, farmers, and shippers, are expected to remain elevated going into next year . Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rubio underscored Reliance's ability to refine heavy crude and referred to India as a "refining superpower" when asked about the role New Delhi and its companies can play in meeting the world's energy demand. Indian and Chinese refineries are good at handling heavy and medium-heavy crude from Venezuela and Russia, Chaudhuri said, adding that this grade of fuel is better-suited for producing diesel.

events.title: AI data centre company cold calling about buying land, inquiry told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts AI data centre company cold calling rural residents about buying Tasmanian land, inquiry told Vica Bayley said locals were told the interested buyers wanted agricultural land close to the north-west transmission line. ( Facebook: TasNetworks ) Locals in a north-west Tasmanian rural area have been telephoned and asked about selling land to a data centre developer, the Greens say. Firmus, which has plans for three data centres in Tasmania, has previously said it was not behind the proposal. The Tasmanian government says the proponent has not yet confirmed a final site. Consultants for an AI data centre company have been cold-calling residents in north-west Tasmania, wanting to buy their land, the Greens say. At a state parliamentary energy committee hearing today, Greens MP Vica Bayley asked the acting coordinator-general whether an AI data centre was proposed for Nook. "We've been contacted this week by locals in Nook, near Sheffield," Mr Bayley said. "They've been contacted by a Sydney consultancy firm wanting to purchase, my understanding is, agricultural land adjacent to the substation there, recently upgraded because it's part of the north-west transmission line, and allegedly for a large data centre." Mr Bayley questioned the appropriateness of locals finding out about the proposal from a "Sydney consultancy firm". ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Acting Coordinator-General Dennis Hendriks said there was "probably not a lot I can say about that". "We are aware that there is a proposal in the north-west that is moving forward," he told the committee. "It's at an early stage of development; we've made some introductions to the planning authority." Proposals for six new data centres were revealed in Tasmanian parliament last month, though the government did not disclose the names of the proponents. Mr Hendriks confirmed the proposal referred to by Mr Bayley was project B — a 200–300 megawatt data centre in the feasibility stage in the north-west. Mr Bayley questioned the appropriateness of locals finding out about the proposal from a "Sydney consultancy firm". Mr Hendricks said the office only had a "very limited amount of information" about the project. He took a question on notice about identifying the proponent to the committee. Government says no final site confirmed Mr Bayley asked Minister for Business, Resources and Industry Felix Ellis if agricultural land should be used for AI data centres. "There's a statutory planning process and environmental regulation and legislation," Mr Ellis replied. The Greens said north-west residents have been told about a potential AI data centre development for Nook, which is near Sheffield (pictured). ( Wikimedia Commons: CucombreLibre ) A government spokesperson said it would continue engaging with the proponent. "This proposal was included in information previously tabled in parliament," they said. "We understand it remains under consideration by the proponent, and no final site has been confirmed. AI data centre company Firmus Technologies has previously said it was not behind any of the six confidential new proposals. Firmus has three data centre projects underway in Tasmania — one under construction in Launceston, another approved for construction at Long Reach in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone, and another waiting for approval at Wesley Vale, in the state's north-west. 'Going to cause huge tension with their neighbours' Wade Rockliff, a farmer in Sheffield, has heard rumblings of consultants asking to buy farmland in the area for AI data centres. "I think they're offering way more than the land's worth," he said. "The people that they're asking, it's probably life changing for them. "Some of them are probably generational families in the community and it's going to cause huge tension with their neighbours because if they build some monstrosity — they're talking bigger than the one that's going in at Bell Bay, so it's a massive data centre — everyone's properties around it are going to devalue." Mr Rockliff does not believe "data centres are going to employ that many locals once they've been built". "And when you look at the ethos of a data centre, it's about replacing jobs.

events.title: Ken Griffin calls Trump’s tariffs on US allies 'a disaster' and predicts it will hurt Republicans in the midterms
events.summary: Citadel CEO Ken Griffin called Trump's tariffs on US allies "a disaster" and said the disputes have been "pro-inflation." Bloomberg/Getty Images Citadel CEO Ken Griffin called Trump's tariffs on US allies "a disaster" and "pro-inflation." Griffin predicts Republicans would lose at least one chamber in the midterms. Inflation has erased nearly all average workers' hourly wage gains since Trump returned to office. Ken Griffin sees trouble ahead for Republicans and says Donald Trump’s fights with America’s allies are part of the problem. The Citadel CEO told Bloomberg's Dani Burger on Tuesday at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York that Trump’s tariffs have fueled inflation and disrupted supply chains as the party heads toward a difficult midterm election. “I think that the tariff battles with Canada, with Europe, with our allies has just been a disaster,” Griffin said. “I talked about this when he first started this in his presidency. To be blunt, I hate to say it, but I've been right.” “It's been pro-inflation. It has certainly taken supply chains around the world and severed them,” Griffin, who said he has been supporting a number of Republican candidates this election cycle, added. Trump's trade disputes with Canada and the EU remain unresolved. The president announced an additional 50% tariffs on certain imports from Canada on July 20, citing what he described as discrimination against American auto, alcohol, and dairy exports. Those duties took effect in August. The economic backdrop is also challenging. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, while inflation has erased nearly all of the average worker’s hourly wage gains since Trump returned to office. Fuel affordability  and the lack of housing supply  have become pain points for Republicans in the midterms. Griffin predicted Republicans would almost certainly lose control of at least one chamber of Congress, describing the midterms as a check on the party in power. “The House almost is in a really tough spot and the Senate's going to be really close," Griffin said. Griffin also has thoughts on Trump’s explanation of the war in Iran and called the administration’s treatment of immigrants "disgraceful." "The war in Iran is very unpopular. I think he's done a very poor job of explaining why," Griffin said. "I think the president has not made that case in a powerful, meaningful way to the American people." Griffin said he believes in securing the border, but immigrants who are already here should be offered "a path to being a contributing member of our society" and help "grow our economy." "If you are here with your family or by yourself and you are gainfully employed and you are working to find a better life for your family, there needs to be a way to stay in our country," Griffin added. events.title: Veggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradise
events.summary: In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them S ixty bowls of slime-green soup sit waiting for the children to arrive. Pupils rush in from their morning lessons, grab the bowls by the handles and start slurping. No complaints, no refusals. (OK, maybe a few “bleurgh” faces.) Chicory soup dispatched, they get stuck into the main course: falafel, Mediterranean vegetable tagine and couscous. Some ask for seconds; most grab a piece of fruit for dessert and run out to play. This is a typical Thursday lunchtime in BS De Stadspoort primary school in Ghent, Belgium. Similar meat-free menus are being eaten in other schools and nurseries across the city, plus community centres, care homes and assisted living facilities, not to mention many work canteens and restaurants. Thursday in Ghent is officially “Veggie Day” , with residents encouraged to eschew any meat or fish. So how did a city get its children – and everyone else – to eat their greens? It didn’t happen overnight. “The success story of Ghent is one where we had an amazing grassroots movement, with people asking for more climate action. But the magic happened when politicians actually listened and implemented policy to introduce the Thursday Veggie Day in 2009,” says Vanessa Debruyne, the head of communications for the nonprofit organisation ProVeg Belgium , who is showing me around town. “It got the ball rolling, companies and restaurants joined, the population got used to it, and more entrepreneurs made the move to plant-based. We’ve been unstoppable ever since! Ghent is the best town in Belgium for plant-based food.” Veggie day was just the start, agrees Hafsa El-Bazioui, the Green deputy mayor of Ghent, who has cycled over to join us (the city centre has been largely car-free since 2017). “A few years ago, we changed to prioritise plant-based protein,” she says. In 2021, the Flemish government launched the Green Deal Protein Shift – a commitment to switch the ratio of animal to plant proteins consumed from 60:40 to 40:60 by 2030. Ghent has already reached the target. As well as vegetarian Thursdays and vegetarian options every day, school caterers have turned traditional meat dishes such as burgers, sausages and meatballs into hybrids, cutting out at least half the beef or pork and replacing them with, say, lentils. Stews might combine meat with chickpeas or beans. An incredible amount of effort is put in to making each dish taste good: they are screened by a “taste panel” made up of dietitians, chefs, childcare professionals and people with sensitivities to flavour, bitterness, texture and mouthfeel. Recipes are constantly modified and improved after feedback from children, parents and school staff. As a result, children get to eat the food they know and like, but the dishes are healthier and better for the planet – Ghent has reduced the carbon footprint of its school meals by 38% since 2018. Although she is a vegan herself, El-Bazioui believes reducing meat consumption across the board is the most effective and achievable policy, rather than trying to convince people to cut it out altogether. “When you approach a lot of people, the impact is more than if you focus on a small group of vegans,” she says. “That’s my philosophy in food, in politics, in life.” This stealth approach is echoed all over the city. I pop in to the Viernulvier art centre , AKA De Vooruit, for a chat with Tom De Vleesschauwer, its kitchen coordinator – De Vooruit is as popular for its large art deco cafe as for its programme of theatre, dance, film and music. “A few years ago, we made oat milk the default: if you don’t ask for cow’s milk, you get oat,” says De Vleesschauwer. “About 90% of customers now have oat milk. If we had a sign saying you can choose, it would only be 10-20%.” There have been other changes in De Vooruit’s cafe, too. The soup is now always vegan; the dish of the day is vegetarian; the staff and performers are served a daily “ Ottolenghi -style vegetarian buffet” instead of cheese and charcuterie. And, as in the school canteens, the few meat dishes on the menu – today just spaghetti bolognese and meatballs in tomato sauce – have been hybridised. “We cut down the meat by 70% and increased the carrots, cutting them to the same size – 30% still gives the flavour and the idea of meat, and carrots give sweetness,” says De Vleesschauwer. “People say plant-based is niche, but we have a very wide audience.” There are plenty of fully vegan businesses in the city, too, such as Madam Bakster , where I drink coffee with homemade hazelnut milk and devour rich, chewy chocolate-chip cookies fresh from the oven. Laura Verhulst, the founder, sees her cafe as more, not less, inclusive. “I wanted to make desserts that everyone could enjoy: vegan, allergen-free, non-refined sugar,” she says.

events.title: Last drinks for Boag's as final Tasmanian beers roll off production line
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Final Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers come off production line as brewer exits home state Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were packaged up in the Launceston factory today. Parent company Lion announced the closure of the 145-year-old brewery in June, with the brand now to be fully produced on the mainland. Decommissioning the brewery is expected to take a year, with the Tasmanian government interested in buying the large CBD site. The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were bottled in Launceston this morning, marking an end to 145 years of local production. In the past century and a half, Boag's has cemented itself as a state icon and often run ads about being brewed with clean Tasmanian water. The final bottles exited the assembly line this afternoon, ahead of the brewery shutting its doors for the final time on November 6, taking with it 42 local jobs. Boag's will cease their Tasmanian operations in Launceston in November after 145 years of local operation. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) While the bottle production finished today, the final brewing day was in September. Brewer Adrian Hinds, who has been a Boag's employee for 22 years, said it was an emotional day. "To be honest, I'm holding it together; it's quite emotional," he said. "Today was the last drop of Boag's put into containers; tanks are empty, everything's on a carton or pallet ready to go out to the public. "Everyone was on the packaging line watching the bottles go through the labeller; it just shows what it means to the staff here. Brewer Adrian Hinds has been a Boag's employee for over two decades. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Mr Hinds said for the last mashing, "everyone came up, got a sample of grain, put it in the mash tuns, so everyone had that final little touch on the last brew of draught that we did". "After everyone left the brew house and I was in there by myself, I just sat there for a while and just listened to all the sounds, the pumps going and then sugar going in and then smelling the hops going in. "To be here for the last fill, it's sad. I didn't think it would ever happen; it's a shame it's happening, but you can't control it. The Boag's Brewery site sits on the banks of the North Esk river in central Launceston. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Tasmania to start importing Boag's from mainland Boag's has existed in Launceston longer than electricity. Originally called the Esk Brewery, Scottish migrant James Boag and his son James Boag II began the operation in 1881. Bottling machines in the brewery's early years. ( Supplied: State Library and Archives Tasmania ) In 2008, Lion Australia, owned by Japanese beer giant Kirin, snapped up the brand for $325 million. But in June, Lion announced an end to local brewing operations in Launceston , citing inflation and long-term declines in beer sales. Brewing of the Boag's brand will continue on the mainland in New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Most of Boag's brewing had already been moved interstate the previous year, leaving the Launceston operation running at one-fifth of its capacity. The Boag's brand will continue to live on, being brewed in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland. Tasmania will now become an importer of its beverage icon. Boag's tour guide Phil Crowden has been taking visitors from around the world into the Boag's Brewery's inner sanctum for 17 years. He said the skills of the local brewers were "unparalleled", but he had faith the mainland-brewed Boag's would still hit the spot for rusted-on fans. James Boag beers can be found in every northern Tasmanian pub, bar and bottleshop. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) "The technology's got so good at the moment," he said. "I mean, breweries are making beers for other breweries around the world, and you can actually emulate the water from any particular place in the world." An online petition was launched in a bid to try and stop the closure of the brewery. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Tasmanian water has long been lauded as the essential ingredient in Boag's, something the brand has heavily promoted in its advertising. Mr Crowden said the exact mineral count of Tasmanian water would be replicated at the other breweries to get as close to the taste as possible. A spokesperson for Lion said the company were considering whether the equipment from the Launceston site may be deployed to its other sites. Decommissioning of the brewing equipment will begin after the November closure date and is estimated to take an additional 12 months. Boag's is easily the bestseller at Launceston mainstay The Gunners Arms.

events.title: Leica’s U.S. boss says F1 ‘goes at incredible speed’ and photography helps ‘stop the moment.’ Now they’ve made $10,000 camera together
events.summary: Some of Formula 1’s most populat drivers are already serious about photography. Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris have both been seen with Leica cameras, and Norris runs a separate Instagram account for his photos. That overlap goes well past the drivers, or even the intricate pieces that goes into both cars and cameras, says Mike Giannattasio, president of Leica Camera North America. “There is such synergy between people who collect cameras and people who collect cars,” he told Fortune . “If you see people who are passionate about vintage cars or racing cars, and if they have anything other than a passenger in the seat next to them, eight out of 10 times it’s going to be a Leica camera.” To Giannattasio, that made a partnership an easy call. On Tuesday, the German camera maker and Formula 1 announced a global licensing deal, Leica’s first official tie-up with the sport. It covers F1 as a whole rather than a single team and includes a special-edition camera, a gallery show in Los Angeles, and events at the United States Grand Prix in Austin this weekend. ‘The decisive moment’ Not everyone saw the workings of a partnership right away. When Giannattasio described the deal to someone he was meeting with, the reply was, “Mike: F1 and Leica? That’s a stretch.” He disagreed, and his case comes down to how both are made. Car and camera manufacturing both involve intricately crafted pieces put together into something the owner will spend countless hours learning. Each time a shutter fires, and each time a tire squeals, involves countless pieces working together to deliver a smooth outcome. Leica Camera AG “When you look at the mechanics of a camera and you look at an M system, inside just a rangefinder, there are over 150 pieces that make the camera work,” Giannattasio said. An F1 team spends months engineering and testing for a race that can be decided within a fraction of a second. Giannattasio compared that to French photographer and artist Henri Cartier-Bresson’s idea of “the decisive moment,” the instant a photographer has to be ready for. “Both photography and racing depend so much on preparation,” he said. “While Formula 1 goes at incredible speed, and it may be really hard to stop the moment, photography helps someone who loves that craftsmanship and excellence stop the moment, so that it can be examined, remembered, celebrated.” Both brands also sell their history. F1 has raced since 1950. Leica still makes film cameras, including the MP and M-A, which have no digital parts. “You can bring an MP or an M-A into the most extreme weathers in the Antarctic, and because there’s nothing digital, the camera will work,” he said. “It won’t freeze. It won’t break.” But he said history only counts if it pushes the product forward: “It’s heritage, but it’s not heritage for heritage’s sake,” he said. “It’s heritage for innovation’s sake.” A camera built ‘in the world of F1’ So what goes into making an F1-driver-approved carbon fiber camera? The result is the Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition, which sells for $9,950. It is the first Leica camera to use carbon fiber, the material that defines modern race cars because it is light and rigid. The carbon covers the grip, the thumb rest, and the soft-release button, the spots a photographer touches most. Giannattasio said the material had to be adapted so the camera still handled the way photographers expect, and that it couldn’t stop looking like a Leica. “You would ask a little child to draw a camera,” he said. “It’s going to be a rectangular box with a little round circle. It is literally quintessential.” “We had to make a product that was quintessentially iconic, immediately recognizable as a Leica camera,” he added. “But yet we had to take the design cues and materials that are big in the world of F1.” The body is wrapped in a black covering modeled on a racing steering wheel, and the red accents on its buttons come from the same place: F1 steering wheels color-code their controls so drivers can find them quickly. From Montblanc to Leica Giannattasio, who grew up in Astoria, Queens, came to Leica from luxury goods, not cameras. He spent more than a decade at Montblanc, rising to president and CEO of Montblanc North America, and earlier worked on Christian Dior watches at LVMH. When he interviewed to run Leica’s North American business in 2020, he said, he was likely the only candidate with that background. “My counterparts were from the electronics or from the camera business and very large companies within that world,” he said. Once he started, staff kept testing his knowledge of aperture and ISO. “What I always said to people is, I love art, I love photography, I love culture, and I am here because I’m passionate about building this organization around those principles, not because I am the best photographer who interviewed for the role,” he said. Despite his résumé, he doesn’t think of Leica as being part of that world: “We don’t by any means consider ourselves a luxury brand. We are a premium brand, meaning we make the best optical equipment in the world.” What sets Leica apart, he said, is what it asks of the owner. With most luxury brands, money is the only way in. A Leica, he said, also takes time and intellect. “You need time in order to develop this relationship with your camera,” he said. “While we don’t position ourselves as a luxury brand, what we do in today’s world is quite luxurious.” He sees that same pull behind a renewed interest in analog products, and he ties it to technology moving faster around us. “In a world that continues to advance with artificial intelligence, I think [there is a] need to slow down to celebrate and be in the moment,” he said. “Whether it’s film, whether it’s books, whether it’s a writing instrument, there’s a real resurgence for things that are real and deliberate.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Singapore’s DayOne said to weigh options for US IPO after data centre rout
events.summary: DayOne was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter. DayOne Data Centers is weighing a delay or smaller US IPO after a data centre market rout, with plans still under review and no final decision made. The Singapore-based firm may cut fundraising to US$2.5 billion-US$3 billion, down from an earlier target of up to US$5 billion and a US$20 billion valuation. Investor caution is rising across data centre and AI-linked listings, after failed or delayed IPOs at Firmus Grid, AirTrunk and others, while DayOne keeps talking to investors. DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US initial public offering , including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases, according to people familiar with the matter. While Singapore-based DayOne has been waiting for the right window to launch the IPO, it has also been considering the possibility of pushing back the share sale until the market recovers, the people said. Other options include going ahead with a smaller listing that may raise US$2.5 billion (S$3.2 billion) to US$3 billion, roughly half of what it had originally aimed for, the people said. DayOne, whose backers include Coatue and Hillhouse, is continuing to engage with potential investors and still wants to move forward as soon as the market allows, the people said. The company was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter, people familiar with the matter said previously. It had been eyeing a valuation of about US$20 billion, the people have said. Deliberations are ongoing and DayOne has not made any final decisions, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. The company could still opt to move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks, according to the people. While data centres have drawn global investor demand amid a boom in sectors related to artificial intelligence, a more negative sentiment has started to have ripple effects on IPOs. DayOne has been raising billions of dollars in private funding rounds as it seeks capital to build out its pipeline. Australian data centre company Firmus Grid pulled its roughly US$5 billion IPO when investors balked at the valuation it sought, while AirTrunk, which also operates data centres, delayed a planned real estate investment trust IPO in Singapore to 2027. South Korean digital infrastructure company Elice plunged 32% in its Seoul trading debut on Oct 20. Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, and Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News reported. On Oct 21, shares of Australian data center operator Nextdc plummeted after it cut earnings guidance. Some investors are hoping that the recent market volatility will pass after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. They are also looking ahead to the performance of Anthropic PBC’s upcoming listing as an important gauge of sentiment toward the AI sector. DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier in October. The offering is being led by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America and Citigroup IFR reported on Oct 19 that DayOne was gathering more investor feedback before launching the share sale. DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia , Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain. Other backers include GDS Holdings, the SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

events.title: An AI slowdown could be exactly what businesses need
events.summary: The artificial intelligence industry has spent years feathering the accelerator of frontier model development in a fierce contest to dominate the technology . Now, it is considering something that until recently seemed almost unthinkable: slamming on the brakes. The prospects of the frontier labs are closely linked to the fortunes of the US stock market, and they buttress vast spending on infrastructure. But for businesses still working out how to harness AI’s illusive productivity gains, a slowdown is not a bad thing. It will give them time to close the yawning gap between AI’s accelerating capabilities and their productive use of them. Still, calls to pace the frontier grow louder. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei made the case in an essay in which he said capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand, align and control them. His proposal was to deliberately slow the improvement enough to give safety research and independent evaluation time to catch up. Is it practical? There remains considerable disagreement over whether this is practical, desirable or possible. But that’s beside the point for businesses, since most of them are nowhere close to exhausting the AI capabilities they already possess. According to the Stanford 2026 AI Index, 88 per cent of organisations surveyed reported using AI in at least one business function last year. But breadth of adoption is not the same thing as depth. The research shows that the use of AI agents remained in the single digits across almost every business function. Relatively few have fundamentally redesigned how work gets done around it. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis found that generative AI accounted for only 5.7 per cent of total working hours by August last year. This tells us that companies already have powerful AI, and are simply failing to make the most of it. They don’t need another massive leap in model capability to claim the productivity gains that are already on the table. A METR randomised study found that experienced open-source developers working on highly familiar repositories actually took 19 per cent longer when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools. The reason is that the bottleneck is increasingly organisational. Companies have to connect models to proprietary data. They have to integrate AI into existing systems. And they need to redesign workflows rather than simply insert a chatbot into them. They also need appropriate governance, security and human oversight, while employees have to learn how to delegate effectively to AI. Managers, meanwhile, need to rethink roles, performance measures and decision rights. Those changes happen at a comparatively glacial pace when compared with the speed at which AI labs have been pushing the frontier. More capabilities OpenAI's enterprise research finds that the heaviest AI adopters use substantially more capabilities across more tasks than the median employee. These intensive users report much larger productivity benefits. Seventy-five per cent of surveyed workers also reported being able to perform tasks using AI that they previously could not do. So the AI productivity frontier inside most companies sits far behind the technological one. This is not unusual. General-purpose technologies typically arrive before organisations learn how to exploit them. Electricity existed before factories were redesigned around distributed electric motors, and computers came along long before companies reorganised processes around digital information. AI is likely to follow the same pattern, which only strengthens the case for hitting the brakes. That will not stall the AI economy , which is so crucial to public equity markets, because it will give companies the badly needed time to extract value from the marvellous capabilities already at their fingertips. That means moving beyond experimentation towards workflow redesign. Moving from individual productivity tools towards end-to-end processes. Connecting AI to enterprise data and systems. Using agents where they genuinely add value. Building governance that allows experimentation without unacceptable risk. And, perhaps most importantly, developing the organisational capabilities required to use AI well. Executives should continue watching the frontier, of course. Better models will create new opportunities, and a substantial slowdown is far from guaranteed. But they should not confuse a slower technological frontier with a slower business opportunity. Even if frontier development paused dramatically tomorrow, companies would still have an enormous backlog of economically valuable opportunities across customer service, software development, finance , procurement, marketing and many other functions. So just because the frontier slows, it doesn’t mean the business opportunity does. The AI race, at least for enterprise users, needs to shift from simply building better AI to building better businesses around it.

events.title: Australian data center operator NextDC's shares plunge 40% after it slashes earnings forecast
events.summary: Australian data center operator NextDC slashed its fiscal year 2027 revenue and earnings guidance due to power supply delays at its Melbourne facility. Citi said in a note that the earnings impact could extend beyond 2027 due to delays in expansion approvals and transformer upgrades. The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million. The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC. Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation. Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades. As Australia grapples with growing concerns over the impact of data center developments on local communities, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was working to establish national standards for investment. Chalmers told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Wednesday that the government welcomes investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, provided it aligns with the country's national interest, adding that the government was finalizing national investment standards to address concerns surrounding AI deployment. Australia is not alone in facing opposition to data center projects, there has been growing push back against data center developments worldwide , amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment. NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.

events.title: Asian stocks climb as strong earnings buoy Wall Street
events.summary: Overnight, stocks on Wall Street were mildly positive, pushing the S&P 500 0.3% higher as oil prices and Treasury yields eased. SINGAPORE – Asian stocks rose and bonds stabilised at the start of trading on Oct 21 following Wall Street’s gain as early indications from the corporate earnings season pointed to strong profits for global companies and bolstered investor confidence. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 1.5%, led by a 4% gain for Korean shares, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 1.3%. S&P 500 e-mini futures rose 0.3%. Stocks in the region have steadied since a wrenching selloff last week but have traded in a tight range since then. With 13% of S&P 500 companies reporting, 86% have beaten earnings estimates, according to LSEG data. “Global equities were mixed, with solid earnings supporting US markets while ongoing concerns around the AI trade and elevated oil and borrowing costs weighed more heavily elsewhere,” Westpac analysts wrote in a note. “Oil prices fell on unconfirmed reports of renewed peace negotiations, before largely retracing the move after the reports were denied.” However, French stocks fell as fears remained around the government’s plans to curb recent unrest . French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would reinforce police with a “massive” deployment of troops to quell protests planned for Oct 24 . The yield on the French 10-year OAT was up 2.7 basis points at 4.94%, nudging the yield differential compared to the German 10-year bund 0.3 basis point higher to 153.1 basis points. Brent crude was 1.1% higher at US$110.03 a barrel as trading resumed in Asia, extending gains after touching a five-month high during a volatile session on Oct 20 as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan’s army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. US envoy Steve Witkoff is due to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin later in the day after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, as US President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war. The yen was 0.1% weaker against the dollar at 158.33 yen after government data released on Oct 21 showed Japan’s exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing estimates. Strong demand for semiconductors and AI-related products offset weakness in other sectors. A Reuters poll found a majority of economists believe the Bank of Japan will refrain from hiking interest rates on Oct 30 before voting for a 25-basis-point increase in December, followed by quarterly hikes. Economists polled also believe the Federal Reserve will skip a hike at its next meeting on Oct 28 before raising rates in December. Fed funds futures are pricing an implied 83% probability of a hold later in October, little changed from a day earlier, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 1 basis point at 5.123%. In emerging markets, traders are awaiting a decision from Indonesia’s central bank , which is battling to halt the rupiah’s slide following a market rout from an MSCI warning that it may exclude the country’s stocks from its major benchmarks. Bitcoin was up 0.3% at US$82,988.76, while ether was 0.2% higher at US$2,452.59. REUTERS

A bitter power struggle over the Tata Group, a 158-year-old conglomerate with more than one million employees worldwide and US$180 billion (S$230 billion) in annual revenue, has become a test of who calls the shots in Indian capitalism: owners, professional managers or the government.

events.title: Tech giant shares plunge 40pc after delays to Melbourne data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NextDC value on ASX smashed by delays to West Footscray data centre The value of NextDC, which operates a data centre in West Footscray, has plummeted. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The value of a multi-billion-dollar tech giant has plummeted amid ongoing delays to its data centre plans in Melbourne's inner west. The community backlash has forced NextDC to drastically cut its earnings and revenue forecasts. NextDC, which has 17 operational data centres in Australia, has another nine centres in the development or planning stages. Community opposition to one of Melbourne's largest hyperscale data centres has smashed the value of one of Australia's biggest companies. A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has forced multi-billion-dollar tech giant NextDC to cut its net earnings and revenue forecasts by tens of millions of dollars, with a planned expansion hit with power supply and government approval delays. The company, among Australia's largest 100 listed companies, notified the stock exchange this morning that its net revenue for the current financial year would be slashed by a third — now $475 million to $500 million — down from $615 million to $640 million. The company's operating profitability was also revised down to $245 million to $265 million, from $385 million to $410 million. Following this morning's announcement, NextDC's stock plummeted by 40 per cent. NextDC attributed the revised estimates to delays to electricity network upgrades by energy supplier Jemena, required to increase power supply to its M3 data centre in West Footscray. The West Footscray data centre, located just 15 metres from homes, has long been the subject of community opposition due to concerns over diesel and noise pollution . Located only 10 kilometres west of Melbourne's CBD, this data centre spans 41,000 square metres. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The installation of towering power poles to accommodate the facility's vast electricity use became another flashpoint earlier this year. In September, Jemena was forced to halt the installation of 15-metre-high power poles in Yarraville after being met with resistance from residents, several of whom blocked crews by leaving their cars and bins out. The power poles can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, approximately 160 times the voltage of previous power poles. Local councils and residents argued that they had not been adequately consulted over the upgrades. The installation of power poles in Yarraville was met with fierce resistance from residents. ( ABC News ) Company 'exploring all avenues' to accommodate facility's power needs In its announcement to the ASX on Wednesday morning, NextDC said the delays meant the next grid supply for West Footscray was now not expected until mid-2027, deferring "the delivery and billing of contracted capacity". "Jemena has advised NextDC that it has suspended parts of the network works required for the next increase in grid supply to M3 Melbourne," NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said. "We have taken the affected M3 contracts out of FY27 guidance until we can reliably estimate their contribution." In a call with investors this morning, NextDC's group chief development officer Simon Cooper said the company was "exploring all avenues", including finding alternative locations for the power poles, or placing electrical cables underground. "Undergrounding does take time and there's not an immediate option that we can work on now. But it is something that we are absolutely considering," Mr Cooper said. Independent senator David Pocock today used a National Press Club address to propose a "modest" 5 per cent levy on data centres operating in Australia from next year. Senator Pocock accused the federal government of being "starstruck" by US artificial intelligence companies, and being "blind" to community sentiment regarding artificial intelligence. He said the levy would generate more than $500 million by the end of 2030. "In the context of a forecast $200-billion investment and little to no corporate tax paid by foreign data centre companies in this country, it's really not much," Mr Pocock said.

events.title: Ambani’s Jio seeks historic IPO a decade after disrupting India telecom
events.summary: Mukesh Ambani’s Jio Platforms, the owner of India’s largest wireless operator, is seeking a valuation that is roughly 10% lower than its nearest sector rival. Mukesh Ambani’s Jio is preparing India’s biggest IPO, valued at US$107 billion, and will open to retail investors on Oct 21. He said it will “unlock great value” for Reliance Industries. Jio still leads India’s telecom market with over 500 million subscribers, but it earns less per user than Bharti Airtel. Bharti has higher ARPU and profit margins, so investors now favour stronger earnings over sheer size. The IPO will help Jio repay debt and strengthen its balance sheet for future battles in telecom, satellite communications, and digital services. Analysts see upside, but Jio must prove growth after listing and may rely on higher mobile tariffs. A decade after storming into the Indian telecom market with free calls and cheap data that decimated its rivals, Mukesh Ambani’s digital venture is aiming for a historic milestone this week with India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO). But unlike in the triumphant fall of 2016, when its aggressive strategy stoked a price war that left only a single competitor profitable, Ambani’s upstart is coming to the market more cautious and humble. Jio Platforms, the owner of India’s largest wireless operator, is seeking a valuation that is roughly 10% lower than its nearest sector rival, Bharti Airtel. The listing marks billionaire Ambani’s return to the capital market after 20 years, an offering that he said will “unlock great value” for parent Reliance Industries. But a closer look paints a more sobering picture. Reliance shares are on track for their worst annual performance since 2011 and the energy-to-entertainment conglomerate had to prune Jio’s valuations to attract marquee investors. It is a reflection of the roller-coaster ride for the nation’s telecom sector, which features some of the world’s cheapest data plans and a massive user base. Jio’s market value adjustment shows that the market is saturating fast and investors now prefer companies that earn more from each customer over those that service more subscribers. “We believe that, following its listing, Jio will likely need to demonstrate growth to public shareholders,” Nomura Holdings analysts Bineet Banka and Abhishek Bhandari wrote in a note dated Oct 10. They added that Bharti Airtel remains their top pick in the sector because of “its higher proportion of premium subscribers, which should insulate it from downtrading and subscriber attrition” if telecom services get costlier. Jio’s IPO opens its books for retail investors on Oct 21, for a subscription period that ends on Oct 23. Anchor investors including BlackRock, Fidelity Management & Research, Capital Group and Allianz SE took stakes worth a combined US$854 million (S$1.09 billion) at the top end of the marketed range. Jio’s US$3.1 billion share sale values the company at US$107 billion at the top end of the marketed price range of 1,065 rupees (S$14.36) to 1,119 rupees apiece, compared with about US$123 billion for billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal’s wireless operator. On paper, Jio is bigger than Bharti Airtel on most counts. It leads in both wireless and fixed broadband markets, boasts more than 500 million subscribers and is ahead of Bharti in new opportunities such as the under-penetrated home broadband. But in average revenue per user, or ARPU – a key metric monitored by sector analysts and investors, Ambani’s venture has lagged Bharti for seven straight years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. For the quarter ended June, Bharti reported an ARPU of 264 rupees, compared with Jio’s 216 rupees – an outcome of its longstanding strategy to prune low-value customers in favour of more inelastic, high-paying users. Profits show a similar trend as Bharti leads the industry with a 57.4% margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, compared with 53.3% for Jio. As a result, Jio is valued at 33.2 times trailing earnings versus Bharti’s nearly 37 times. Nomura and Motilal Oswal Financial Services valued Jio Platforms at a premium to Bharti based on enterprise value-to-Ebitda. That is a long way since Ambani unleashed Jio on India’s once hyper-competitive telecom market in 2016. In the tycoon’s signature style, the upstart came to disrupt and eventually dominate a fragmented industry. Its inaugural plan of free call and data services kicked off one of the most intense price wars in any sector the country had seen, causing rivals to exit, merge or consider bankruptcy. The strategy triggered courtroom battles and accusations of predatory pricing by rivals, with Bharti Airtel – then the market leader – warning it would “kill the rest of the industry and create a monopoly”. For Mukesh Ambani, this was his second attempt at getting mobile phones right and follow his father’s advice to make phone calls as cheap as postcards.

events.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
events.summary: Voters in Alberta have overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with four-fifths of votes counted showing 75% support for staying EDMONTON, Alberta -- Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in the country, referendum results showed Tuesday, delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their country. With more than 1.9 million votes counted and results reported from 90% of voting areas and locations, 75% of voters supported remaining in Canada , while 25% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada . “It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Carney told reporters Tuesday before a Cabinet meeting in Ottawa. Carney said the roughly one-quarter of voters who backed beginning the separation process did not necessarily want independence, suggesting only a smaller “hard core” favored leaving Canada. Some voters said they wanted to send Ottawa a message rather than separate. Alberta separatist organizer David Parker acknowledged the scale of the defeat. “Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on social media. In a televised address Tuesday night, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the result and pledged not to hold another referendum on separation while she remains in office. “Yesterday, Albertans voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining a province of Canada,” Smith said. “The voter turnout was historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for our country and our province.” Smith said Alberta would continue pressing Ottawa for greater provincial autonomy, but disputes would be settled within Canada’s political and legal institutions rather than through separation. Carney said he spoke with Smith on Tuesday morning about the results and greater federal-provincial cooperation, including immigration. “Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves , is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Despite the overwhelming rejection, separatist leaders vowed to continue pressing for independence. Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.” Rath said before the vote that he would be thrilled with 30% support. He also said he wanted Smith ousted as UCP leader and believed the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Ian Brodie, a University of Calgary political scientist and former chief of staff to Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper, dismissed Rath and fellow separatist organizer Mitch Sylvestre as “nobodies,” saying they failed to gain traction even in a district that elected a separatist to Alberta’s legislature in 1982. “Even on a very soft question — whether to hold a referendum on separation — they couldn’t gain real traction," Brodie said. Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the separation process even though he doesn’t want Alberta to leave Canada. “It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy,” he said. Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united. Instead we’re fighting among ourselves.

events.title: The people of Serbia v the Trump family
events.summary: Serbia’s authoritarian president personally intervened to remove the protection of a historic landmark – then came protests and prosecutions. Tom Burgis on the murky tale of Trump Tower Belgrade In the heart of Belgrade, near the banks of the Danube, stands the General Staff building. Built in the 1960s, it embodies the difficult history of Serbia . It was designed to resemble a canyon of the Sutjeska River, where one of the most significant battles of the second world war was fought. Then suddenly, in November 2024, it was announced that the building was no longer protected from development. Instead, a tower with Donald Trump’s name on it would go up in its place. Protests and prosecutions followed, as opposition to the plan mounted. Investigations correspondent Tom Burgis tells Helen Pidd : “This isn’t just about the fate of a building, important though that kind of monument to Serbia’s history is. It’s about what is happening to the world when the US president is open for business.” The Trump family insist no political favours were sought or received in Serbia and that all they ever wanted to do was transform the site into “a symbol of healing and reconciliation”. But what does the murky tale of the Trump tower that was never built tell us?

events.title: Australian AI data centre operator NextDC shares shed 44% on revenue delay
events.summary: NextDC shares fell 44% and wiped about A$3.1 billion from its market value in early trade. NextDC shares fell 44% after it cut revenue and earnings forecasts, saying delays to power upgrades at its M3 Melbourne site will defer about A$140 million in contracted revenue. The company will pause all new development projects and land buys for now, and it may sell selected sites as it reviews capital recycling options. Jemena’s delayed network works pushed the next power increase for M3 to 2028, showing how community opposition and power limits can threaten data centre growth. SYDNEY – Australian data centre operator NextDC shed nearly half of its market capitalisation on Oct 21 after sharply cutting revenue forecasts for the year ahead and putting future developments on hold, extending the burst of negative sentiment towards global artificial intelligence stocks. The company said delays to electricity network upgrades at one of its major Melbourne assets would mean about A$140 million (S$126 million) worth of contracted customer revenue this financial year would be deferred. It would shelve all new development projects and land acquisitions for the foreseeable future and would evaluate capital recycling opportunities, including potential sales of selected development sites. The news sent NextDC shares down 44% and wiped about A$3.1 billion from its market value in early trade. The stock, now at its lowest since Jan 18, was also the biggest loser on the broader ASX200 benchmark index. Investments for data centre operators continue to pour in on expectations that surging demand for AI will drive a new wave of spending on digital infrastructure. However, sentiment has weakened in recent weeks as investors question whether massive AI spending can justify soaring computing, land and power costs. Signs of strain are emerging in some of those bets, with a data centre initial public offering withdrawn in Australia last week and credit investors becoming increasingly selective towards AI-linked companies. NextDC now expects net revenue of A$475 million to A$500 million in 2027, down from its prior outlook of A$615 million to A$640 million, excluding the affected M3 contracts. The company also cut its 2027 underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million, excluding the affected M3 contracts. Delays to works by Jemena Electricity Network meant the next increase in supply to its M3 Melbourne data centre was now expected in 2028, it said. Jemena had suspended parts of the electricity-network works needed to increase power supply to M3 due to opposition from the community and stakeholders and does not expect to recommence them before February 2027. “Whilst out of the company’s control, delays to power supply and development applications relating to NXT’s (NextDC) M3 data centre is evidence that community concerns around data centre developments present a real risk to the timing of delivery of contracted capacity for data centre owners,” said Tom Beadle, RBC Capital Markets analyst. Separately, NextDC lowered its 2027 capital expenditure outlook to A$4.5 billion to A$5 billion from A$5.25 billion to A$5.75 billion and said it had begun a detailed review of its spending programme.
