events.title: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal
events.summary: Alejandro Betancourt, a 46-year-old Venezuelan energy baron, is the key figure in a historic oil deal with the Trump administration. Venezuelan opposition leaders and U.S. congressional Democrats have criticized the agreement because Betancourt has been the target of investigations of alleged corruption. Antonio Heredia/El Mundo In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.  ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text. One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.  The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.  The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial 15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.  Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to the Miami Herald , federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company. NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr. Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims against them are baseless.”  Do You Know More About This Topic? We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our reporting team. Cate Brown I’m interested in talking to people who understand how members of the Trump administration, or their family members, are doing business, at home or abroad. Contact Me Key aspects of the plan differ from the Trump administration’s public pronouncements. Trump has said the deal will secure America’s energy dominance for the next century. But the text indicates that U.S. purchasing rights expire in half that time and that the underlying operating rights appear to run afoul of Venezuelan laws limiting oil concessions to 25 years. The agreement does ensure the United States a deep discount from fair-market value on 20% of NABEP’s oil, as Trump has said. It does not, however, explicitly guarantee that Betancourt’s company is obligated to pay the estimated $200 billion in royalties and tax payments to Venezuela that the White House has said would benefit the country .  There are also significant caveats related to Trump’s central selling point to Americans — that the deal will bring a gusher of low-cost oil imports.  The agreement gives the U.S. the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s oil at a discounted rate of $30 a barrel, or less than a third of what oil has sold for in recent months, according to one of three supporting documents reviewed by ProPublica.  But this fee does not account for the cost of getting Venezuela’s oil out of the country. Much of Venezuela’s raw crude is so thick that it won’t flow through pipelines unless it is first blended with 20% or more of oil thinner products. Under the deal, the potentially significant cost of importing millions of barrels of those blending materials is not included in the price. The White House, the State Department, the Pentagon and the energy company NABEP all defended the agreement, saying in statements that their new public-private venture will provide meaningful and lasting economic benefits to both countries that cannot be captured in a legal document. “This historic deal marks a major step toward stabilizing Venezuela’s economy after years of hyperinflation and almost no new investment, while more than doubling the United States’ oil reserves,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers. Wade emphasized that NABEP was chosen because of its track record of expanding oil production in Venezuela in recent years and that the agreement was between the company and the U.S. government, not Venezuela. “Thanks in large part to the agreement,” Wade said, “there is a surge in confidence about the future of Venezuela’s oil industry and, as a direct result, substantial new investments are flowing into the country.” He added that much of NABEP’s oil comes from fields that require little or no blending materials and that blending costs would not meaningfully impact the price of production. “Our barrel economics are strong.” The newly revealed details of the agreement are nonetheless likely to raise more questions about whether the unorthodox marriage of the United States and a foreign energy baron can bring lasting benefits to either country — and which private parties might benefit along the way. Trump’s oil deal is likely to face scrutiny in both the United States and Venezuela, especially if Democrats win one or both chambers in the midterm elections, according to former U.S. diplomats and congressional staff. “Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?” said former Ambassador James Story, who served as the top U.S. diplomat in Caracas from 2018 to 2023, in an interview. “Why did he get this deal? And was he involved in criminality? events.title: The reporter who exposed Theranos loved the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary but says its ‘artistry’ shouldn’t obscure the fraud
events.summary: Just over a decade after Elizabeth Holmes threatened him with lawsuits and tried to kill his reporting, author John Carreyrou has become a perhaps unlikely fan of “You Can See Everything,” a new documentary exploring the disgraced founder’s home life as she prepares for prison—in fact, he’s seen it twice. Carreyrou is the author of the 2018 book “Bad Blood,” in which he reports on Theranos’ collapse and Holmes’ downfall in a captivating narrative that topped the New York Times’ bestseller list. The new documentary, in which comedian Nathan Fielder lived in the guest house of the home Holmes shared with her partner Billy Evans and her two children for 34 days before she went to prison, has thrust Holmes, and indirectly, Carreyrou, back into the spotlight, while also earning rave reviews and an estimated $15 million during its first weekend—the second-biggest opening for a documentary ever. Carreyrou, for his part, told the New York Times ’ “Hard Fork” podcast that he saw the film twice, the first time being during a virtually private screening with his wife at the Manhattan offices of A24, the studio behind the film. He said he enjoyed the film even more the second time he watched it. “I guess, over two viewings, I was really won over by the artistry of the way they filmed this thing, but also the structure, the amount of meta-thinking that went into it, how unusual it is,” he said on the podcast. In a post on X, Carreyrou went even further, saying the documentary deserved best picture. But he warned it doesn’t cover the full story. “The film is a great piece of art, but let’s not confuse that art with the underlying facts,” he said in a statement to Fortune . Some people have told Carreyrou that Holmes is “unknowable and everything is ambiguous,” he wrote in a post on X . He said what these people are missing are the details of what he experienced during his reporting. This includes legal threats that Theranos’ lawyers leveled against him as well as against two of his sources, Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung. “She went after Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung with everything she had. I was threatened with litigation on a daily basis for months on end. It was a ruthless cover-up of a breathtaking fraud, and she was at the controls,” he wrote in the post. At the center of that fraud was Holmes’ promise that Theranos could perform hundreds of medical tests with just a few drops of blood from a finger prick, which she sold as a way to make testing more accessible and cheaper. Yet, the company’s machines really could only perform a limited number of tests and often produced unreliable results. Some tests also required much more than the small portion of blood Holmes said they needed or had to be done with conventional methods, rather than with Theranos’ product. Holmes also misled investors, falsely stating that Theranos had been validated by numerous large pharmaceutical companies and telling investors the company would bring in $1 billion in revenue in 2015, while knowing that the actual revenue figure would be negligible, according to the Justice Department . Further details of the campaign to stop Carreyrou’s reporting are revealed in his book, including Holmes’ attempt to kill his original story by appealing directly to the Wall Street Journal ’s billionaire owner, Rupert Murdoch, who was also a Theranos investor. Theranos’ lawyers also confronted Carreyrou at the newspaper’s offices in a meeting that lasted about five hours. Carreyrou now works as a reporter at the New York Times . To be sure, Carreyrou was frustrated by the movie the first time he watched it, he said on the “Hard Fork” podcast. When Fielder repeatedly asked Holmes whether she did anything wrong and she denied any wrongdoing, Carreyrou said he “would have liked to jump in and grab the mic from Fielder, and drill down a little bit more, and not be so polite.” One of Carreyrou’s sources, Tyler Shultz, whose grandfather, former Secretary of State George Shultz, served on Theranos’ board, said in an interview with CBS that despite Holmes’ denials, “she knows she did something wrong.” “She created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies,” he said. Holmes in 2022 was convicted of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud for deceiving investors. She was sentenced to just over 11 years in prison, and she and her former boyfriend and business partner Sunny Balwani were ordered to pay $452 million in restitution. A federal appeals court upheld her conviction last year, but in March a federal judge reduced her sentence to 10 years and three months following changes to federal sentencing guidelines. She is scheduled to be transferred to a halfway house in 2027 and slated for release in 2030. Despite his history with Holmes, Carreyrou said the film ultimately helped highlight some of Holmes’ contradictions. In one scene, Holmes insists she has never told a lie in her life, a claim Carreyrou called “preposterous.” While some have argued the documentary is part of a ploy for Holmes to restore her broken reputation, Carreyrou said her statement about never having lied is evidence for him that it had the opposite effect. “It comes off as this absurd statement that can’t possibly be true,” he said on the podcast. “And if anything, she looks worse for it.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Tesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backing
events.summary: Billionaire, on SpaceX earnings call, says ‘special committees’ exploring idea but no agreement reached yet As SpaceX released its second-ever public earnings report Tuesday, Elon Musk declared his support for combining the aerospace and AI company with his electric vehicle company, Tesla. He said both companies had created special committees to explore a potential merger, but have not reached any agreement on terms of a transaction. “Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders and these special committees are, uh, consist of independent directors,” Musk said on the call. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees.” Musk also expressed his backing for the move, while cautioning about the hurdles involved achieve it. He stated that it would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said, adding it would require shareholder approvals and special committees at both firms. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.” The company revealed a far better financial quarter than Wall Street projected. SpaceX company, which encompasses rockets, artificial intelligence and satellite communications, reported a 161% growth in revenue year over year, driven by its Starlink and AI segments. The company declared $14.58bn in revenue against analysts’ projected $12.72bn. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents and a net income of $4.4bn. The company’s stock, which started the day down around 8% for the year, shot up 2% in after hours trading immediately after the results. Musk appeared alongside SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and CFO Bret Johnsen at his Starlink factory in Texas to deliver the earnings report, touting the company’s growth and plans for future rocket developments. Musk also highlighted its artificial intelligence segment, which the company refers to as Super Intelligence, that drew $7.6bn in revenue and now outperforms its Connectivity business, which provides internet services. Musk’s company once again found itself in the spotlight in recent weeks as investors have speculated about the potential merger with Tesla, the second-most valuable part of the tech mogul’s empire. Musk has also been at the center of geopolitical tensions after Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, last week accused SpaceX of restricting access to its military-grade Starlink internet service. The disruption in service to StarShield allegedly led to several failed Ukrainian combat missions and left the country more vulnerable to Russian drone attacks, as well as highlighted how global internet infrastructure has come to rely on Musk’s products . Musk denied responsibility for the disruption, stating that StarShield was controlled by the US government, not SpaceX. The White House has likewise denied hobbling StarShield. Moments before the SpaceX earnings call on Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the throttling of StarShield, citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter. Musk faced no questions about the reports on the investor Q&A portion of SpaceX’s earnings call. While SpaceX’s role in international affairs faces scrutiny, Musk has taken on a resurgent role in US domestic politics. The world’s richest person has contributed $366m in political spending this election cycle, backing Republican-aligned Super Pacs and pouring money into influencing key midterm races. Musk also agreed earlier this month to co-lead a Pentagon project on the future of warfare, bringing him back into government work after his time as the de facto leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge). A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Musk recently pledged to give every child in the US one of his SpaceX stocks next year, which Donald Trump stated would be facilitated through the president’s “Trump accounts” initiative that creates savings plans for children. The prospective share giveaway is a rare display of philanthropy from Musk, who has criticized traditional aid organizations and has taken credit for dismantling the world’s largest single provider of humanitarian aid by gutting the government agency USAID. “Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” Musk posted on X, the social media company he owns. Tech leaders such as Musk have faced increasing public pushback over their extraordinary accumulation of wealth and power in the US, while this year AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic both announced big investments to their grant-making and non-profit arms. Musk’s announcement came after Anthropic announced earlier this week that it plans to donate 5% of its shares to a newly created public benefit fund within the company.

( ABC News: John Gunn ) The RBA deputy governor says there are signs some people do not expect inflation to come back to the RBA's target, which is "central banker's nightmare". Markets are putting the chance of a November rate hike at more than 50 per cent. The RBA's rate-setting board will next meet at the beginning of November, with a decision handed down on Melbourne Cup day. Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook is "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike as soon as November. Just under a fortnight out from the next interest rate decision, Mr Hauser warned high inflation was becoming entrenched in the Australian economy. "We are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we're going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period," Mr Hauser told the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney. The RBA targets headline inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average over time. Inflation currently sits at 4 per cent, according to the August consumer price index . Mr Hauser said the central bank's liaison program and surveys showed there was "an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that, maybe, sort of 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent [inflation] is the new normal". "Look, that is the central banker's nightmare. "We can't allow expectations to shift away from target." Australia's 'quirky' obsession with housing is fuelled by necessity Market pricing now puts the chance of an interest rate hike in November at 51 per cent, based on Bloomberg data. The odds of a hike next month had dipped below 20 per cent last week, after the unemployment rate reached a five-year high in September . UBS chief economist George Tharenou described Mr Hauser's remarks as "hawkish" and said the investment bank was forecasting a November rate hike. "Hauser's comments today are consistent with our view of the likelihood the RBA staff provide an explicit recommendation at the November meeting to raise the cash rate," Mr Tharenou said. The RBA will release its quarterly forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy on November 3, the same day the interest-rate-setting board next hands down a decision. Betashares chief economist David Bassanese agreed that the RBA official was setting the stage for a Melbourne Cup day hike. "Despite the steadfast claims that the Reserve Bank is no longer in the business of offering forward guidance, its signals to the market in recent weeks have rarely been clearer," Mr Bassanese said. "It remains possible the RBA board vote will be split, and the external members have a majority to hold rates, and hence effectively 'outvote' Bullock and Hauser," Mr Tharenou said. However, even if the RBA holds rates in November, he still would expect "a 'hawkish hold', with the RBA retaining a tightening bias … and also setting up a hike at the subsequent meeting in December". 'Laying shorter-term pain on top of pain' Mr Hauser reiterated the "hard choices" facing the RBA as it balanced the pressures on prices from the Middle East crisis, the AI and technology boom and weak productivity growth. Asked about the pain of higher interest rates hitting many households, on top of cost-of-living pressure, the deputy governor said: "It's a continuous challenge to explain this." "The reason is that, even though we are laying shorter-term pain on top of pain, it's to prevent a longer and potentially far worse pain down the track if inflation expectations get locked in," Mr Hauser said, echoing comments RBA governor Michele Bullock has made as the central bank has lifted rates. Mr Hauser downplayed concerns about the state of the jobs markets, saying there was potentially "noise" in the numbers, after the unemployment rate rose to 4.7 per cent in September. "That said, it clearly was a little weaker than we and others have been expecting," he said. "I stress the 'little'. These unemployment numbers in Australia are still right at the bottom or very near the bottom of G20 out-turns on labour markets.

events.title: When AI models refuse to fight hackers
events.summary: In the race to fend off AI-enabled cyber threats , security teams are confronting a new problem: The AI models they rely on to investigate attacks can suddenly refuse to help. Why it matters: While AI giants race to build AI tools that can respond quickly to hacking or other malicious online threats, strict guardrails on their most powerful models lock out defenders mid-investigation, leaving them scrambling for alternatives at critical moments. What's happening: OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, said it was compromised over the weekend, allowing attackers to obtain API keys belonging to some customers, including keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google services. OpenCode said the breach was "related to a large scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users." OpenCode co-creator Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting its systems continuously for 48 hours, forcing the company to keep its own AI agents running around the clock to respond. OpenAI , Google and Anthropic have said they worked with affected customers to revoke exposed API keys and address unauthorized usage charges. Zoom in: Raad said on X that frontier AI models initially helped investigate the breach but then "started refusing." The models' safety restrictions reportedly began blocking requests as the investigation turned to potentially malicious code, even though OpenCode was trying to defend its own systems. OpenCode then gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted cybersecurity defenders access to models with fewer restrictions. "We definitely need to be more proactive and we've made so many improvements over the last few days," Raad wrote on X Monday. The big picture: The incident underscored a dilemma facing cybersecurity teams trying to figure out when to use powerful proprietary AI models, which come with built-in restrictions, or open-weight alternatives that offer greater control over how they're deployed. When Hugging Face discovered suspicious activity on its systems that it later linked to OpenAI's own agents, its security team turned to a Chinese open-weight model to help investigate after encountering restrictions on frontier models. Yes, but: AI companies maintain that they need to gate access to their most powerful models to ensure that malicious actors can't abuse their cyber capabilities. Between the lines: Cybersecurity teams will have to figure out how to balance the need for faster AI-powered defenses with restrictions designed to keep those same capabilities out of attackers' hands, Chris Jones, chief technology officer at Nightwing, told Axios. "We're all going to have to figure out how that race gets modulated over time," Jones said. "That's a big piece here." Go deeper : Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

events.title: Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7%
events.summary: Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%. This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown. Shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%. Japan's exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing market expectations by a huge margin. Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%. This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown, after hitting a near four-year high in July. Growth was supported by continued strong semiconductor exports, with shipments rising 49.4% year on year by value. Exports of machinery also bolstered growth, with semiconductor-related machinery shipments up 43.9% and power generation machinery exports climbing 22.6%. In terms of destinations, shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%. Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth for the first two quarters of 2026, helping the world's fourth largest economy beat expectations in the first quarter, and supporting growth in the second. Japan's imports in September grew 18.9%, also missing expectations of 19.6% from Reuters. Tokyo's imports of petroleum climbed 51.1% by value in September, with inbound shipments from the U.S. surging nearly 820%, while those from the Middle East inching up just 1.5% as the conflict in the region continues to impede supplies. Following the data release, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 1.8%, while the Topix gained 1.14%. The data comes as the Bank of Japan is set to meet next week, and Reuters poll estimates indicate that the central bank is set to hold its policy rate steady at 1%.

events.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes following call with Rubio
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian attacks that he said occurred without enough notice to Ukraine KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice , leaving civilians vulnerable. For at least a week , the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles. Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio . “We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I’m speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming,” Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. “So we are thankful to American side now that it works.” Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue. In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help. Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff , who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war . Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital. Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues. “Today was a good day for peace,” Stubb said. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn’t expect any “miracle” from Washington. At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again . “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing.” The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes “some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us.” Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations . Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia , a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow’s full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February. Zelenskyy said he had “a substantive conversation” with Rubio. “I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position,” Zelenskyy said on social media. The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he said. European countries, worried about Russia’s plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made. events.title: Netflix posts higher Q3 profit but revenue growth worries pull shares lower
events.summary: Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street’s expectations Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street's expectations, but investors sent shares down after the streaming company lowered its ad sales guidance, prompting worries about slowing revenue growth. Netflix said Tuesday it earned $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, for the July-September period. That's up 44% from $2.55 billion, or 59 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 12% to $12.87 billion from $11.51 billion. Analysts surveyed by FactSet predicted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $12.87 billion. “With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it’s concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business,” said Emarketer senior analyst Ross Benes. “Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge but it is a worthwhile start. Guidance is not as aggressive as investors have grown accustomed to.” Last week, the Los Gatos, California-based company announced that it plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions, as the company makes wider “organizational changes.” At the end of 2025, per regulatory filings, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees worldwide. The most recent layoff announcement marks the biggest round of cuts that the company has rolled out in years. Netflix also announced last week that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. Bajaria was with Netflix for nearly a decade. Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions. He takes over the post on Oct. 26. While Netflix has benefited from membership sign-ups and price increases, the company is dealing with intense competition in the streaming sector from companies such as Amazon’s Prime Video and Disney+. There's also Skydance , after Paramount’s $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery put HBO Max and Paramount+ under the same roof. Netflix walked away from its offer to buy Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming business in February. The company is also competing for people's attention with YouTube and TikTok, where short videos are extremely popular. New shows and movies coming this quarter include “East of Eden” and season four of “The Diplomat” as well as the sixth and final season of “Emily in Paris.” Netflix also released “La Bola Negra,” a Spanish film about the interconnected lives of three gay men across a history that spans the early 20th century, the Spanish Civil War and the modern day. “La Bola Negra” — which cost $15 million to make — is expected to challenge “The Odyssey” for best picture. Netflix disclosed box office numbers for the movie, for the first time in its history. It made $313,391 over the weekend through Monday with a release in just four theaters. As of Tuesday's close, Netflix's stock is down about 25% for the year to date. Analysts see several factors contributing to its difficulties. “Investors are concerned about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes,” said John Belton, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. events.title: Exclusive: Ramaswamy doubles down on explosive ad featuring rival's mother, despite backlash
events.summary: Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is pouring $4 million into a bombshell ad in which his opponent's estranged mother attacks her daughter — doubling down on the message despite fierce bipartisan backlash, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Ramaswamy is gambling that the deeply personal attack by Amy Acton's mother — who Acton has said sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted Acton when she was 12 — will resonate with voters. After the ad began appearing Tuesday on social media, many fellow Republicans urged Ramaswamy to distance his campaign from it. They warned it could backfire at a time when the controversy over the Epstein files has elevated the sexual abuse of children as a national campaign issue. Driving the news: Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed to Axios that it produced the ad, which began circulating on social media late Monday without language identifying its sponsor. Sources close to Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with "persuadable" voters, prompting the decision to launch a $4 million statewide campaign that began streaming Tuesday night. Catch up quick: The minute-long commercial features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. "She lies about her past," Arthur says. "She's lied her entire life." Arthur also disputes Acton's account of experiencing homelessness as a child. The other side: Acton, a physician, has said she was sexually abused at age 12 by her stepfather, who faced criminal charges, and that her mother sided with him. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. According to her brother, their mother remained married to Acton's alleged abuser until his death. Acton, 60, has said she hasn't seen her mother since childhood. In a statement posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Acton said that "between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me." "I've always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it's sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain." Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, called Ramaswamy's ad "disgusting." What they're saying: Despite bipartisan criticism, Ramaswamy's campaign continued to treat the mother's statements as campaign gold. "This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton. The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing told Axios. Several prominent Republicans and conservative commentators blasted the ad, arguing that it could generate sympathy for Acton. Republican strategist David Urban on CNN drew a parallel to the Epstein controversy, warning that voters are especially sympathetic to victims of sexual assault and that the ad could backfire. "It seems crazy to me one would assume this would work and not backfire," conservative commentator Mary Katharine Ham posted on X. Yes, but: Some conservatives defended the commercial, including Donald Trump Jr., who urged Ohio voters to "watch [it] and think about what it means." By the numbers: A mid-October Marist survey showed Acton leading Ramaswamy 50% to 43% among likely voters. What's next: Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted are set to campaign with Vice President Vance in Cincinnati on Wednesday.

events.title: Football regulator has ‘absolute power’ to force Manchester City sale if verdict upheld
events.summary: IFR chair David Kogan insists regulator has power to act City have appealed against Premier League’s charges The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) will have “absolute power” to force Manchester City’s owners to sell if they are ultimately found to have run the club improperly, the watchdog’s chair has said. Manchester City have been found guilty of circumventing Premier League rules by an independent commission, which found they set up “sham” commercial arrangements to inflate revenues or reduce costs by over £900m over a nine-season period. They were also found to have made “concerted efforts” to “stop and frustrate” the Premier League’s investigation into those arrangements. City have lodged an appeal, claiming the verdict “contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. David Kogan, the chair of the IFR, told podcast The Rest Is Football it was premature to talk about any action his organisation might take while the appeal was ongoing. Kogan did confirm, though, that the IFR had “absolute power” to force a sale by the club’s ownership, if that was felt to be appropriate. “We have the power to ask an owner to step away from a club if we believe that they run a club in a way that is neither fit, fair or done with propriety,” Kogan said. Asked if an owner could refuse to divest, Kogan replied: “No, no, no. We’ve got absolute power to do so.” On the possibility of the IFR investigating City, Kogan said: “I am not going to get pushed into making any judgement on this until we’ve seen all of those questions being answered. Then we will have to decide whether we’re going to mount our own investigation and come to a conclusion on that and what we’re going to do. And pre-empting that would be a colossal mistake.” Manchester City are majority-owned by Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug), an investment vehicle owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family. Kogan has already pledged to resign if there is any political interference in any investigation the IFR may undertake into City, amid concerns it could create a diplomatic issue between the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates. Kogan’s comments came amid fresh scrutiny of Manchester City’s finances by the UK’s accounting watchdog. In a letter to the House of Commons business, innovation, science and trade committee, the Financial Reporting Council (FRC) confirmed it assumed “regulatory consideration” of the matter on 30 September. The FRC said it was examining the independent commission’s findings and making “preliminary enquiries” to establish whether there were grounds for a formal investigation.

events.title: House Democrats forced to make tough choices with limited midterm cash
events.summary: House Democrats' main super PAC is winding down its spending in several races where the party has struggled to make headway despite national trends working in their favor . Why it matters: Democrats' ambitions of winning heavily Republican districts are running into the reality of finite resources at the end of a long and expensive midterm campaign. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and its corresponding super PAC, House Majority PAC, have struggled to keep pace with their GOP counterparts' monster fundraising this cycle. Republicans also have the bonus advantage of a network of cash-rich outside groups, namely President Trump's MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk's America PAC . Driving the news: HMP pulled back its spending this week in three Republican-leaning districts, according to AdImpact and a source familiar with the matter. TN-05: Democrats were bullish about their star recruit, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, until redistricting made the district redder and embattled Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost his primary to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher . HMP has drawn down its ad reservations in the district from nearly $1.6 million this month to a little over $500,000 as of Monday. Trump carried the newly reconstituted 5th district by 21 percentage points in 2024. Cook Political Report rates the race as "solidly Republican." FL-07: Facing a situation similar to Tennessee, Democrats liked their odds of unseating scandal-tarred Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), who lost his primary to former local news anchor Ryan Elijah. Like Molder, Democratic candidate Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff, was a top DCCC recruit and is part of the committee's coveted "Red to Blue" program. HMP essentially halved its investment in the district on Monday, cutting ad reservations from $3.9 million to just $1.95 million. Cook rates the race as "likely Republican," though a poll released by the DCCC on Tuesday had the two candidates tied at 45% each. CO-03: A top target for Democrats when Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) represented it, the seat has become a heavier lift for the party since she abandoned it and Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) took office last year. Democrat Dwayne Romero, a real estate company CEO and Army veteran, is seen by party operatives as having failed to build the kind of momentum shown by Jessica Killin in the neighboring 5th District. HMP halved its investment in this district too, from more than $2.1 million last week to less than $1.1 million as of Monday. Between the lines: The group has also made partial cuts — what it calls "shaves" — in districts where Democrats have struggled to gain traction but still see a glimmer of hope. That includes Arizona's 2nd District, where Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is locked in a rematch with former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in a race Cook rates as "likely Republican." HMP has also taken some money out of Texas' 23rd District, where Republican Brandon Herrera, a right-wing YouTuber, is facing Democratic lawyer Katy Padilla Stout in another race rated "likely Republican." Yes, but: Some HMP triages are in districts where they feel confident the Democratic candidate will prevail. That includes Reps. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.), both of whose races are rated "likely Democratic" by Cook. The PAC has also pulled back in the districts of retiring Reps. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.), which Democrats are increasingly bullish about flipping. The money from these cuts is funneled to districts the party views as more core battlegrounds — including some seats Trump carried by double digits in 2024 that Democrats nevertheless view as winnable. HMP has added at least $4.7 million to its existing investments in nearly two dozen districts over the last two days. What they're saying: Phil Gardner, a senior adviser for Blue Dog Action — a centrist group backing Dalton — told Axios of the cuts in Florida, "I'm not sure what HMP was thinking here." "The rest of the party is not triaging this seat," he said, citing the DCCC's poll and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark's (D-Mass.) plans to campaign there on Wednesday. Gardner said he agrees with "95% of the decisions HMP's made this cycle," but that it is "bonkers they're dumping so much money" into Maine's 2nd District "while leaving one of the party's best recruits high and dry in Florida." Blue Dog Action spent nearly $500,000 to help Dalton win the primary, but it hasn't yet invested any money in the general election. The bottom line: "We're focused on taking back the House," CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for HMP, told Axios in response to Gardner's criticism. Said Gardner: "I'm confident they'll rethink and make the right decision for the final week. Bale can win and hold that seat with everyone's help."

events.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
events.summary: Crime scene evidence is often not enough to identify suspects Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois. The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma. The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found. For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator. The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US. Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases. The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer. They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms. Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual. Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the suspect's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member. "That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime. It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who police say then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year. Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this." Albert Zigler was charged with murder in May The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved. It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations. Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map." Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect. However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed. An Othram scientist prepares a bone for DNA extraction DNA science isn't the only technology that is helping detectives solve cold cases. One of the challenges facing detectives on major investigations like the hunt for Sperino's attacker is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up. Officers investigating her murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993. They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case. The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot. This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence. But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them." Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique." "But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds. While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data. "There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London.

President Trump's son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner will join the meeting virtually. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. Driving the news: Witkoff will arrive in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. The U.S. official said Ukraine "brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail." The official said the parties made "meaningful progress" and now have "strong alignment at the working level" on next steps. Behind the scenes: Kushner joined the meeting virtually and again pressed Trump's demand that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to a source with knowledge. "Jared was very direct," the person said. Zelensky said after the meeting that he's prepared to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow takes reciprocal steps. What he's saying: Trump said on Tuesday that he thinks "Russia would like to get it done" but expressed doubt that Zelensky wants to end the war. "If he does not, it's gonna be a very bad thing," Trump added. "We want Zelensky to make a deal … If they don't make a deal, it's just gonna get worse [for Ukraine]."

events.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry. Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution. Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes. The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53 , which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.” Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes. It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes. Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework , which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said. The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death , the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking . A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls. In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions. Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse. Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all . events.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … It’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call. Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm; Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair; former Tesla CTO JB Straubel; Joe Gebbia; Jack Hartung; James Murdoch; and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing . Neither Musk nor his brother Kimbal Musk is independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance. SpaceX lists six independent directors , including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelof Botha are also considered independent directors. Antonio Gracias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Gracias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Gracias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements. Musk said he supports the idea of the merger but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.” The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said. The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX. events.title: Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX are weighing a $3.5 trillion merger—without him in the room
events.summary: It’s official: Tesla and SpaceX are in talks. Independent board members at the two Elon Musk-led companies have formed special committees to hash over a possible merger, Musk told investors during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call Tuesday. “These special committees consist of independent directors, and because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” said Musk, who was asked about a potential combination during the call. “This is definitely the kind of question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.” Tesla stock rose just over 1% in after hours trading, while SpaceX rose above 5% following the Q&A with Wall Street analysts featuring Musk, SpaceX president and COO Gwynne Shotwell, and chief financial officer Bret Johnsen. Musk said the committees haven’t reached any kind of an agreement on the terms of a potential transaction, and there’s no guarantee that they will. He noted that “some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it.” Musk also has to walk a fine line as a conflicted party. As the CEO of both companies, he owns a roughly 20% stake in Tesla and 45% of SpaceX—and wields control over about 82% of the voting power at the latter. “It’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” said Musk. At the same time, Musk has made clear he believes a tie-up would be a fine idea. He cited collaboration on AI software, chip design, robotics, and connectivity, plus the planned Terafab chip plant, which is a colossal manufacturing complex being developed by SpaceX and Tesla jointly. The committees were formed “at the request of shareholders,” said Musk and on the Tesla side it would need support from a majority of all outstanding shares, which Musk described as “quite a high hurdle.” Tesla filed its annual shareholder proxy report on Monday, and it doesn’t include a merger proposal for shareholders to vote on. Rumors of a tie-up, however, have swirled for months, even before SpaceX’s blockbuster IPO in June. A $3.5 trillion company At Tuesday’s closing prices, a combined Tesla-SpaceX would have a total market value of about $3.5 trillion, with SpaceX at about $2 trillion and Tesla at nearly $1.5 trillion. A formal deal price wouldn’t come until much further down the road, if at all. Musk would own about a third of the combined entity. The companies are already financially entangled, including a $2 billion investment by Tesla in SpaceX, Tesla’s Monday proxy statement confirmed. There are also multiple areas of overlap between the Tesla and SpaceX boards.  Ira Ehrenpreis, founder of venture capital firm DBL Partners, chairs SpaceX’s compensation and nominating committee, which is a single committee at SpaceX, as well as the two separate committees at Tesla. And Tesla board member James Murdoch, who has been a director at the electric-vehicle maker since 2017, testified in a previous legal challenge over Musk’s pay package at Tesla that he had previously invested in SpaceX.  The disclosure from Musk came as SpaceX reported its first operating profit since its June IPO.  Revenues for the third quarter fiscal 2027 year rose 161% to $14.58 billion, well above the $12.86 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. Operating revenue clocked in at $2.79 billion, apnd net income was $4.4 billion.  Revenue from SpaceX’s AI business, which was renamed “Super Intelligence,” nearly tripled from the second quarter to $7.56 billion, surpassing Starlink’s $5.25 billion for the first time since the company went public.  In his usual fashion, Musk offered up aggressively optimistic thoughts about the future of SpaceX, claiming SpaceX’s breakneck buildout pace implies annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, Johnsen reaffirmed a target of $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of this year. At its third-quarter pace, SpaceX is bringing in about $58 billion a year. Hitting the $100 billion figure would take about $8.3 billion of revenue in December, roughly 70% more than its average month last quarter. Musk’s range would require about $42 billion to $83 billion a month by December 2027.  Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Infrastructure startup Fireworks AI is in early talks for new funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion
events.summary: Fireworks AI CEO and co-founder Lin Qiao Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference Fireworks AI is an AI-infrastructure startup founded by former Google and Meta AI engineers. The company is seeking to raise a new round of funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion. Fireworks AI was last valued at nearly $18 billion in July of this year. Fireworks AI is seeking to raise fresh funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after the AI-infrastructure startup was valued at $17.5 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. The potential valuation leap reflects investors' appetite for the companies selling the computing power and tools fueling the AI boom, even as Fireworks AI works through the fallout from a recent security incident. The talks around the financing are still early, and valuation targets could still change. Fireworks declined to comment. Founded in 2022, Fireworks was built by veterans of Meta and Google's AI efforts. Chief executive Lin Qiao previously led the PyTorch team at Meta, while cofounders include former Meta infrastructure engineers and a former leader of Google's Vertex AI. The company rents out computing infrastructure and software that lets businesses run, fine-tune, and deploy open-weight and custom AI models. In July, Fireworks announced a $1.5 billion Series D funding round at a $17.5 billion valuation, led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures, and TCV, with participation from Nvidia, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Menlo Ventures. That round followed a $250 million Series C at a $4 billion valuation in late 2025, co-led by Lightspeed, Index, and Evantic. Last month, The Information reported that Fireworks has been considering a round at a $30 billion. Rather than trying to build a consumer chatbot to rival ChatGPT, Fireworks sells what it calls specialized intelligence: models customized on a customer's proprietary data, workflows, and use cases. The company said in July that it had surpassed $1 billion in annualized revenue and was serving more than 40 trillion tokens a day; it said 95% of those tokens came from models tailored to customers. The company operates in a highly competitive layer of the AI stack. Rivals include model-infrastructure startups such as Together AI, Baseten, and Replicate, as well as cloud giants such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle. The fundraising talks come shortly after a security incident at Fireworks AI. The company said it identified unauthorized use of internal credentials earlier this month that allowed an intruder to access data from some customer accounts. "We take this seriously and will be transparent about what happened and what we find," Qiao posted on X. "I'm personally committed to turn this attack into the most formidable security response in AI Infra." Please send along your tips. events.title: Tesla and SpaceX have set up committees to explore a merger
events.summary: Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX have created committees to discuss a potential merger. Bloomberg/Getty Images SpaceX and Tesla have each established exploratory committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said. Musk, who said he can't participate in the talks, gave the update during Tesla's Q3 earnings call. Musk said he thinks a merger is a good idea, but cautioned investors that shareholder approval is "quite a high hurdle." Houston, we have an update on all that SpaceX-Tesla merger chatter . During SpaceX's Tuesday earnings call , Elon Musk said both of the companies had created "special committees of independent directors" to discuss a potential merger. Musk, who helms both companies and owns billions of dollars in stock of each, said he can't be part of those exploratory groups. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," he said on the call. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this, and particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders." He said clearing that bar would be "quite a high hurdle." It's the most detailed update investors have received yet on the idea of a tie-up, which has been the subject of much chatter since SpaceX went public earlier this year. If the companies ultimately decide to merge, it would further consolidate Musk's business empire, often referred to as Musk Inc. His businesses have been on a consolidation kick. In 2025, xAI acquired Musk's social media company, X (formerly Twitter), and in February, SpaceX acquired xAI . Musk also runs the brain-chip startup, Neuralink, and the tunnel-building firm The Boring Company. Both operate independently, but have had business collaborations within Musk Inc. Tesla and SpaceX's stocks were up in after-hours trading following the news. SpaceX was up around 6.6% and Tesla 1.6%. Musk sees clear benefits in tying the knot "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity," Musk said during the call. SpaceX and Tesla have worked together on a host of projects, including artificial intelligence software , chip design, TeraFab manufacturing efforts, robotics, Starlink satellite connectivity , and SpaceX's ability to launch payloads into orbit, Musk and SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said. The most recent result of that partnership: On Thursday, Tesla demoed its long-awaited Roadster , which includes a version with SpaceX technology. The high-powered sports car's top trim will include cold-gas thrusters. The car launched, hovered, and flipped in the air during the demo. While Musk is for the two companies tying the knot, he said investors shouldn't think it's a sure thing. "I don't think we should necessarily assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty," he added. "That would be overstating it." Read the original article on Business Insider

SpaceX reported spending $16.4 billion on AI-related capex in the third quarter, continuing the acceleration of AI spending seen in recent quarters. SpaceX spent roughly $19.6 billion on overall capital expenditures in the third quarter as Grok maker continues its AI buildout. That was squarely in line with what Wall Street analysts were expecting. Of that $19.6 billion, SpaceX reported spending $16.4 billion on AI-related capex. Analysts were expecting $16.9 billion. SpaceX expects capex to balloon in the current quarter, with CFO Bret Johnsen forecasting $35-$40 billion due to new compute coming online. Johnsen also said SpaceX expects to quickly see returns on its investments. "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year," he said. SpaceX's stock was trading up 4% after hours following the results. The company is broadcasting the earnings call on X, becoming one of a small list of companies to broadcast video of the gathering. Q3 2026 Financial and Operational Results https://t.co/Qrb0qeVG15 — SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 20, 2026 During the earnings call, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that chips are no longer the biggest constraint to AI buildout. "So talking about SpaceX superintelligence, SpaceXSI — "sexy," whatever — so as I think people are starting to realize the constraints on deployment of superintelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips," he said. SpaceX's AI revenue grew significantly quarter-over-quarter to $7.6 billion — ahead of analysts' estimates of $6.3 billion. This report also marks the first quarter since SpaceX purchased Cursor. That revenue means that SpaceX's AI segment officially brought in more revenue than its Starlink business. Starlink brought in $5.2 billion for the quarter. SpaceXAI has since rebranded as SpaceXSI , following Musk's alignment with President Donald Trump's preferred rebranding of "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence." One area where SpaceXSI has found some success is leasing its compute to Anthropic, Google, and Reflection AI. During the company's last earnings call, SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said the leasing arrangements had generated $1.6 billion in additional revenue. Musk said that SpaceX is being inundated with lease requests. "We are also frankly hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute," he said. "So we could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone." Overall, he said the allocation for SpaceX compute is something "that's going to change from one month to the next." events.title: Netflix posts third-quarter earnings beat, but shares fall on advertising and revenue guidance
events.summary: Netflix reported third-quarter earnings per share that surpassed Wall Street expectations and revenue that was in line. The streaming giant in its shareholder letter said, "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," but added, "engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy." Wall Street and investors will be looking for Netflix to provide additional details about the company's strategy following recent organizational changes. Netflix on Tuesday reported third-quarter earnings that topped analyst estimates and revenue that was in line as Wall Street eyes the company's engagement and advertising metrics. Here's how Netflix performed for the period ended Sept. 30, compared with projections from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 87 cents vs. 82 cents estimated Revenue: $12.87 billion vs. $12.87 billion estimated The streamer's revenue was almost 12% higher year over year, boosted by growth in membership and an increase in subscription prices that went into effect in March, the company said. Netflix said the response to those price hikes has been consistent with prior changes and with its expectations. Net income for the quarter was $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, compared with $2.55 billion, or 59 cents a share in the same period last year. Netflix said the year-over-year jump in profit was due in part to the timing of expenses. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise more than 11% to $13.44 billion, driven by growth in memberships, pricing and ad revenue, it said. The company narrowed its 2026 full-year forecast, saying it now expects revenue to reach $51.1 billion, a 13% increase over the year prior. This is on the low end of the range Netflix provided during its previous earnings report of between $51 billion and $51.4 billion and below Wall Street's expectations of $51.2 billion for the year, according to LSEG. Wall Street and investors will be looking for Netflix to provide additional details about the company's strategy following recent organizational changes and headwinds including stagnating viewership and growing competition from the likes of YouTube. "With intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention, strategic clarity and excellent execution are critical," the company said in a shareholder letter Tuesday. "In Q3, we delivered well across all three priorities, but we see room to do even better with focused, continuous improvement." Last week, Netflix said it was laying off about 6% of employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, and that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria was departing from that role. The company said Tuesday it expects its fourth-quarter results to be impacted by those reductions in head count, with a negative impact on operating margin of about 120 basis points. Former Disney executive Peter Rice has been tapped as the new CCO, but it's not yet clear how he'll address concerns around viewership. Netflix in its shareholder letter said, "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," but added, "engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy and … we continue to deliver strong value to members." The company seeks to accelerate growth in those view hours and plans to do so with a three-step strategy, it said: deliver more entertainment value to members; leverage technology to improve all aspects of the service; and improve monetization. Central to Netflix's value offering has been its cheaper, ad-supported tier. Yet, the company on Tuesday lowered its full-year revenue guidance for its ad business. Netflix said it now expects 2026 ad revenue of around $2.7 billion, down from the roughly $3 billion the company had previously forecast. That lower guidance is due to a slower-than-expected rollout of some ad product capabilities, the company said. "Our ads business has delivered really impressive growth since we've launched, and we do see a long road of continued growth ahead of us," co-CEO Greg Peters said on the company's earnings call. "We set big growth targets for our ads business this year. We established an aggressive product road map that was consistent with that strategy. And, just note, I think that the build-out that we've been on is the fastest build-out of a comparable ad stack in our industry, but we are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year." Earlier Tuesday, Netflix announced new features for advertisers that it says will help better connect brands to the right audiences and measure the impact of their ads.

events.summary: Netflix's Ted Sarandos said the streamer needs to step up its US content. Noam Galai/Getty Images Netflix's co-CEO said its US movies and shows need to improve. "We do need better execution in the US," Ted Sarandos told investors. The streaming leader replaced its content chief and film head before its Q3 earnings report. Netflix needs to make better shows and movies in the US, its co-CEO said after its third-quarter earnings report . "We do need better execution in the US," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said on the company's Q3 earnings call on Tuesday. Netflix's global content — including Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia — "is largely working," Sarandos told investors. "The US is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could, or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos said. Netflix's biggest market is the US and Canada, which made up about 44% of its revenue this quarter at $5.6 billion. Next are Europe and the Middle East, followed by Latin America and the Asia-Pacific region. Sarandos said the US "had some really solid doubles and triples this year" but added that "the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs, so that they'll travel around the world." Netflix announced last week that it will be replacing content chief Bela Bajaria , who had overseen the streamer's movies and shows since 2023, with former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice. The streaming giant is also moving on from film chief Dan Lin . Rice will oversee Netflix's movies until the company fills his role. Co-CEO Greg Peters said on the earnings call that Netflix's goal is to take its content slate "from very good to great." Besides subbing out content execs, Netflix also cut roughly 1,000 workers in what was its biggest round of staff reductions since 2022. Netflix shares entered Tuesday's earnings report down about 44% in the last 12 months. The stock fell 6% in after-hours trading following the company's report, which showed a third consecutive quarter of slowing revenue growth. Wall Street has grown concerned about Netflix's engagement growth , especially as the paid streaming leader competes with free streamers like YouTube . "There is a lot to be excited about, but I know that we could do better," Sarandos said. Read the original article on Business Insider
