events.title: 17 actors who transformed into real-life tech company CEOs and founders
events.summary: Elizabeth Holmes (and Amanda Seyfried's portrayal of her) is back in the news. A24; Hulu Amanda Seyfried is making headlines for again playing Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." Seyfried first played the Theranos founder in the Hulu series "The Dropout." She's part of a growing class of actors who've taken part in the latest trend: playing tech moguls. We've all heard of musician and actor biopics — now, it's all about the stories of tech CEOs. These days, startup founders can be just as famous (or infamous) as any other celebrity, and the dramatic lives they've lived in business or at home make great fodder for TV and film. To play these figures, some of the best-known actors had to ditch their signature looks to take on Steve Jobs ' turtleneck and wire-frame glasses, Elizabeth Holmes ' red lipstick and frizzy blowout, or SBF's signature curls. Here are 17 celebrities who transformed to play some of Silicon Valley's most prominent figures. Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in 'The Dropout' and 'You Can See Everything' Hulu; David Orrell/CNBC/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/ Getty Images In the 2022 Hulu limited series " The Dropout , Seyfried played Holmes from her time at Stanford in 2003 (when she did the titular dropping out) through the fall of her company, Theranos, after The Wall Street Journal's 2015 exposé. Theranos purported to manufacture a device that could do a litany of blood tests from a single finger prick, but, infamously, it did not work as promised. In 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison after being convicted of defrauding investors. Four years after the Hulu series, comedian and documentarian Nathan Fielder asked Seyfried to once again play Holmes in some reenactments he wanted to do in his doc about her final days before prison, " You Can See Everything ." We won't say much else besides that you need to see it to believe everything that goes down. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in 'Artificial' Neon; Mike Coppola/Getty Images for TIME "After the Hunt" wasn't enough for Garfield and director Luca Guadagnino — the two have since teamed up to tell the story of OpenAI CEO and cofounder Altman. " Artificial ," which is set for release in select theaters on Christmas Day, will focus on Altman's 2023 firing by cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) and subsequent rehiring one week later. Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Reckoning' Sony Pictures Releasing; David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images "Succession" star Jeremy Strong played the Facebook founder in " The Social Reckoning ," a film about the release of Facebook Files , a staggering number of internal documents leaked by whistleblower and employee Frances Haugen and published by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, and the subsequent congressional scrutiny that followed. The film, released in October 2026, was written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, the screenwriter of "The Social Network," making this something of a sequel to the 2010 classic. Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Network' Sony Pictures Releasing; Adam Berry/Bloomberg/Getty Images "The Social Reckoning" wasn't the first time Zuckerberg has been portrayed on screen — most famously, Eisenberg played the founder in " The Social Network ," which chronicled the earliest days of Facebook, back when it still had a "the" in front of it. It juxtaposes the wild, early days of the website with two lawsuits Zuckerberg settled a few years later: one from cofounder Eduardo Saverin and another from his Harvard classmates, the Winklevoss twins. Justin Timberlake as Sean Parker in 'The Social Network' Sony Pictures Releasing; Ramin Talaie/Corbis/Getty Images The other famous "disruptor" portrayed in "The Social Network" is Parker, one of the cofounders of Napster , the original music streaming platform. He's played by Timberlake in a career-best performance. Parker comes in as an early believer and executive at Facebook, which ruffles the feathers of cofounder Eduardo Saverin. Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in 'The Altruists' Netflix; Craig Barritt/Getty Images for CARE For Special Children Sam Bankman-Fried , also known as SBF, will get the biopic-miniseries treatment this November on Netflix in a series titled "The Altruists." Bankman-Fried co-founded the crypto trading firm Alameda Research in 2017 and later co-founded the cryptocurrency exchange FTX in 2019. After making millions, FTX collapsed in 2022 , and Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted of several crimes , including fraud and money laundering, in 2024. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison. SBF's onetime girlfriend and former CEO of the FTX-affiliated trading firm Alameda Research, Caroline Ellison , will also be in the show, portrayed by Julia Garner. Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Travis Kalanick in 'Super Pumped' Showtime; D Dipasupil/FilmMagic/Getty Images Gordon-Levitt played Uber cofounder and former CEO Kalanick in "Super Pumped," a 2022 Showtime limited series. It focuses on the rise of Kalanick and his eventual fall from power, culminating in his 2017 resignation from the company. Ashton Kutcher as Steve Jobs in 'Jobs' Open Road Films; Tom Munnecke/Getty Images The first mention of Jobs on this list goes to Kutcher, who played the Apple founder in the 2013 biopic "Jobs." It traces his career from Apple's founding in 1976 to the introduction of the first iPod in 2001. Michael Fassbender as Steve Jobs in 'Steve Jobs' Universal Pictures; William STEVENS/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images Two years after "Jobs," the late founder was portrayed again on screen, this time by Michael Fassbender in "Steve Jobs." Instead of a standard cradle-to-grave biopic, " Steve Jobs " checks in with the enigmatic figure at three different points in his career: first in 1984, before the introduction of the first Apple Macintosh computer; second, in 1988, when Jobs is the head of a new company, NeXT, and is preparing to launch its first computer; and finally, in 1998, as Jobs gears up to release the iMac. Noah Wyle as Steve Jobs in 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' TNT; Matthew NAYTHONS/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images In 1999, the TV movie "Pirates of Silicon Valley" aired, starring Wyle as the Apple founder. It chronicles Jobs' career from the '70s to the '90s, from the founding of Apple to his return as CEO. Anthony Michael Hall as Bill Gates in 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' TNT; Doug Wilson/CORBIS/Corbis/Getty Images The other half of the "Pirates of Silicon Valley" narrative focuses on Gates, the cofounder of Microsoft . He's played by "Breakfast Club" star Anthony Michael Hall. The film's climax is based on the real-life falling out Gates and Jobs had in 1985, when Jobs felt that Gates had ripped off Apple. events.title: Mamdani takes on AI chatbot ‘doom loops’ in New York
events.summary: New York City could be the first place in the country where consumers are protected from a “doom loop” of AI-powered customer service chatbots, per a rule proposed today by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration. The rule would require businesses to connect people to a human customer service agent quickly if a chatbot cannot fulfill their requests. “When corporations force you to fight your way through an endless doom loop of AI-generated responses to speak to another human being, they’re stealing your time, money, and patience,” Mamdani said in a release. “This rule makes clear: Customer service cost-cutting can’t come at New Yorkers’ expense.” Businesses would have to disclose when customers are talking to AI and offer an “easy off-ramp” to a human representative, with violators subject to fines that would start at $525. At the helm of Mamdani’s consumer protection efforts are several Biden administration alumni: Samuel Levine, commissioner of the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, previously led the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection under the agency’s then-chair Lina Khan, and Deputy Mayor Julie Su was acting labor secretary during the Biden era. Khan is also part of Mamdani’s administration, serving as board chair of the city’s Economic Development Board. — Ashley Gold

events.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
events.summary: Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. One word: bonkers The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide. events.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
events.summary: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago. A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out. Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations. The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds. District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case". "Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order. The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri. In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12. However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing. The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help. The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue". Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022. events.title: Trump goes full apocalypse in anti-Dems midterms message
events.summary: President Trump is escalating his doomsday warnings about a Democratic takeover of Congress, painting a nightmarish vision of an America consumed by burning cities, economic collapse, mutilated children and the destruction of Western civilization. Why it matters: Trump has long portrayed Democrats as an existential threat to the country. But in an effort to preserve Republicans' grip on Washington, he's taking that rhetoric to new extremes as he casts the election as a choice between Republican rule and national catastrophe. At the same time, Trump is offering voters a financial incentive to keep Republicans in power: $5,000 checks for every adult American citizen if the GOP retains control of Congress. The pledge would cost more than $1 trillion and has no clear path to becoming reality. What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Axios in a statement. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Reality check: Even if Democrats take control of Congress, Trump will remain president and retain veto power over legislation they pass. Here's what he's been telling voters. America will burn like France On Monday night, Trump told Kansas voters that under Democrats, America will burn like France, which is facing widespread student and union protests over public spending cuts and deficit concerns, per Reuters . "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America." Trump has blamed the riots in France on immigration , suggesting that border policies under Democratic Party leadership would unleash the same chaos in America. Yes, but: The unrest in France has been driven by disputes over living costs and public funding. There's no evidence that Democrats in the U.S. want to take up similar forms of violence. America will fall into another Great Depression Trump predicts Democrats will cause economic catastrophe and trigger a depression similar to the one that began in 1929. "If the Democrats win you will have a 1929-style economic depression," Trump told Tennessee voters on Saturday. "I hope I'm wrong on that." By the numbers: Unemployment peaked at roughly 25% during the Great Depression, compared with about 4% today. What's next: House Democrats, should they gain power, plan to repeal Trump's tariff policy, bring back Affordable Care Act tax breaks and undo Medicaid cuts as part of a general affordability push. Democrats will "mutilate your children" In Arizona, Trump warned last week that Democrats want to "mutilate, cut your children." "I mean, they can do whatever they want, and they do. Your son leaves as Jimmy and comes back home in three days as Janet, and they don't even ask you," Trump said . "They can take your child out of school and do whatever the hell they want." Reality check: Trump's claims about schools secretly performing gender-transition procedures misrepresent how such medical care works. Schools cannot perform gender-transition surgeries. Those operations take place in medical settings under relevant state laws. Democrats will "get rid of the border" Trump warned Democrats would dismantle the border and allow criminals from around the world to enter the U.S. He told voters in Kansas that "the Dumocrat agenda is a plan to extinguish Western civilization. They want to open the borders." Trump claimed prisons around the world will empty prisoners into the United States. The other side: A coalition of Democrats have proposed using advanced technology to protect the border, while rejecting mass deportation strategies. Trump: Democrats will take your guns — and wild animals will feast Trump also warned that Democrats will "take away your guns" if they control Congress. "You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like eating you," he told voters in Montana. "... They would gain a lot of weight." Context: Mainstream Democrats have not called for repealing the Second Amendment. While some Democrats support banning certain types of guns, that's different from eliminating the constitutional right to own firearms. Democrats will destroy farms Trump also warned that Democrats would "decimate Kansas farms." On Monday, the Trump administration announced $8 billion in relief for farmers facing soaring fuel costs, driven in part by Trump's own policies and the Iran war. What's going on: Democrats have been making a push in farm country by appealing to rural voters in Kansas and Iowa . House Democrats have also proposed expanding support for rural development and family farms .

GM is closing a battery-assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch. events.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
events.summary: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies. The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August. The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers. The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses". The White House has been contacted for comment. Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border. Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry. "These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday. The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks. That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises". The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 31 August The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338. Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol. It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began. Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said. The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada. "The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said. The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection. It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year. Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear". events.title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
events.summary: Fresh data points from September showed the housing market continues to deteriorate just as the Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates again. Building permits, new starts and pending sales all were considerably worse than Wall Street forecasts. Under some circumstances, Fed officials would use easier policy to spur demand. However, the central bank is currently battling inflation, which it could prioritize over a flagging housing picture. The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist. Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates. Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage. "The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze." The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%. Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday. Privately owned housing starts fell at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data. Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023. "Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates." The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily . Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices. Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years. Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs. But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009. Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing. However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months." Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall. The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels.

events.title: 'Dark fleet' under spotlight in latest US move to ease rising energy costs
events.summary: The US is turning to an unlikely saviour in its latest efforts to ease rising energy prices: the “ dark fleet ” that it has spent years sanctioning. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright revealed the administration's latest endeavour on Monday, telling those at a New York event that Washington wants to “move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet'". The dark fleet, sometimes referred to as the shadow fleet, refers to a group of ships that sail outside conventional shipping regulations. These vessels use deceptive shipping practices to transport cargo that is under sanctions or high risk, deliberately concealing it to avoid detection. Estimates on the size of the fleet vary. Mr Wright said he believes there are about 1,600 vessels. Data from TankerTrackers set the number at 1,480 active ships, while maritime company Windward said it has identified 1,100 dark fleet vessels. The dark fleet has grown in recent years after sanctions were imposed on Russian oil in response to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. Many of these vessels are past the 15-year threshold that marks the point at which technical failures begin to mount, adding to environmental safety risks. Mr Wright said the administration's plan would involve investors buying and refurbishing these idle sanctioned vessels before using them to transport legitimate oil. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more,” he said. The US has delisted sanctioned vessels before. In March, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control removed sanctions on the Panama-flagged crude oil supertanker Kiara M, which had been placed as part of the Trump administration's pressure campaign on Venezuela . This morning, U.S. military forces, in support of the Department of Homeland Security, apprehended… pic.twitter.com/UPADtiw681 — U.S. Southern Command (@Southcom) January 20, 2026 Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University's Centre on Global Energy Policy, said the move does little to address the security issue facing seafarers today in the Strait of Hormuz. At least 15 container ships have been struck in the waterway in the past 10 days. “You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets,” Mr Nephew said. War risk insurance premiums have surged since the start of the conflict. Rates have climbed to as high as 10 per cent of hull value, compared to 0.25 per cent before the conflict, adding millions to the premiums ship and cargo owners pay. Mr Wright's comments also come less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russian diesel in an agreement with President Vladimir Putin. Mr Trump said the agreement would include Moscow supplying millions of barrels of diesel to US and global markets. You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets Richard Nephew, senior research scholar at Columbia University With only two weeks until the US midterm elections on November 3, diesel prices at the pump have risen to more than $6 a gallon [$1.59 a litre] on average, compared to about $3 the same time last year. Wholesale diesel prices passed $200 a barrel in Singapore in mid-September and hit all-time highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US, the International Energy Agency said in an October 14 report. The seven-day moving average for tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz was seven vessels for the week ending September 18, a small fraction of its pre-war levels, according to the International Monetary Fund's PortWatch monitor. Analysts at Kpler estimate only 24 of the about 160 vessels under sanctions from the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. “If this is about getting ships out of sanctions, fine, no problem, proceed as you wish. If this is about solving the problem with whether we can get enough diesel and other products to market, this is not it," Mr Nephew said.

events.title: If Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catch
events.summary: Elon Musk posted on X that he will give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year. The world's richest person appeared to suggest that he would use the Trump Account program to make this historic gift. Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X . Posts from the White House and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also referenced Musk's gift as benefiting Trump Accounts. But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached. Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble. Treasury's temporary regulations, subject to revision after public comment, aim to encourage stock gifts. But they also give donors unusual influence over children's investments, according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 In the broader world of charitable giving, donors can typically express preferences about how their gifts are managed, but the receiving organization or trustee retains final authority, said Carolyn Schenck, an attorney and former national fraud counsel at the IRS. Under the new Trump Account rules, however, it's "the donor that's dictating the terms of the gift," she said. Representatives for Musk, Gerstner and the Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the proposed gift. According to the Treasury, about 70 million Trump Accounts have been created, including more than 60 million through a recent auto-enrollment effort . Trump Accounts are available to all children with U.S. citizenship under age 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Musk would be the second philanthropist to publicly announce a stock pledge to Trump Accounts: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell pledged earlier this summer to use the Trump Account program to gift some 2 million shares . That gift has not yet been distributed. What stock sale restrictions mean for children Trump Account beneficiaries do not have the latitude to sell under circumstances that other investors might otherwise. Under the new rules, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Before then, early sales are permitted only in limited circumstances, such as certain corporate transitions or when the stock is formally delisted from a national securities exchange — not when financial or legal problems emerge that might prompt an investor to sell. "Giving families more choices and more ability to hold the assets that they think are best for them and their kids' future ... would be a good thing," said Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. "But this is not really that, because you have no choice in the asset that is being deposited into your child's account, and then you also have no ability to sell it for the five-year holding period." The temporary regulations also mandate that if any gifted stock is sold too early, the trustee must purchase the same number and class of shares "as soon as practicable." This increases beneficiaries' risk of loss if the share price rises before the trustee repurchases the stock, according to Schenck. Beneficiaries would ultimately bear that cost. "If the fiduciary makes an investment mistake, then the focus is typically restoring value to the beneficiary. But here, the focus seems to be restoring the specific security itself," said Schenck, who left the IRS in 2025 for law firm Caplin & Drysdale. CNBC has learned the buyback provision is intended to quickly correct trading errors, though the regulations do not explicitly state that purpose or limit the requirement to accidental sales. Donor incentives behind the holding rule The temporary regulations cite donor interests.

events.title: What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?
events.summary: Decision has implications for household energy bills, the UK economy and the climate crisis UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea About four years and six energy secretaries after it was given the green light, the Jackdaw gasfield has been given consent to begin production 150 miles east of Aberdeen. So what does this long-awaited decision mean for the Labour party, household bills, the economy and the climate crisis? Does this break a Labour manifesto promise? No, because although the party vowed to “not issue new licences to explore new fields” in the hydrocarbon-rich basin, it made clear it would honour licences granted before it came to power. These fields include Jackdaw, which was granted a licence in 2022 , and the larger Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, which was approved the following year . Oil and gas licences give broad permission to explore an area for fossil fuels but consent is still needed to extract them. Although Jackdaw and Rosebank had both, they were blocked from starting production after a legal challenge by campaigners at Greenpeace and Uplift early last year. That ruling compelled the companies behind the project to resubmit their applications with extra information on the climate impact of the fuels produced. Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norway’s state oil company, Equinor. Adura also hopes to develop Rosebank in conjunction with Ithaca Energy. A decision on Rosebank’s new application for consent is expected soon. Will the Jackdaw decision lower energy bills? Probably not. Household bills are based on the price of gas in the UK wholesale market, which is determined by international prices that have surged amid disruptions to global supplies. These have included the loss of Russian flows to Europe and disruption to Gulf exports to buyers around the world – shocks far too big for the relatively small output from Jackdaw to outweigh. The Tories have claimed drilling could still help to lower bills under their plans to use tax revenues to cut VAT on gas and electricity bills for three years. However, this does not mean energy costs are fundamentally lower – or sustainable. Meanwhile, Labour has cut VAT from electricity bills from this month until next March and ministers are understood to be planning to offer billions in energy bill support for low-income households at next week’s budget. What about the UK’s carbon emissions? Gas from Jackdaw could release between 23.6m and 35.8m tonnes of CO 2 equivalent over its 11-year operational lifespan, but the carbon impact of new North Sea fields is “not clear cut”. That’s the view of the Committee on Climate Change (CCC), which advises the government on meeting its legally binding climate targets. There are two sorts of emission to consider: firstly the “scope 1 and 2” kind, created from getting fossil fuels out of the ground and transporting them to users. These are relatively low in the British North Sea and make up about 3% of the UK’s total. In fact, the CCC has said there might be “emissions advantages” to the switch because scope 1 and 2 emissions from UK gas are by some estimates four times lower than from US and Gulf fossil gas imports. The second, far bigger impact is from the “scope 3” emissions created from burning the fossil fuel. Although Jackdaw’s gas would release CO 2 when used in homes, businesses, factories and power plants, there is no evidence it would lead to higher overall gas consumption. As Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in July : “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.” A better way to reduce UK emissions would be to replace gas boilers and fossil fuel vehicles with electric alternatives powered by low-carbon sources. What about the impact on global emissions? Here too, the answer is unclear. Some academics have suggested that more UK oil and gas would push up fossil fuel production globally unless output fell elsewhere. In 2024, the CCC said new fossil fuel developments would have a “minimal impact on UK carbon budgets” but that if others followed the UK’s lead in increasing production the cumulative impact could lead to “an oversupply that would pose a risk” to international targets. It urged the UK government to “reassess whether further exploration for new sources of fossil fuels” was aligned with its global climate obligations. This supports the government’s ban on new licences but would not rule out Jackdaw – which is not a new source. Moreover, a global oversupply of fossil fuels does not necessarily lead to greater emissions. In 2025, China’s crude oil imports hit a record 11m barrels a day but its emissions continued to fall because it was building its crude stocks to a record high of 1.4bn barrels. In short, emissions are largely due to energy consumption, not energy production.

events.title: Mystery mailings put Congress and election offices on edge
events.summary: Over three dozen congressional lawmakers and election offices in at least 32 states have been targeted with suspicious letters, many containing a white powder. Why it matters: The letters have forced evacuations and disrupted election offices just weeks before the 2026 midterms , raising concerns about political intimidation . Driving the news: Rep. Adam Smith's (D-Wash.) district office received a letter Monday, prompting staff to evacuate. In an emailed statement, Smith's office confirmed it "received a suspicious letter containing a powdery substance, like others sent to Congressional offices across the country." Staff returned to the office Tuesday. What they're saying: "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices, and Congressional offices," an FBI spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident." Catch up quick: The U.S. Capitol Police, the House and Senate sergeants at arms and other officials sent notices to congressional offices last week warning about letters containing suspicious substances and urging staffers to be vigilant. Over 100 letters were estimated to be circulating around the country, law enforcement sources told ABC News. The USCP referred Axios to the FBI for comment. Here's what we know about the suspicious letters: Who was targeted At least three dozen lawmakers have been targeted with the letters, including both Democrats and Republicans. That includes prominent leaders such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.). Election offices in at least 32 states were targeted with similarly suspicious letters, according to WIRED . Authorities intercepted many of the letters, including those addressed to election offices in Ohio , Minnesota and Connecticut . But in places like Oklahoma , Arizona and Delaware , the letters arrived and prompted evacuations. What's inside Many letters contained a white powder-like substance. So far, preliminary testing of the powder has found no hazardous materials. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also reported receiving suspicious letters but did not disclose their contents. Nebraska officials received a letter that they didn't open and instead turned over to the FBI for further analysis. Flashback: The Capitol Police's notice went out on the 25th anniversary of the anthrax attacks that terrified Capitol Hill in the wake of 9/11. On Oct. 15, 2001, a staffer opened an anthrax-laced letter in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle's office, forcing the Hart Senate Office Building to close for months. Anthrax attacks killed five people that year. Where are they coming from Law enforcement has not yet determined where the letters are coming from or if they're part of a coordinated attack. The FBI declined to say if the letters are linked, nor are they confirming "specific instances or letters." However, the bureau told Axios in an emailed statement it is working to identify whoever sent the letters. Worth noting: Some of the letters claimed to come from the Democratic Socialists of America, the left-wing insurgent organization that denies any involvement. Some letters bore a New York City return address that DSA previously used but has not occupied since 2013, a spokesperson said . DSA did not respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs. PyTorch is the popular open source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects. Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no rewriting of their apps. Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it’s going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default. Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM), RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does. Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite , to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops, and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps. None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Steven Bartlett started ‘The Diary of a CEO’ with a $100 microphone. Now he says it’s on track for $60 million in annual revenue
events.summary: Steven Bartlett started his podcast with just a laptop and a sock pulled over a $100 microphone. Before there were guests, it was just Bartlett, reading from his diary at 2 a.m. and trying to make sense of what he had written that week. He eventually began interviewing other people about theirs. Now, The Diary of a CEO is one of the world’s biggest podcasts and is on track to overtake Joe Rogan as the most-subscribed podcast on YouTube. The show has grown into a business Bartlett forecasts will generate about $60 million in revenue this year. But growing it has also meant turning down money—including a deal that would have required more advertising and taking the show off YouTube. He described the proposed arrangement as a trade: Accept a large payment, put 12 advertisements in the podcast, and have little say over those ads. “One of the central reasons why I turned down such an offer is because that is four times more ads than I have to put in now,” Bartlett told Fortune’ s Ellie Austin on Fortune Daily . Working with what he calls “fragmentation vultures”—companies seeking exclusive podcast distribution deals—can mean sacrificing revenue or control over the relationship with an audience, Bartlett argued. Instead, he sees the relationship with his audience as worth protecting, even when a lucrative offer like that comes along. The business he aims to preserve already makes money beyond advertising through products, subscriptions, and events. Beyond the podcast ad Bartlett, who dropped out of college to pursue entrepreneurship, launched The Diary of a CEO in 2017 by turning his own diary entries into podcast episodes. He later began interviewing other people about their own diaries, finding it more intellectually stimulating to learn about their own lives than to read about his own. Those conversations explored his guests’ motivations, insecurities, and ambitions, eventually broadening the show’s scope to subjects ranging from neuroscience and psychology to performance and sports.  And with it, the business has expanded too. When asked where the show’s projected $60 million comes from, Bartlett pointed to brand partnerships, products his business owns and manufactures, subscriptions, memberships, and events. On top of that, he runs an investment fund.  “It’s a wide range of things and again, this goes to the point of diversification,” he said. Steven.com, Bartlett’s holding company, houses the podcast and his other creator businesses. It also includes other creators, helping them build media brands and develop products and ventures. Bartlett forecasts about $90 million in revenue for his broader media company this year, including the projected $60 million from The Diary of a CEO . He also put next year’s holding-company forecast at about $160 million. But he’s not the only person to see nine-figure valuations as a result of the podcasting business: Call Her Daddy podcast host Alex Cooper’s holding company Unwell raised investment at a $500 million valuation in August . Bartlett sees that evolution as part of a wider shift of how creators work with brands. Early in his career, he said companies treated influencers like billboards: Pay them, and they would post something. Then came the creative-director titles, equity arrangements, and opportunities to cofound businesses. That is most evident with Sydney Sweeney, who became an equity partner and creative director at sports prediction market Novig, shaping its advertising rather than just simply appearing in it. He believes the next stage involves creator businesses making acquisitions and operating more like large holding companies.  “You’re no longer an influencer, you’re no longer an equity partner, a creative director,” he said. “You are an owner or cofounder.” The business of audience trust Distribution has become a point of negotiation across podcasting, perhaps most famously in 2024, when Spotify ended Rogan’s exclusivity and allowed his show to stream on rival platforms. Bartlett prefers fewer partnerships, and only with businesses that matter to him personally. About 70% of his podcast partners, he said, are companies whose founders he approached himself.  Choosing sponsors is only one part of maintaining audience trust—what guests say on the podcast matters too. On Fortune Daily, he was questioned about a 2024 BBC investigation into health claims made on his show. He said his team had contracted a full-time medical PhD to review health episodes, adding context on screen and removing material that could not adequately be contextualized. Now, an independent review team fact-checks every episode —not just those focused on health—before it is published.  When asked whether an unsupported scientific statement would be removed from the audio, he said the decision depends on its framing: A definitive claim would be treated differently from a guest discussing a hypothesis based on early research. But despite his growing influence, Bartlett doesn’t consider himself a journalist. He described his interviews as an exercise in pursuing his own curiosity, whether he’s sitting across from Kamala Harris or JD Vance. Viewers will always have questions they wish he had asked, he said, but he believes his approach needs to remain anchored in that curiosity. “If you’re not anchored to, like, your own curiosity, you’re going to be a plastic bag in the wind,” he said. As the business continues to grow, Bartlett’s advice to other creators is to think beyond the next deal—while acknowledging that his own success gives him more freedom to choose.  “If you want to build a durable business in this creator economy, you have to prioritize sovereignty,” he said. “You’re renting your audience at the moment.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices. Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time. The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat. The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations . Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled. OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting. Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results. With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats. OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN. Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings. Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT
events.summary: Former New York Mayor Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democratic candidates in November's midterm elections, The New York Times reported. The billionaire's contributions are part of a Democratic effort to regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections. President Donald Trump has vowed to spend $400 million to help Republican candidates this election cycle. Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democrats regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections, The New York Times reported Tuesday, citing his team. Shortly after The Times published its article about Bloomberg's campaign spending, his fellow billionaire, President Donald Trump , in a social media post reiterated his vow to spend $400 million to boost Republican candidates. The dueling announcements came as Republicans are increasingly worried about retaining their majorities in both chambers of Congress. Many political analysts expect Democrats to win control of the House, and multiple polls show Democrats within reach of winning a majority of seats in the Senate. Bloomberg "is of the view that resources matter in campaigns," his political advisor Howard Wolfson told The Times. Bloomberg, a former New York City mayor, "expects a result," Wolfson said. With the $80 million in spending, Bloomberg is among the top five largest individual Democratic donors according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings for the 2025-2026 election cycle. Wolfson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Before Tuesday's announcement, Bloomberg was known to have donated $23 million to Democrats and affiliated causes this election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records through Tuesday. As of the beginning of October, Bloomberg had put $11 million behind a super PAC supporting Micah Lasher in New York's 12th Congressional District and $2.5 million toward Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's reelection, according to campaign-finance records . Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Trump, in a Truth Social post, said that he and his affiliated political action committee have spent more than $300 million to help Republican candidates with advertising, voter contacts, rallies and turnout efforts. Trump promised that his spending will top $400 million by Election Day, Nov. 3. FEC filings as of Tuesday afternoon so far show roughly $200 million in identifiable spending and ad reservations tied to Trump's political operation, leaving a gap between what's publicly visible and Trump's broader claim. In September, Trump said he had " close to a billion dollars " in his super PAC, MAGA Inc., and planned to spend $400 million to $500 million on the midterms. At the time, MAGA Inc. reported about $403 million in cash on hand — less than half the amount Trump cited.

events.title: At least $963K in trading cards were stolen from a FedEx truck in California
events.summary: Police in California are investigating the theft of trading cards worth at least $963,000 from a FedEx truck SANTA ANA, Calif. -- Police in California are investigating the theft of trading cards worth at least $963,000 that were taken from a FedEx truck parked outside of a company that verifies memorabilia. The truck was broken into on Oct. 13 near Professional Sports Authenticator, also known as PSA, which authenticates trading cards, autographs, comic books, and other memorabilia and grades their condition, Santa Ana Police Department spokesperson Natalie Garcia said in a news release. Pokémon and sports cards were among the items that were stolen, the release said. The driver had left the truck unattended, Garcia said in a follow-up email Tuesday. How long the driver was gone is part of the investigation, she said. The truck's lock was gone and two pallets were taken, she said. A third pallet was disturbed. “The estimated value of the stolen cards at the time of the incident was $963,000. However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined,” Garcia said in the news release. Nick Andrews, a card collector near Boston, told The Associated Press the value of what was taken could be much higher. PSA's parent company, Collectors, said it has “deactivated the certificates for the stolen cards and notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items.” The company also said it contacted affected customers directly and arranged for compensation based on fair market value. Both FedEx and Collectors said they are working with law enforcement. “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority,” FedEx spokesperson David Westrick said in a statement. FedEx referred additional questions to police. They were worried they would never see them again or receive proper compensation. Andrews, who collects vintage sports and Pokémon cards, told the AP in a phone interview that he was not affected by the theft but has heard from at least two dozen people who were. “Thousands of cards, most likely, and millions of dollars, most likely,” he said of the losses collectors suffered. He said one person who submitted cards for grading on behalf of several people told him that they lost half a million dollars in declared value. PSA's parent company did not get into specifics on losses in its statement. “We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset,” the statement from Collectors said. “Our team is focused on supporting them. We take this incident seriously, and we will continue working with law enforcement to hold those responsible accountable." events.title: Right after my ex and I broke up, I started packing my things. Then, we decided to continue living together.
events.summary: I've been living with my ex while saving money and building a life abroad. Aaliyah Alexander I was living with my boyfriend when we broke up, and he suggested that we stay roommates. After looking into my options, I realized that living together might be the best financial move. It was awkward at first, but acknowledging the situation and setting boundaries helped. I met my ex in Spain, on a warm October night in 2024. He approached me as we were both walking home from a boxing class and confidently started a conversation. About two weeks later, we went on our first date . A few months after that, we took our first weekend trip together. In April, he surprised me with a key to his home. By June, I'd moved in. Our relationship was built on genuine care for one another. Throughout our relationship, we always sought to support each other's well-being and growth. Of course, we had bumps here and there, but they were never significant enough to change our respect for each other. That's why, when we agreed to break up in August because we saw our lives going in different directions, I wasn't at all surprised that we found a way to continue living together. We broke up, but I stayed at my ex's house I normally wouldn't have continued living with an ex, but it felt like the best option. Aaliyah Alexander Under normal circumstances, I would've moved out as soon as possible. I've always believed that you can't start to heal from a breakup until you cut all ties and communication with your ex. So, I bought the boxes, tape, and bubble wrap, started looking for apartments , and began packing. But then two weeks later, I lost a freelance contract that contributed a significant portion to my income. This, coupled with the fact that I was already in the middle of a lengthy visa process to make Spain my long-term home, only added to the stress of going through a breakup. Seeing the distress I was enduring, my ex sat me down and suggested that I continue to live with him until I was able to get back on my feet again. My first thought was that people would think I was out of my mind for choosing to live with an ex . Then, I started weighing the pros and the cons. If I stayed, housing would be one less thing I'd have to worry about … but every day, I would have to see someone I'd just broken up with. Worst of all, I'd have to treat my ex like a roommate, as if we didn't just spend the past two years in an affectionate relationship. If I decided to move out, I wouldn't have to see my ex every day, and I could focus on healing my broken heart alone — but I'd be in a tough financial situation. Unlike my ex — who's lenient and open to pulling some extra weight when I can't make rent or contribute 50/50 on utilities — I knew that a landlord wouldn't necessarily care about my personal situation once the first of the month rolled around. I chose to keep living with him. At first, there was an adjustment period Having honest conversations and setting boundaries helped. Aaliyah Alexander Those first few weeks were awkward. We'd already had separate bedrooms because of my ex's insomnia, but the changes to our routines and interactions felt foreign. Instead of getting a text inviting me to come cuddle with him on Sunday mornings, my phone remained silent. Instead of getting ready and walking to the gym together in the afternoon, I started going in the morning. Instead of sitting down to have dinner together, we ate at different times in different rooms. Whenever we saw each other, we would force a smile, say hi, and go our separate ways. We didn't acknowledge the strangeness of our situation until one moment broke down the barrier. I was used to having crying sessions in my room, but this time, one snuck up on me while I sat in the living room. The stress of my breakup, finances, and living situation had just built up too much. My ex was passing through the living room when he saw me crying and gently asked if he could give me a hug. I nodded. This interaction prompted us to finally discuss the elephant in the room (well, house): Living with your ex is weird. Simply addressing the situation and talking about how we were both coping instantly made it feel a little bit lighter. We found a new way to live together What followed was a conversation about how we wanted living together to look like. We knew we were doing something unusual, which was daunting, but also meant we were free to make our own rules. Our first decision was to stop acting like strangers. Barely acknowledging each other's existence just didn't work for us, so we welcomed a level of friendliness into our new relationship. Then, we decided we'd continue offering each other a certain level of emotional support. My ex recently took a leave of absence from work to heal from burnout and contemplate his next career move. Meanwhile, I was struggling to find full-time work and sustain the life I was building abroad. Being there for each other when one of us needed a listening ear felt important. Lastly, we agreed not to cross any lines that would confuse the other person. We weren't in a romantic relationship anymore, so we decided that any affection beyond a friendly hug would be prohibited. With this, our living situation went from something that felt unbearable to something that works for us. In the next few months, I plan to save enough from my freelance work to move out. Until then, I'm happy knowing I have a home, even if it's with my ex. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
events.summary: Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts. The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday. Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online. The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience. "We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening. They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard , external , where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally. Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres. In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London. It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b. These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest. The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings. Banks appeared to be among the most badly affected, with customers reporting problems ranging from being unable to access funds abroad to struggling to complete a property purchase. Rachael Ellen, 25, a Revolut customer from Glasgow, told BBC News she was left unable to access her money. "Today I was unable to pay for my parking at a shopping centre because my Revolut account wasn't working properly," she told the BBC. "This left me in a difficult situation as I had no way to access the money I needed at the time." She said the outage also meant she could not view a transaction from a relative and was told by the app's help bot that there were no pending incoming transactions. "It's frustrating not knowing where the payment is or when I'll receive it," Rachael added. Rachael Ellen said the outage caused her "real inconvenience" when she couldn't access her funds on Revolut More than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services were flagged to platform outage monitor shortly after 08:00 BST on Tuesday. A spokesperson for the company said some Revolut services were disrupted earlier as a result of the Google Cloud outage. "We can confirm that services are now fully restored. Our customers' money and data are safe and remained safe throughout. "We apologise for any inconvenience caused." Customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by the Lloyds Banking Group - also reported issues affecting some online banking services. A Lloyds spokesperson did not confirm the cause of issues affecting some of its services, but told the BBC later on Tuesday "we understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon". Guy Baybutt, who works for a family-run business The Veg Box Company also said he was "severely affected" by Tuesday's outage. Baybutt, who is from Preston, told the BBC the firm - which supplies fresh fruit, vegetables and other produce to customers across the UK - could not access its website to download and process customer orders amid the technical issues. "We were also unable to book parcels onto DPD's system for collection, meaning orders that should have been dispatched today were at risk of being delayed," he said. "To make matters worse, customers were unable to access our website to place new orders, meaning we lost valuable sales during the outage." He said that such disruptions can have "serious financial consequences" for small businesses like his own. "We don't have the resources of larger companies to simply absorb lost revenue, particularly when we're dealing with fresh, perishable produce that needs to reach customers promptly," Baybutt added. Guy Baybutt told the BBC its services had recovered, but it was frustrating "that a technical failure completely outside our control brought so much of our business to a standstill" Tuesday's incident came exactly one year after more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline for hours during an outage at AWS' largest cloud site .

events.title: The Wall Street Journal has been planning a big push into streaming TV, and courted Feed Me's Emily Sundberg for a show
events.summary: Emma Tucker has been involved in a video push at The Wall Street Journal. John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images The Wall Street Journal has been planning a big streaming TV push with an ambitious slate of shows. It's explored shows around editor in chief Emma Tucker and creators like Feed Me's Emily Sundberg. Sundberg dropped out of talks a few weeks ago, Business Insider has learned. The Wall Street Journal has been ramping up its push into video and had plans for an ambitious slate of streaming TV shows. Internal documents viewed by Business Insider described an initial six-series offering that would include a flagship live morning program and an interview show hosted by the Journal's editor in chief, Emma Tucker . The docs are from the summer, and a person familiar with the Journal's strategy said that its plans, including dates and partners, are in flux. The docs said the Journal had been "in negotiations" with creators such as Feed Me Substacker Emily Sundberg, as well as with the restaurant discovery platform The Infatuation . Sundberg dropped out of the talks a few weeks ago, Business Insider has learned. The plans called for the shows to launch on the Journal's own channels, YouTube, and social media. Journal parent company Dow Jones is also hiring a head of programming and content, who would be tasked with building "something ambitious in video." The live job description says the role will pay up to $330,000 in base salary, and involve developing talent that includes employees and external creators, translating the company's journalism into streaming formats, and creating live and on-demand shows. The Journal and Dow Jones's effort shows how news outlets traditionally known for the written word — including The New York Times — are racing to beef up their video offerings in a media landscape that's seeing both the rise of social video and the decline of cable TV news. It also demonstrates that Tucker is taking a flexible approach to the market by looking to both build shows around in-house talent, including herself, and partner with creators and other media companies. "Expanding our video presence across Dow Jones and The Wall Street Journal is a major strategic priority, as we have widely communicated," a Dow Jones spokesperson said. "We are actively hiring leadership to shape and execute our go-to-market strategy for video across Dow Jones, and we look forward to sharing our updated plans when ready." The Journal explored a show with Substacker Emily Sundberg. Aurore Marechal/Getty Images for The Business of Fashion The Journal name-checked familiar figures The internal docs viewed by Business Insider described the live morning show as a 60-minute-long anchor of the initial slate. The docs said the Journal enlisted some familiar names in morning news and video to help execute the show. They said the Journal has been working with the production company EverWonder, which was cofounded by the former Time Studios executive Ian Orefice with backing from Jeff Zucker's RedBird IMI. Another show in the proposed slate in the docs was "The Exchange with Emma Tucker," which was billed as a "prestige interview franchise" that would put viewers "in the room with the people running the global economy." The documents name-checked top CEOs, including Microsoft's Satya Nadella, JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, and BlackRock's Larry Fink, as potential guests. The person familiar with the Journal's strategy said the documents represented one of a number of different avenues the outlet was exploring and didn't reflect the current status and form of its efforts. The person said the company is in active conversations with a number of external people for potential partnerships. The documents said the Journal had been "in negotiations" with Sundberg — which have since ended — for a show called "Feed Me, On Camera" that would introduce her "highly engaged, younger creator audience to WSJ while bringing WSJ's scale, authority, and affluent professional audience to her world." The docs envisioned each episode beginning with a "tip, obsession, or question from the Feed Me universe," and following Sundberg to its conclusion while integrating business context and reporting from the Journal. Other shows the docs said the Journal had explored included one called "Market Price with The Infatuation" that would tackle the "business behind taste, literally." It would combine the cultural authority and young audience of The Infatuation, now owned by JPMorgan Chase, with the Journal's business reporting chops. Another was "Inside Sports" ("title to change"), a "next generation reboot of 'Real Sports' for the sports-as-an-asset class era," potentially helmed by Emmy-winning TV journalist Armen Keteyian. The documents said the Journal had been "in negotiations" with The Infatuation and "in discussions" with Keteyian. Business Insider could not confirm the status of those discussions. The last series listed in the docs was an AI show that aimed to get a big-name host. The docs said the Journal was in talks with TV journalist Armen Keteyian to helm a sports show. Patrick McMullan/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images The Journal compared its plans to 'The Daily' In the docs, the Journal expressed big ambitions for a live morning news show, and said there had been "nothing new" in the category for a professional audience "in a decade." The last entry on a timeline included in the planning docs was The New York Times' "The Daily" in 2017, which has become a reliable top show on the podcast charts and one of the paper's most successful launches. "We see an opportunity to reinvent the category," the documents said. The Journal also has its own daily news podcast, called "The Journal." Like the Times, the Journal is in a rare position in a challenged media environment to make a transformative investment. The Journal, part of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp., is profitable, helped by an early move to paywall its journalism. The documents said that in its video push, the Journal aimed to produce 20 hours of video a week, expand to a free, ad-supported streaming (FAST) channel, and add subscription options and other formats as demand warranted. Between WSJ TV, existing video shows, licensed shows, and co-productions with creators, the Journal aspired to be an "always-on streaming channel." The person familiar with the Journal's strategy said those goals didn't represent its current plans. The Journal wanted to make an impact on the level of The New York Times' "The Daily," hosted by Michael Barbaro. Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival Tucker took the helm at the Journal in 2023, moving from the Murdoch-owned UK Sunday Times with a plan to increase engagement with the Journal's digital products .
