events.title: Paddy Power owner blames tax rises for plan to shed up to 1,400 jobs
events.summary: Flutter says one in 10 UK and Ireland workers at risk of redundancy because of a ‘material increase in betting and gaming duties’ The gambling company behind Paddy Power and Sky Bet has announced up to 1,400 job cuts, blaming tax rises imposed by Rachel Reeves . Flutter Entertainment revealed plans on Tuesday to restructure its UK and Ireland division, affecting staff in Leeds, Dublin and Sunderland. Redundancies are also expected to hit offices in Porto in Portugal and Cluj-Napoca in Romania. But Flutter’s domestic market, where it employs 8,960 people, is expected to bear the brunt of the cuts, indicating that more than 10% of its UK and Ireland workforce could lose their jobs. The announcement is likely to echo loudly in the Treasury a week before John Healey’s first budget. The chancellor is considering an increase in machine games duty (MGD), a tax levied on slot machines. Industry figures warn this would trigger thousands of job losses. Flutter’s bombshell will heat up the debate over whether tax rises are wholly to blame for job losses in the sector, or whether companies are using government policy as cover for strategic cost-cutting, amid lacklustre conditions in the UK market. Paddy Power’s founder, Stewart Kenny, has accused the industry of “scaremongering” about jobs to avoid paying more tax. But Flutter pinned the blame squarely on the “significant” increase in gaming duties announced by Reeves in the 2025 autumn budget. The then chancellor increased remote gaming duty – levied on online casino games – from 21% to 40%. She also raised duty on online sports bets from 15% to 25%. Several major gambling companies, including Ladbrokes owner, Entain, and Evoke, which is owned by William Hill , have blamed Reeves for poor financial results or job cuts. One industry insider, who asked not to be named, said Flutter’s absorption of Sky Bet, which it bought in 2020, was likely to be a contributing factor. “Government policy changes ran alongside existing integration of its [Flutter’s] brands with inevitable job cuts,” they said. Many of the job cuts are expected to fall in Leeds, which was Sky Bet’s key centre of operations. Flutter said it expected to take a one-off hit of $90m (£67.3m) from the redundancy round. Its shares rose more than 2% in early trading in the US as investors looked forward to the prospect of a leaner business with fewer employees. “The material increase in betting and gaming duties announced in the UK budget last year has fundamentally changed the economic model of the regulated betting and gaming industry in the UK while helping to fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market,” said Kevin Harrington, Flutter’s UK and Ireland chief executive. “As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed-cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future. We remain confident that we are well placed to benefit from share gains given our position as the largest scale operator in the UK.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Leading figures in the gambling industry, which takes £13bn from British punters every year, have warned Healey to expect further contraction among the major operators if he goes ahead with plans to increase MGD. The Social Market Foundation, a cross-party thinktank, has called for a doubling of the levy from 20% to 40%, saying this could raise up to £460m. Adult gaming centres, slot machine venues that can be open 24 hours a day on high streets, are understood to be one of the main targets for any such rise. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been a vocal critic of the centres. The Guardian has exposed exploitative practices in the sector, which disproportionately clusters its shops in deprived areas . Some industry insiders say that gaming centres, which have lower overheads than bookies, could survive a tax rise relatively unscathed, whereas betting shops and casinos would face closures.

events.title: Figma co-founder Dylan Field thinks MCP is not a perfect protocol
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Despite Figma co-founder Dylan Field’s concerns about MCP (model context protocol), which standardizes how AI agents connect to external data sources and tools, the company is expanding its support for the open source standard. At the design company’s first Config conference held in India, the company announced 20 new MCP partners, including Amp, ClickUp, Dia, Junie by JetBrains, Linear, Meta Muse, Mistral, Notion, OpenCode, and Sarvam Agents. Field has expressed his misgivings about MCP before. Days before this announcement, one of MCP’s co-creators complained about Figma not supporting the open source tool Pi. As part of his response, Field made a comment about Anthropic not making its various resources available via MCP. “I find it interesting that Anthropic (creators of MCP standard) do not expose artifacts/other cloud resources created via MCP,” he wrote on X. “The debate is framed as open vs closed. Everyone always prefers open … obviously. And meanwhile issues of asymmetric context sharing are ignored.” (Field later added that Figma plans support Pi. ) Can you help me understand why you don't make various Anthropic resources available via MCP? Maybe I'm missing something. At a media briefing, I asked Field about this debate. The co-founder explained that while Figma wants to be open, he doesn’t think MCP is a perfect protocol. “I’m really excited about what we’re doing in terms of opening up our ecosystem. I also think that MCP is not a perfect protocol. And I think that it is something that has tons of room for improvement,” the co-founder responded. “It is advantaged more to frontier labs. Also, I understand everyone online who just wants a protocol that they can use when they want to use their Figma data, and I want them to use it, too.” Figma’s CEO said that the reason the company doesn’t want to be fully open is that the more data the company exposes through MCP, the higher the chance of abuse. He also clarified that while most users don’t intend to use MCP or Figma data in a malicious way, the company still has to think about those potential risks. events.title: How the energy crisis could become a food security crisis
events.summary: The Iran war and the Ukraine- Russia conflict are creating a "multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture" that could spiral into a crisis, a new report finds. Why it matters: Wars and extreme weather are colliding to threaten global food supplies and drive up prices, especially in vulnerable economies. The report explores how the El Niño phenomenon could compound the problems of restricted supplies of key fertilizer ingredients, higher fuel costs on the farm and more. The S&P Global Institute report is an unusually holistic look at the topic. Driving the news: The analysis comes alongside new warnings about food from the International Monetary Fund. Its World Economic Outlook last week sees an overall 10% increase in fertilizer prices this year and food costs rising by 5% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, though it depends on the region. "Higher energy and food prices could have severe effects on poverty and food security" and threaten political stability in vulnerable economies, the IMF warned. State of play: Food producers need steady supplies of natural gas and sulfur for fertilizer, diesel for farm machinery and food transport, and open sea lanes for trade, S&P notes. "Conflict is now testing all of them at once, just as El Niño tests the harvest," states the report from the research and consulting firm. "The risk is increasing, especially for low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of household spending," it states. Zoom out: The disruptions could affect agricultural production worldwide, from soybeans and corn in Brazil to wheat in Australia, S&P finds. The intrigue: The S&P report also warns of something that has received somewhat less attention. The diesel supply crunch doesn't just raise costs for farmers. It also works alongside pro-biofuels policies to make biodiesel production more attractive. "The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food." Zoom in: A few stats via S&P illustrate the overlapping threats. Middle Eastern prices for exported sulfur, a fertilizer ingredient, reached a record $1,000 per metric ton in July, after starting the year at a historically high $500 per metric ton. 47% of the global sulfur trade normally goes through the Strait of Hormuz. In Indonesia, industrial use of palm oil, largely for biodiesel, is expected to be roughly five times its 2015-16 level. The bottom line: A global food crisis is by no means certain. But if wars keep disrupting energy and fertilizer supplies, and weather cuts harvests in key regions, "the elements of such a crisis will be falling into place," S&P warns.

events.title: UAE and France deepen defence ties with Rafale F5 fighter-jet deal
events.summary: Defence co-operation is among the areas covered by a series of agreements signed by the UAE and France as the two countries look to bolster ties amid geopolitical uncertainty triggered by the Iran war. They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi. The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties. Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations. The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group , a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella. The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war. Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit. Edge , set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare. The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency. Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement. The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space. The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons. Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French government said. France and Bahrain signed a defence co-operation agreement in February during a visit to Paris by Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa. The UAE and Bahrain were among the Gulf countries France helped protect with air defence and anti-drone assets during Iranian attacks this year. France has also co-operated closely with Bahrain at the UN Security Council to find a diplomatic solution to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . Energy, AI and advanced technology The UAE and France signed new deals in energy, AI and advanced technology as the two countries seek to strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in Abu Dhabi. In AI and advanced technology, three agreements were signed with France's AI start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several key sectors, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office. The deals involve Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), Abu Dhabi's G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI will focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog's deal with AMI Labs focuses on exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications, creating new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technologies and identify opportunities to enhance operational efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts covering a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. In his opening remarks at the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan in Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled underscored the importance of bilateral co-operation in ensuring reliable energy supplies and building resilient supply chains amid changes in the global economy. The UAE and France have strong economic ties, with more than 600 French businesses currently operating in the UAE and $4 billion worth of goods exported annually from France to the UAE, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website. UAE investments are also growing in France. In 2021, UAE-based Gulf Islamic Investments made a $301 million investment in Altais Towers, while Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company signed an initial agreement with Bpifrance, committing to invest €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in the LAC1 Fund, a €10 billion fund managed by Bpifrance.

events.title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward. The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date. “We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer. And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress. Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight. Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months. The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station. Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added. “This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027. The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.) While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant. “It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: No cancellation of planned FDI in UAE this year despite Iran war, Ministry of Investment says
events.summary: No planned foreign direct investment in the UAE has been cancelled this year, despite the uncertainties created by the US-Iran war, a senior government official has said. The overall stock of FDI in the UAE this year might be fractionally lower than the record levels achieved in 2025, as global investors assess the impact of conflict in the region. However, the Emirates remains firmly on course to achieve its 2031 FDI targets, Mohammad Abdulrahman Alhawi, Undersecretary of the UAE Ministry of Investment, told The National in an interview on Tuesday. “Everyone we've spoken to has said: 'We haven't cancelled our plans. We are just either waiting, or we're delaying a little bit, or we're decreasing the quantum a little bit but the country is capable of making up,'” Mr Alhawi said on the sidelines of the 10th HSBC Future Forum in Dubai. “Very understandable [that] people will wait and see how the conflict is resolved.” The good thing, Mr Alhawi said, is that even though the conflict been going on since late February, it has helped investors better understand the resilience of the UAE and the capabilities of its government in dealing with a crisis. “I think that's the message that our investors have received over time and I think, maybe not immediately but in the next few years, that will definitely be a positive thing, as more investment is coming,” he said. FDI into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development ( Unctad ) data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. The UAE has maintained consistent FDI inflow momentum over the past few years and was expected to continue on the growth trajectory this year before the war-driven disruption to economy and trade. Like its peers in the six-member economic bloc of the Gulf Co-operation Council and its Arab neighbours, the UAE has faced waves of missile and drone attacks, but Mr Alhawi said it remains “100 per cent” on target to achieve the $65 billion annual FDI targets by 2031. “You'll have some years when it'll grow slightly less or slightly more,” he said. “But now that we've reached the $40 billion [plus] range, we expect to keep that for a couple more years before jumping to the next level, which is the $65 billion range, which is where we want to be.” While various governments at the emirate level are incentivising investors to boost FDI inflows, the UAE federal government is focused on investing in its own economy. Special attention is being paid to developing ports and related infrastructure on the East Coast, as well as improving and expanding rail connectivity, and oil and gas pipeline infrastructure. “Now, that investment does two things: one, it shows our confidence in our economy, and two, it shows that we're building different routes and paths for our main value proposition, which is being a logistical hub,” Mr Alhawi said. “We're investing in the right places, which means the investors that are already here can see the impact this will have and they will see it over the next year or so.” Partnerships with investors The UAE is more than capable of executing those projects on its own but it is seeking participation of foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story. Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said. “We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term. “We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.” Infrastructure pipeline Investment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant. HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding requirements to build the planned infrastructure projects. The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Menat Infrastructure report indicates. “Ultimately, these large-scale projects, such as Al Maktoum [International] Airport, the Dubai sewage system and developments in Fujairah, have strong government backing,” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE, told The National . “So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.” The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”. HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors. Opportunity knocks The sheer size of the MENAT pipeline underpins the scale of the region’s medium and long-term investment potential despite geopolitical headwinds, HSBC said in the report released on Tuesday. Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said. The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline. The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows “Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

events.title: Orlando Bravo on AI’s 'giant sucking sound'
events.summary: The death of software has been greatly exaggerated, said Orlando Bravo, who has more riding on its comeback than perhaps anybody in the world. The firm he runs, Thoma Bravo, oversees $170 billion in investments, nearly all of it invested in corporate software under threat from cheaper replacements spun up by AI coding bots. “Right now it’s a really, really hard time to buy and sell a company,” Bravo said on an episode of Semafor’s . “There have been four times the software industry has been doubted, and this is one of them. Every other time, it’s boomed after it’s been doubted. People got it wrong. It’ll be the same thing this time.” The sharp decline earlier this year in software stocks ground dealmaking in the sector to a halt, as CEOs were reluctant to sell at the bottom and private-equity firms struggled to raise the debt . That freeze is starting to thaw, with deals like Schneider’s $23 billion acquisition of PTC and the $6 billion takeover last week of AI cybersecurity company Varonis by a Thoma-backed competitor. The only questions that matter, he said, are “what is your level of domain expertise and how difficult it is to replicate it.” Dayforce, an HR-software provider Thoma Bravo bought in 2025, “is not selling you code. [It] is selling the following: ‘I will pay your employees on time, their deductions will be right, and their amount on their paycheck will be right. And if they’re not, I take the liability for it.’” “Yeah, somebody could try to recreate their code,” Bravo said. “Great. The business is not about that.” He also said the coming IPOs of “monster companies” like Anthropic and OpenAI will crowd others out of the capital markets — bad news for the private equity industry, which is sitting on an estimated $3.8 trillion backlog of unsold companies . “Who’s gonna pay attention with this stuff when they have to make big decisions on this enormous capital?” he said. — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

events.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security . The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, and covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said. The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the U.S. and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an offic i al briefing . “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off of Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. events.title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models. That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime. “They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raghuram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch. In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders. Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.” Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to 10 years ago. Take a look for yourself: What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?” When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch. These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks , say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point. “Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.” Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes. “Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.” Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California–Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gig workers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them.

events.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
events.summary: Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and Elon Musk, pictured here at President Donald Trump's 2025 inauguration, have seen their wealth soar thanks to the stock market boom and beneficial tax changes. Chip Somodevilla/Pool Photo via AP The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability , but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment. A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this. This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. Inequality by the numbers Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow . The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999. These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026. Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories. Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall . The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom. How taxes play a role Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive , often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth. Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940 . While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from. Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership , allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash , usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. The new drivers of inequality Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed. One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil. Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “ A Brief History of Equality ,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.” Markus Schneide

events.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
events.summary: Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned. Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free. Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own. The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman. However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait. The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK. Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases. Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases. Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills. Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says Published 12 February Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions Published 29 January Retired civil servants left in pension limbo Published 23 January According to the latest figures up to 30 September , external , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old. Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days. The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved. The Cabinet Office said that while the number of individuals approaching the two-year threshold was currently fewer than 10, "we are treating every case with urgency". If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance. The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate. Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty". His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability. Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim". He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month". He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear." Writing in response to Sir Geoffrey's letter, Minister Sally Jameson said neither the Cabinet Office nor the pension scheme administrator had the power under tax law to alter or waive these tax charges. However, she said where delays lead to an avoidable tax charge people "will not be left out of pocket" and the pension scheme "will ensure compensation is processed swiftly". She added that the Cabinet Office was working with Capita to ensure the oldest outstanding cases were prioritised. Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong? Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensions Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death. On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed. Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on. "It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said. "It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult." Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings. However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive. Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".

events.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug – and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
events.summary: Would this bother you? 500px/Getty Images Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like “the one” when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it. Consumers do this all the time. They replace phones that still work , furniture with a scratch and sweaters with a small snag. Often, what has changed is how people see these items. We are marketing researchers who study why people buy, use and get rid of stuff. This obsession with perfection began when one of us, Aprajita Gautam , moved from India to the U.S. in 2019. She was struck by how different the culture of buying and owning things was in the two countries. In our peer-reviewed research paper , published in August 2026 in the Journal of Consumer Research, we identified one reason for this pattern: Some people care much more than others about having flawless things. We call this penchant a desire for perfect products. Not the same as perfectionism We began by interviewing 17 people in Austin, Texas, in 2023. They included real estate agents, entrepreneurs, stay-at-home mothers and people employed by an nonprofit that promotes reuse. We asked them about their possessions and what made things seem perfect or imperfect. We then surveyed about 540 more people, some online and some in a university research lab. The results suggested that people who strongly preferred flawless items had more elaborate ideas about what their ideal product was and were sensitive to even small deviations from those ideas. Their standards also kept rising. Seeing something better than what they owned could raise the bar further for them. Next, we developed questions to assess how much people care about having flawless possessions. We used people’s answers to determine how strongly they desired perfect products. We also found that this tendency is related to but distinct from perfectionism . While perfectionists hold themselves to high or even impossible standards, people who want perfect stuff hold what they buy and own to lofty standards. You might easily shrug off a bad day at the office but be far less forgiving of a scratch on your new coffee table. For people who feel they have to own perfect products, even a small imperfection can overshadow everything else they like about something they own. Finally, we conducted 12 experiments where we recruited participants – University of Texas at Austin students and online workers participating in crowdsourcing marketplaces – to test the behavioral effects of the desire for perfect possessions. It can affect how you shop In our first online experiment, we asked 402 consumers across the country to imagine booking a hotel in California’s Napa Valley using filters like those on travel websites, such as star rating, Wi-Fi or a spa. Consumers who desired perfect products used more filters and set higher cutoffs, narrowing their search to hotels that came closer to meeting their standards. Newness itself also had value for them. In another online experiment with 301 consumers, those who cared most about owning flawless possessions were quicker to upgrade to the latest iPhone, even when it offered little real improvement over the previous one. This urge can be costly. It can mean paying extra for something new when the old one works fine, or spending more time searching for a product that meets every standard that may not actually matter. If you can live with imperfections, you can buy some of your stuff used. Moment/Getty Images Makes people less open to repairs This preference also affects what people do with the stuff they already own. In our next online experiment, we asked 1,004 U.S. participants to chose between two options: an insulated coffee mug and an insulated water bottle. When told that the product they chose had a small dent on the bottom, those who were most bothered by flaws in their possessions were more likely to swap it for the other option. We found a similar pattern with repairs . In an online experiment with 601 consumers, we found that those who want to own perfect products were less interested in fixing a broken keyboard when the replacement key wouldn’t match the color of the other keys. This highlights a problem with repairs that isn’t usually part of discussions about sustainable consumption : Fixing something can restore its function without necessarily making it look as good as new. A factor for donations Consumers with exacting standards for their things also applied their high standards to items they were getting rid of. In an experiment we conducted in a university behavioral lab, we asked 339 students to help with a “Clean Out Your Closet” drive. They examined pieces of clothing that others had discarded and sorted them into two bins: one to donate and one to recycle. Those who strongly preferred flawless items were less likely to donate imperfect but still usable clothing. This attitude can shorten a product’s useful life. That finding has implications for sustainability . Much of the academic research about sustainable consumption focuses on what people buy. But another way to consume less is to keep products in use longer. That becomes harder if small imperfections make otherwise useful products seem less valuable. Learning to value imperfection Our research suggests that how someone responds to flaws in their possessions can vary depending on what those flaws mean to them. We were inspired in part by the Japanese concept of wabi-sabi , which finds beauty and value in imperfection and change. In our final online experiment, 1,203 consumers learned about hoodies with subtle variations in color and pattern. When those variations were described as making each hoodie unique, consumers who love having perfect products responded less negatively to them. A mark on a well-used object can be seen as a flaw, but it can also become part of its history. And replacing products because of minor imperfections can lead consumers to waste their money. None of this means consumers should keep everything forever. Mugs break and clothing and shoes get worn out. Sometimes people simply want something new. But consider that bag again. Its scuffs could mean it is no longer the perfect bag you originally bought. Or they could mean you’ve carried it hundreds of times because you like it. The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
events.summary: Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek , as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector. A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices. The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment. “DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice. Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned. Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said. DeepSeek has been contacted for comment. One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance. The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4. The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals. Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents. The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

events.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
events.summary: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. events.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
events.summary: I’m a chief technology officer. AI still needs your human expertise AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment A utonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center . In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become. The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong. Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems. A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like. As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale. Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a 2026 study , after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result. Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break. Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010. But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it. The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable.

For an industry behind such a large share of global CO₂, that’s a real breakthrough. Gregor Ellegast and I both come from the sealing and building materials industry and we see so much potential in Germany. Satya Nadella if AI shortens time-to-market for new materials this much, does the competitive advantage shift from who owns the best labs to who owns the best data? In industrial governance and asset management, addressing the heavy carbon footprint of sectors like construction requires transitioning from reactive emission controls to systemic material science innovation. Leveraging digital discovery tools to optimize the lifecycle and efficiency of critical materials bridges the gap between ambitious climate targets and practical, large-scale execution. From an industrial strategy perspective, what key scaling framework do you find most effective to ensure that AI-accelerated material innovations move swiftly from laboratory discovery to widespread deployment in heavy infrastructure? AI is making it possible to discover new materials much faster. But how quickly can we test them under real working conditions? A promising discovery still has to prove itself in manufacturing, installation, and years of everyday use. events.title: A concrete vision: Saint-Gobain and Microsoft Discovery build for the future
events.summary: PARIS — Saint-Gobain’s business is construction materials. It got its start in 1665, when King Louis XIV charged the company with making the mirrors for his lavish new palace in Versailles. And he needed a lot of mirrors. The idea was to break the monopoly that glass-making power Venice had at the time, cutting costs and improving efficiency. These days, Saint-Gobain has 161,000 employees in 81 countries making construction materials — glass is still important, but there’s also gypsum for plaster board, insulation and concrete admixtures and cement additives. These last elements — products for cement and concrete — represent one of the company’s most important product groups, and like glass in 1665, one of the most challenging. Cement production uses a lot of energy, and accounts for around 7% of annual CO2 emissions globally. Saint-Gobain is looking for chemical elements that could reduce those carbon emissions and improve the strength of cement. “It would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager at Saint-Gobain, said that using Microsoft Discovery saved months of time for researchers working to improve an additive for cement. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. So, when the company’s researchers collaborated with engineers from Microsoft earlier this year in using Microsoft Discovery , a new AI-powered agentic platform for scientists and engineers, to find solutions, the results stunned them. “We actually gathered 62,000 patents and 44,000 abstracts,” says Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager overseeing the project to find lower-carbon, less expensive options. “Without using this technology, it would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” With a broad smile, she says Microsoft Discovery helped the team to narrow the data, analyze some novel possibilities in the chemistry involved and come up with several hypotheses about new ingredients for cement additives worth testing in about six weeks. A breakthrough in how research is done “So, yes, the researchers are very happy with Discovery,” Rastgoo-Lemaitre says. “It’s a great tool to help them have new ideas, and to go faster.” Saint-Gobain was one of Microsoft’s first clients to use Discovery in private release in March of this year, and teams from both companies worked on fine-tuning the platform. The team from Microsoft was from a new operating business called the Microsoft Frontier Company, which places Microsoft engineers inside companies like Saint-Gobain to deliver solutions using AI applications and tools like Microsoft Discovery. Discovery lets scientists orchestrate AI agents to search literature, connect information, generate hypotheses, design experiments and run analyses. “The construction industry, from production to running, is 40% of the world’s carbon footprint,” Ursula Soritsch-Renier, chief digital and information officer at Saint-Gobain says. “We’re not going to stop constructing, but we can make change, and who is better placed to do that than us?” She says Saint-Gobain is embracing technology as a means to cut waste, reduce energy use and be more efficient. The efforts to decarbonize the making of cement is just one illustration, she says. “You don’t just push technology for the sake of technology. You need to always understand the ‘why’ and the ‘what for’.” Ursula Soritsch-Reiner, chief digital and information officer, at Saint-Gobain’s headquarters in Paris. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. Technology that creates real-world impact For example, Saint-Gobain has changed the way it delivers plaster board to construction sites. Before, it came in a standard size, and workers cut the board to fit the rooms being built. But the leftovers just went to the dump. “We have now a cut-to-order system,” Soritsch-Renier says. “So, we get the building information model, we optimize the cuts, then nothing goes to the landfill.” She says the new system improved time-to-installation by 30%. “In construction, time is money,” she says. “And the environment wins because in the end it is less raw material and less energy. And that’s thanks to the digital tools we’re using.” Microsoft has been a key partner, Soritsch-Renier says, and the framework agreement the two companies signed in July will benefit both companies by accelerating the search for sustainable construction materials and processes. “You don’t just push technology for the sake of technology,” she says. “You need to always understand the ‘why’ and the ‘what for.’ And with that understanding you develop and you evolve and you push things forward with new tools, like with the research platform.” Saint-Gobain’s efforts to embrace cutting-edge technology took another step at the beginning of September, when it appointed Annica Hagen to a newly created role as the company’s first chief artificial intelligence officer. She will work with Soritsch-Renier to define how AI can support the Saint-Gobain Group’s strategic plan. “It’s important not to talk about AI as a means to an end,” Hagen says. “It’s an enablement to get where we want to go. My main task is to enable growth — and how can we use AI to enable that? Now is the time to shape the future.” Annica Hagen is the new (and first) chief artificial intelligence officer at Saint-Gobain. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. An exciting time to be an applied scientist Rastgoo-Lemaitre says the teams at Saint-Gobain’s Innovation Hub Europe in the Parisian suburb of Aubervilliers were already thinking about other projects where they could apply Discovery, but that research and development on the cement additives would continue. Saint-Gobain already has a cement-additive called EnviroAdd that reduces the need for clinker in cement by about 20%. Clinker is the ingredient in cement that binds, and it’s made by super-heating limestone, which is where the production of CO2 is most significant. By searching across domains outside of the construction industry, Rastgoo-Lemaitre says, the scientists using Discovery were able to find some molecules they otherwise would not have considered. The idea is to create a new chemical additive that could further reduce the need for clinker in cement while making it stronger. “They are right now testing those molecules for the behaviors and chemistry they are looking for,” she says. If the potential bears up under scrutiny, the next steps would be passing the potential solution to the development team, which would test the additive in physical conditions. A new era of discovery at Saint-Gobain “Every day that I’m using AI today, I think, if I had only had this my life would have been so much easier, and I could have done so much more.” Silvia Mariani is the managing director of the Saint-Gobain Innovation Hub Europe in Aubervilliers, France.

events.title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
events.summary: Oct 20, 2026 | Douglas Phillips - President and Chief Technology Officer, Microsoft Specialized Clouds Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure. Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements. These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve. Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate. Sovereign Control Panel , entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required. This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian , which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger , also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed. Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure. Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms , now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information. Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements. Designing for resilience and operational independence For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption. To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns . These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed. For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions.

events.title: The AI boom doesn’t answer to the Fed
events.summary: Liz’s view One rule of investing is “don’t fight the Fed.” Playing the contrarian to the Federal Reserve’s plans to stimulate or dampen the economy only ends badly. But Big Tech is not run by rule-followers. AI giants have been almost willfully indifferent to the rising cost of money. Rates go higher, and they borrow more. It’s a problem for the Federal Reserve, which is trying to tamp down inflation that, as Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told us last week , is “jumping out of its lane” — spreading from AI-linked sectors into unrelated parts of the economy. The Fed’s main lever, at least so far, isn’t working. Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei aren’t giddy consumers whose spending cools when borrowing gets expensive. They see themselves as great men of history, securing super intelligence for the West and ushering in an age of intergalactic abundance. They also believe customer spending on AI has only just begun, and so the coming revenue can justify their investments. That kind of existential drive can’t be discouraged by an extra 75 basis points of bond interest. Both the AI companies and the Fed are desperate for goodwill and credibility. If mortgages cost 15% and hyperscalers are still spending like there’s no tomorrow, people are going to be very mad at both of them. Notable Speaking at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok last week, Warsh recognized that AI investment was creating a “shock” on prices, but reiterated his conviction that the technology would bring wealth and productivity in future.
