events.title: Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge
events.summary: There are more signs that Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge and inventories dwindle ahead of the Northern Hemisphere winter. One tanker is now sailing toward Poland through the Red Sea, according to Bloomberg, and at least 20 more shipments have passed through the Strait of Hormuz to other destinations since early September. The gas could help halt the surge in consumer prices and slow the decline of Qatar’s $200 billion economy, which the IMF expects to contract by 15.6% this year. It’s unclear how the LNG is getting out: Qatar’s prime minister said last month that buyers had negotiated passage with Iran for the few cargoes that made it through during the first six months of the war. But Doha also seems to have adopted the “Hormuz shuttle” strategy Gulf crude exporters are using. Tracing the journey of Al Rayyan, one of Qatar’s oldest LNG tankers, Bloomberg tracked the vessel transferring its cargo to another ship in the Gulf of Oman before returning to Ras Laffan to reload. LNG ship-to-ship transfers are more complex than oil transfers, requiring cryogenic hoses to handle gas chilled to minus 162 C (minus 260 F). The effort is paying off, however: QatarEnergy restored LNG exports in September to about a third of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Trump isn't out to hurt Ukraine, Rubio tells Zelensky
events.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a phone call Tuesday that President Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Why it matters: The call was an effort to prevent the crisis between the U.S. and Ukraine from escalating further — and to push back on Ukrainian accusations that Trump is trying to coerce Zelensky into making concessions to Russia. The 45-minute call took place several hours ahead of a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to present to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Driving the news: The crisis broke out 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia at the same time his envoys were in negotiations with Ukrainian officials in Miami. Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he says are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Behind the scenes: Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that he clarified to Zelensky that the Pentagon hasn't changed anything when it comes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, weapons sales or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system. "No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said. Rubio acknowledged to Zelensky that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptors that have already been paid for by NATO countries. But the reason, he said, is that the U.S. needs to make sure it has enough to protect its own military bases around the world. "Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine." Rubio also asserted that the several cases in which Ukraine didn't get advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were a result of technical failures, not a U.S. order. What he's saying: "No doubt there are tensions," he said. "That is why we had the call. The president is frustrated. The president is responding to the insinuation that he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine, which is not fair and not true." Rubio said Trump is "angry and frustrated" about the lack of progress in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine after two years of efforts. The other side: Zelensky wrote on X after the call that he is "grateful" for Rubio's "readiness to help and his clear position." He said Ukraine needs ballistic missile interceptors and early warnings to protect Ukrainian citizens and stressed that "the situation with Starlink and Starshield needs to be restored." State of play: Witkoff arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelensky and European leaders. The talks there are expected to include Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Following Oslo, Witkoff plans to travel to Russia to meet with Putin and present ideas developed in consultation with Ukrainian and European leaders.

Text of this article October 20, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple announces new American Manufacturing Program partners for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro From U.S. titanium to advanced camera technology, American suppliers are producing key components in the latest iPhone lineup CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced new and expanded partnerships with American companies that are supplying critical materials and components for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro. Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made. Apple works with suppliers in all 50 states and supports more than 450,000 American jobs. Last year, the company deepened that commitment by launching AMP, aimed at bringing even more advanced manufacturing and critical component production to the United States as part of Apple’s $600 billion, four-year commitment to U.S. manufacturing and innovation. “We’re thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer. “American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.” The grade 5 titanium enclosure on iPhone Duo is exceptionally strong, providing amazing durability to the first foldable iPhone. Apple will commit up to $100 million over the next three years with Perryman, a family-owned business and a global leader in manufacturing specialty titanium products. At its site in Houston, Pennsylvania, Perryman melts, forges, and rolls titanium with a minimum of 80 percent recycled content for iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics to build key camera technology for iPhone 18 Pro in the U.S. Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. Variable aperture is at the heart of the new 48MP Fusion Main camera, which enables incredible light and depth control. It’s powered by on-device intelligence that automatically lets in more light for darker settings and helps get sharper detail in brighter ones. Nearly 100 components in iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro — from wireless chips to the silicon that powers key functions across the devices — are produced by American companies and drawn from suppliers in more than a dozen states. The multiyear agreement will produce more than 15 billion U.S.-made chips. Corning , an Apple partner since the original iPhone in 2007, produces specialty glass for Apple in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, including Ceramic Shield. By the end of 2026, all of the cover glass for iPhone — including iPhone Duo — and Apple Watch sold worldwide will be produced at this facility. Coherent continues building on its multiyear agreement with Apple, supplying new vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser technology from its Sherman, Texas, facility. events.summary: The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year. However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring. The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring. ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment". "The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said. "The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor." Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff. The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs. Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms. Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty". However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment". The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added. But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X , external that "businesses can't afford to hire". "This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said. The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year. Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment. Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover". But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said. Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened". But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising". The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body . The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates. In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? events.title: For investors, the Iran war redefined energy security
events.summary: Nearly eight months of war in Iran have produced one of the most severe energy shocks in decades, exposing a sharp divide between the countries that absorbed it with surprising ease and those forced into painful tradeoffs. Resilience, it turns out, comes less from any single technology or policy than from systems-level thinking, long-term investment, and deliberate planning. The countries that coped best were not always those with the most energy resources. They were the ones that had built flexibility, redundancy, and alternative pathways into their energy systems. China drew on strategic reserves, alternative pipeline imports, and fuel switching. The US benefited from record domestic oil and gas production, regional storage and solar to improve summer grid stability, and secure North American supply chains. Highly electrified countries such as Norway relied on hydropower, heat pumps, EVs, and infrastructure located far from the conflict zone. Emerging markets fared worse. Bangladesh and Pakistan imposed electricity restrictions and other demand-reduction measures. Wealthier economies across Europe and Asia largely avoided shortages only by paying sharply higher prices for LNG and other fuels. The dividing line ran not between producers and consumers, but between countries with options and countries without them. Three lessons stand out for governments and investors: Domestic electrons are safer electrons. The principle is straightforward: The shorter and more secure the energy chain, the fewer vulnerabilities a country carries into a crisis. Energy that is produced, generated, or stored at home is often more reliable than energy that must travel through vulnerable supply chains and geopolitical chokepoints. Few countries can achieve outright energy independence, but all of them can reduce their exposure to single points of failure. Solar and storage have scaled quickly in recent years on cost and technical readiness alone. Some producers will expand oil and gas output as demand shifts away from the Middle East to places with safer access to global trade routes. The Iran war is also unlocking public and private money for nuclear and geothermal energy. Nuclear deserves renewed attention as both an energy and national security asset, since reactors provide reliable electricity largely insulated from short-term geopolitical shocks. Small modular reactors could go further, supplying dependable power close to military installations, advanced manufacturing facilities, and AI data centers. Meanwhile, breakthroughs in deep drilling and new enhanced geothermal systems could vastly expand access to around-the-clock power beyond “traditional geothermal regions.” Electrification is now as much a security strategy as a climate strategy. Every domestically produced electron reduces exposure to disruptions in global fuel markets. That shifts the burden onto the grid. The challenge is no longer simply generating enough power. It is building the systems required to deliver that power where and when it is needed. The US electric grid is one of the largest on Earth, and it is aging rapidly. Some 70% of transmission lines are more than 25 years old, and the average large power transformer has been in service for nearly four decades. Demand for transformers has surged, yet the US has only one domestic producer of the specialized electrical steel needed for transformer cores. In 2025, 80% of power transformer supply and 50% of the distribution supply parts came from abroad. The American workforce is thinning too. The power sector will need more than 500,000 additional workers by 2030, just as hundreds of thousands of existing energy sector employees retire. Permitting compounds the problem: Major US infrastructure projects can take four to five years to secure approvals, delaying as much as $1.5 trillion in investment. As energy supply struggles to keep pace with demand, those delays have drawn political attention and, finally, action, including significant legislation passed at the state level and a new bipartisan permitting reform bill proposed in the Senate. The countries that cope best with the next crisis will not necessarily be those that build the most infrastructure. They will be the ones that make the best use of what they already have. Not every energy security challenge can wait a decade for a new power plant, transmission corridor, or major industrial project. In the US, with its aging grid infrastructure and rapidly growing power demand, that constraint bites. But many of the answers already exist: Long-duration batteries can store electricity during periods of surplus and release it when shortages emerge. Grid-enhancing technologies can raise transmission capacity, ease congestion, and improve the efficiency of existing assets. Smart-grid software and demand-management tools can shift consumption away from periods of peak stress without new steel in the ground. Every crisis is said to carry opportunity. The lesson from 2026 is that the most successful energy systems of the next decade will not merely generate more power. They will store it better, move it more efficiently, and protect it more successfully.

events.title: £30 rise in payments for crisis-hit households
events.summary: Sheffield City Council's crisis resilience fund can be used to pay for essentials such as utilities Crisis payments for people in Sheffield who are facing severe financial difficulties have been raised by £30. Single person households which qualify for help from Sheffield City Council's crisis and resilience fund will now be entitled to a one-off payment of £95, up from £65 previously. Meanwhile, two-person households can apply for a payment of £110, while homes with three or four people are entitled to £120 if they qualify and households with five or more people can get £130, the authority confirmed. Announcing the change, councillor Elle Dodd, chair of the authority's finance and performance policy committee, said life was "difficult and expensive" for "too many people" in Sheffield. The fund can be used to help people buy essentials such as food, toiletries and utilities, the council's website stated. The increase was put in place after a cost-of-living review conducted by the committee, which is made up of a group of Sheffield councillors. The review found almost 50,000 households in Sheffield were struggling to make ends meet and could not pay their bills . At least 7,000 crisis grants, totalling nearly £600,000, have already been awarded by the council since April. Dodd said: "Behind every statistic is someone making impossible decisions, feeling stressed and looking for a little breathing room. "We are determined to tackle the root causes of poverty, and to provide immediate support to those who need it. "We are keeping tackling poverty and the cost of living firmly on the agenda." events.title: DIY repair clubs are helping Americans save money and fight big tech
events.summary: US community repair clinics teach people how to fix their belongings, pushing back against throwaway culture O n a recent Monday night, a volunteer-run workspace bustled with dozens of fixers in Brooklyn, New York . Some tinkered with sewing machines while others soldered circuit boards at a workbench. Caleb Young, a co-founder of the Brooklyn Spark space, fit a DIY suction device on to the handle of a Dyson vacuum cleaner. “It’s in our culture to throw things away, but sometimes the fix is easier than you’d think,” Young said. The Fixit Clinic is open every Monday night to walk-ins. Anyone with a broken item they’d like to fix – from torn clothes to malfunctioning electronic devices – can drop by during open hours and get the repair help and tools they need. It’s a way for people to push back against tech companies, making their phones and gadgets deliberately unrepairable so they buy newer devices while creating large amounts of e-waste . The clinics also foster community: once people learn to repair their possessions, many get addicted and like helping others, Young said. “We like to tell them, ‘Why not take a few seconds to try and open something up?’” he said. “It’s broken anyway.” The Brooklyn clinic is part of a nationwide network offering community repair. Peter Mui, who founded the first Fixit Clinic in Berkeley, California, in 2009, said that he has seen the number of clinics explode during the past few years; at least 2,000 have been hosted across the country. “We’re offering these workshops in libraries, at colleges and in public spaces where fixers and community members can come together,” Mui said. Similar, unaffiliated clinics have seen success, too. The community-run Repair cafe , originally founded in Amsterdam, now has about 250 US locations. Neighborhood repair events at local community centers are also popping up around the country. Policy proposals have even matched this grassroots demand. Since 2012, 24 states have successfully passed some form of right-to-repair legislation, mandating that manufacturers make their products repair-friendly instead of destined for the landfill. This year, 57 right-to-repair bills have been introduced in 22 states that would make machines such as phones, wheelchairs and construction equipment easier to repair. Members of Congress have also introduced a bipartisan federal automotive right-to-repair bill, called the Repair Act , but it has yet to be brought to a full House vote. Mui attributes the growing interest to people questioning the environmental and economic costs of our consumer culture. “So much of our capitalist system is tied up in our endless consumption,” he said. “But if we come together to take agency and empowerment over the things we own, we can build a more sustainable future.” Starting a bottom-up repair culture The first modern right-to-repair state law was passed in 2012, when Massachusetts granted car owners the right to fix their cars at independent service shops. Congress passed a bill in 2014 that legalized “phone unlocking”, which allowed consumers to change their cell service carrier without buying a new phone. Farmers and states have also filed lawsuits against the agricultural equipment manufacturer John Deere over repair restrictions to their equipment, resulting in settlements with the company . Right to repair reached a new level of public consciousness in 2024 when customers across the country were upset over broken McFlurry machines. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) protected the software on these machines, meaning only their manufacturer, Taylor, could fix them. After petitions from consumers and consumer advocacy groups, the US copyright office granted a copyright exemption that would allow third-party repairs on McFlurry machines. Nathan Proctor, the senior director of the Right to Repair campaign at the Public Interest Research Group, said that corporations’ responses to right-to-repair laws have ranged from compliance to active resistance. For example, Apple has gradually made some parts and manuals available for repair, while the automotive industry has fought back against right-to-repair laws. “Some companies are hostile and refuse to provide repair materials, while others have made national policies to sell spare parts,” he said. But the growing grassroots movement of community repair brings Proctor hope. “We need to both change the law and build out a culture of repair,” Proctor said. “To see these community events start up with no institutional backing – that’s a signal that something about repair is clicking with people.” Educating the next generation of fixers At San Jose State University in California , the Fixit Clinic student organization was recently voted the most influential club on campus. The student-led group holds monthly clinics for fellow students and community members at libraries around the city.

events.title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
events.summary: Oil prices hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continued attacking Saudi Arabia, further stoking concerns over supply and higher inflation that could prompt interest rate increases. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.52 per cent higher at $111.30 per barrel at 2.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 2.30 per cent to $100.80 a barrel. Crude prices were last at these levels in mid-May. On Friday, Brent hit $110 for the first time since May, while WTI topped $100 for the first time in a month. The Houthis claimed responsibility for renewed strikes on ⁠Saudi energy, airport and military targets ⁠on Monday, escalating tension in the region and bringing down stock markets in the Gulf. The rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks on the kingdom, which included strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a military airbase near Abha International Airport, a naval task-force camp and a Saudi radar in Bir Askar. With the US-Iran conflict continuing, crude supplies from the Middle East remain choked, prompting moves to ensure adequate supplies globally. The International Energy Agency last week said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . The fighting has kept energy prices elevated, nudging inflation upwards and, in turn, raising the probability of another interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, which is scheduled to meet next week. Analysts are now expecting a second straight raise as Fed officials seek to tame inflation. "Brent crude hovering near five-month highs following geopolitical tensions in the Middle East has reignited fears of sticky inflation," analysts at US energy company Duncan Oil said. "Surging energy costs have led investors to believe the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tame inflation." Ship movements in the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, remain under pressure. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday that Washington was willing to allow oil tankers placed under sanctions to begin a process to legitimately ship crude. Analytics firm Kpler said easing sanctions on the shadow fleet would have little effect on record freight rates. It estimated that, as of Monday, only 24 of the nearly 160 vessels under sanctions from the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. Wholesale diesel, meanwhile, already surpassed $200 per gallon in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US, the Paris-based IEA said last week.

events.title: Tesla’s Roadster represents a feat, and a defeat
events.summary: Andy’s view The new Tesla Roadster is science fiction: It can zoom into the air, perform barrel rolls, and then plop down softly using cold-gas rocket thrusters. Unveiled last week at a rocket facility in Texas, the Roadster is a triumph of engineering — an exquisite toy for the super-rich, if it ever reaches production (the disclaimers on the advance orders suggest CEO Elon Musk himself has doubts). Yet, paradoxically, it also represents a defeat: The Roadster isn’t a vehicle that will turn the tables on China, outcompeting the likes of BYD in the consumer market. Instead, it represents the future in another way, one in which China owns global mass manufacturing not just in cars but everything else — machine tools, pharmaceuticals, ships. As low-priced Chinese exports swamp global markets, politicians from Washington to Brussels to Berlin diagnose the problem largely as one of Chinese overproduction, and are putting up trade barriers to protect their domestic industries. The EU and China, for example, recently agreed to set quotas with tariffs for Chinese hybrid cars, and are considering similar restrictions on other industrial categories. But this misses the broader challenge. China’s surging shipments are much more than just surplus production, the difference between what comes out of Chinese factories and what can be sold domestically in a sagging economy. They are a deliberate strategy, clearly stated in the country’s five-year industrial plans and, ultimately, represent China’s quest for national power. The implication for Western industry leaders is existential: They can either climb the technological ladder into increasingly rarefied niches — like Tesla, with its Roadster — or risk being destroyed by Chinese rivals, as is currently happening to Volkswagen in China, still its largest single market. In fact, influential Chinese strategists don’t recognize the concept of overproduction at all. Lu Feng, a professor at Peking University’s School of Government, sees a showdown on the way between China’s “industrial socialism” and the US’ “financial capitalism” — and he warns that caving to foreign pressure to curb “overproduction” would be “ tying our own hands .” In this way of thinking, since China’s desire for power is limitless, there can be no question of producing too much. Kyle Chan, a researcher specializing in China’s industrial policies at the Brookings Institution, labels Lu’s brand of economic nationalism, “industrial maximalism.” Perhaps, then, we should call the Roadster a prime example of its opposite: “industrial minimalism.” Among leading global automakers, Tesla had the best chance of owning the future of mobility. Indeed, its Shanghai gigafactory, built in 2019, and the local supply chains it developed were a catalyst for the entire Chinese EV industry. But Musk is now clear-eyed about the competition he helped spawn. Without trade barriers, he warned in 2024, China would “pretty much demolish most other car companies in the world.” Musk is now betting Tesla’s future on becoming a robot maker. But he’ll run into the same issues in that sector, too. The challenge from China is systemic, not industry specific. The country’s industrial machine is set up to commoditize products through overwhelming economies of scale, to bring down prices, and conquer global markets — regardless of financial return. This is not about profit maximization. It’s about power maximization. Writing in The Guardian, the tech reporter Chang Che, who recently visited 11 Chinese robot makers across five cities, sees a future where the US leverages its advanced research capabilities to try to build the ultimate robotic machine — one that can “mow your lawn, walk your dog, and babysit your children” — while China cranks out functioning robots for each of those tasks at a fraction of the price . Already, China accounts for 60% of all the world’s new factory robots. It also has the capacity to supply 100% of global demand for EVs. Michael Dunne, the author of the forthcoming , told The Wall Street Journal that what remains for Western carmakers “ is to move up or get pushed out. ” The Tesla Roadster is, quite literally, aiming for the skies. Other carmakers will have to make a similar vertical ascent, or bite the dust. Notable Zeroing in on the term “ scenario innovation ,” a recent Sinocities article explained China’s state-sponsored process of opening up real spaces, like roads and factories, so that companies can test new technologies in real-world settings.

events.title: Europe to see 'biggest-ever' increase in air fares next year, Ryanair chief says
events.summary: Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary has forecast a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to push up oil prices , forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers. Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, Mr O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels on Tuesday. As a result, airline margins will be squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said. “You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say in history, in Europe in the next 12 months,” Mr O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.” The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic rise in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets. Mr O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry. “We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said. Ryanair's shares dropped as much as 2.1 per cent, bringing the decline to 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018. The chief executive used his news conference to dish out against regulation in markets such as France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He repeated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment. Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet. Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability. Mr O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected up to April.

events.title: Today in Paris, we announced new capabilities across Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, expanding choice and control for organizations running their most sensitive workloads across public and private cloud, and our growing partner ecosystem.
events.summary: Today in Paris, we announced new capabilities across Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, expanding choice and control for organizations running their most sensitive workloads across public and private cloud, and our growing partner ecosystem. https://lnkd.in/gDjmHetu Intriguing to hear what Microsoft is defining as sovereignty. My understanding of EU digital sovereignty is that we want independence from manufacturers who retain control of how we use their products/services. If your vendor can shut down your service — by definition — your use is not Sovereign. After reading the article I noticed one potential challenge here is vendor lock in. Even if organizations gain more control over where their data lives and how workloads operate, how easy is it to move away from the Microsoft ecosystem entirely without major costs or disruption? True digital sovereignty should include not just control, but the freedom to switch providers when needed. What are your thoughts? The fundamental contradiction remains very visible. The US cloud act legally compels American service providers to produce data upon request, meaning absolute digital sovereignty via a US corporation is an ongoing legal impossibility. The proposed solutions in the blog expose the technical limits of this approach, why ? Operating an Azure local environment on disconnected private hardware is simply traditional onpremise hosting reliant on a proprietary software stack. A company might own the physical servers & sever the network cables, but they are still running a closed source system. True digital sovereignty requires the ability to audit the technology independently. Local security agencies are legally prohibited from inspecting the compiled binaries of Microsoft software. They cannot verify the underlying mechanics and/or write their own internal security modifications. The organisation remains permanently dependent on a foreign software supply chain. EU public institutions are actively shifting toward open source platforms & domestic providers specifically to escape this type of extraterritorial legislation. Rebranding disconnected virtualization as a new product does not alter the underlying jurisdictional reality. Sovereignty isn’t about where the servers sit, it’s about which law applies to them. In June 2025, Microsoft France’s legal director told the French Senate under oath he could not guarantee that French data would never be handed to US authorities. The CLOUD Act still applies, and will always. A sovereign cloud under US jurisdiction should be an oxymoron. Europe doesn’t need sovereignty under licence Great to see digital sovereignty evolving beyond data residency toward a more comprehensive approach to control, resilience, and operational independence. As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise workflows talking from the first hand experience, questions around where they run, what data they can access, what actions they’re authorized to take, and how those actions are governed become increasingly important. The workload-based approach is particularly compelling: combining cloud innovation with the right level of control, security, and resilience for each workload. Trustworthy agentic AI requires not just intelligence, but also clear boundaries, governance, and operational accountability. Mehr Optionen bedeuten für stark regulierte Sektoren leider nicht automatisch mehr Kontrolle. In der Praxis verlagert die wachsende Feature-Vielfalt das Problem oft nur auf die Compliance-Ebene, weil technische Souveränität ohne echte operative Unabhängigkeit die Auditoren am Ende selten überzeugt. What would be the key outcomes and business values it brings for MS cloud user Satya Nadella Does Microsoft have a road map for CADA compliance offerings, by 2028/2029? for a government buyer the test of sovereignty is simple: does the service keep running, with keys held locally, if the vendor's home jurisdiction says otherwise. residency is the easy part to certify. the exit plan is the part procurement teams rarely ask for. Control over where data lives is turning into a real buying factor. I see the same in tracking work, where clients now want their data in their own server-side setup instead of fully on someone elses platform. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze. In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama ’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves. events.title: 'Gulf security is our security', says former UK defence secretary
events.summary: Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis , because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Sir Michael Fallon has told The National . The US , he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”. That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”. With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.” For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis . “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024. Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion. Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.” It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given. However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.” 'Gulf security is our security' “Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.” The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”. “So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said. The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia , declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran. Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”. “Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.” The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”. Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.” Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course. Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”. Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism ”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS. Europe's turn to do more The same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow. He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress. “I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said. The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness. “He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine 's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”. Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.” Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.” Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.” The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September. Pressure on Kyiv The stakes are highest in Ukraine . “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.” A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato ”. Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. But it will also send a signal right round the world to other countries that want to extend their borders”. “China, of course, has ambitions to bring Taiwan formally back inside China, to extend its influence across the South China Sea.” The idea that might makes right, Sir Michael warned, “is very dangerous for the international community”. events.title: Europe has few alternatives to counter China other than costly protectionism
events.summary: The Scene Pascal Lamy negotiated China’s accession to the WTO in 2001 on behalf of the EU. A decade later, in a speech in Shanghai, Europe’s former trade commissioner lauded what he called a “win-win” outcome. But like a growing number of current and former European leaders, he’s grown alarmed as China’s trade surplus with the EU has ballooned. Lamy, now with the Jacques Delors Institute, was one of the authors of a recent policy paper that called for restrictions on Chinese exports using a quota system — an idea that the EU has now embraced. Q&A Andy Browne: Is the EU-China trade war now off? Pascal Lamy: I interpret the recent deal on hybrid cars’ export restraints as a first step in the right direction. I think the European side will consider this as a down payment. In my view, we need further steps to seriously address this rocketing Chinese trade surplus with Europe. So is this a tactical concession by China or a strategic shift? Both interpretations are possible. But from the EU side, this will not be seen as sufficient. Is the car deal a model for other sectors? Yes, indeed, although voluntary export restraints raise a series of technical issues. It’s certainly easier for hybrid cars than it is for chemicals or pharmaceuticals. And, of course, when you look at the numbers you need quite a lot more given the [EU’s] €350 billion annual trade deficit with China. You once called China’s WTO accession a “win-win.” Recently, you said that “China is killing open global trade.” What changed? I changed my mind because China changed. None of us predicted the speed of economic growth in China. A lot of people now say ‘you made a mistake by not forecasting that China would become an enormous elephant.’ My usual answer is: Who said that at the time? Give me some evidence that we had a choice between those who said ‘be careful’ and those who said ‘that’s a great idea.’ [Former Chinese Premier] Zhu Rongji thought that the Chinese miracle was a clever mix of Chinese characteristics and good old Western liberal capitalist market recipes. This is not the view of Xi Jinping. He believes that the incredible economic success of the past 20 years is due to the fact that China is led by the Chinese Communist Party. Also, the state-owned sector is larger today than it was in 2010. What’s changed, too, is that China no longer plays the game of comparative advantage, which is the ideological basis of the World Trade Organization. If you are better — cost and quality wise — than I am at everything, where’s the comparative advantage? Isn’t a big part of the problem that China now out-competes Europe? I’m not saying that all of China’s comparative advantage is, let’s say, WTO illegitimate. There is their education system, their engineers, their planning system, and the size of their market. But there’s another part which is not in line with an open rules-based trading system. By the way, what’s also changed is that a lot of markets that were open to China — the US, Turkey, Japan — have taken protectionist measures. China’s exports are now going to Europe, the only large and deep market that is still wide open. Germany and France have proposed a “kill switch” that could shut China out of European markets completely. Is that a good idea? I disagree with that formula. It’s like the US using Section 301 to determine whether a trade partner is playing fair or not. The Jacques Delors Institute has proposed a WTO compatible quota system with in-quota tariffs and out-of-quota tariffs. That’s a big difference — it’s predictable, rules-based, with benchmarks and numbers, and everyone understands clearly how the system works. There is no unilateral determination except for the size of the quota. China also has a ‘kill switch’ — rare earths. Can Europe really afford to risk a trade war? China’s rare earth dominance is time-limited. The US, EU, and Japan have started working on alternatives. If you over-use market dominance, markets adjust, and there’s a big price incentive to innovate. Tariffs raise prices. Are European consumers ready to pay a premium? Some prices will be higher, yes. Protection is costly. But what’s the alternative? You have to choose between that and industry closures, social problems, and the growth of extremism on the right and left of European politics. Can China be persuaded to compromise? I’ve been trying to convince my Chinese friends that they should care about this. We have to convince them that if the people who will govern Europe are the products of industrial and social shocks that China is creating, they will be much tougher with China than we, traditional center left or center right, are.

events.title: AI takes on great experiment in self-rule
events.summary: Slowly but surely, the leading AI companies are creating a national self-governing structure to oversee their technology and its societal impact. With the federal government largely hands-off, Anthropic, OpenAI and others are self-regulating their technology and now setting up their own plans to redistribute their wealth. Why it matters: Not since the age of the robber barons have America's industrial titans wielded such sweeping power to shape society — and decide how their private fortunes should serve the public good. In the modern era, Washington has largely exercised those powers through regulation, taxation and public spending. The big picture: President Trump has no interest in new regulations. Instead, he has blessed a basic framework for the AI companies to regulate themselves — and potentially each other — outside of formal government monitoring. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Elon Musk's XSI, Meta and Nvidia are working on different versions of this. This is all voluntary and rests on the public trusting companies the size of industrialized nations to responsibly police themselves. These companies are in a frantic race to create human-surpassing superintelligence. All are pressing ahead, even as their leaders — particularly at Anthropic — warn of potentially catastrophic risks and profound economic disruption. At the same time, some AI leaders are promising to direct a portion of their vast wealth to benefit those outside their companies. Zoom in: At least three competing visions are emerging for sharing the spoils of the AI boom, each with a different answer to who should control the wealth. Anthropic: The company. On the eve of its blockbuster IPO, Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund that could grow into one of the largest philanthropic institutions in history. At a hypothetical $2 trillion valuation, its stake would be worth $100 billion — more than the Gates Foundation's current endowment. Including earlier founder and employee pledges, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares are earmarked for the public good. Musk: The people. Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement by urging the company to give shares "directly to the public." On Monday, Musk pledged to give every American child a share of SpaceX next year — a staggering $10.5 billion giveaway at current prices. Musk called it the "first of many," though he offered no details on how the unprecedented distribution would work. OpenAI: The government. CEO Sam Altman has floated giving the U.S. government a 5% stake in OpenAI through a sovereign wealth fund — potentially handing Washington a multibillion-dollar interest in one of the world's most powerful AI companies. Altman envisions an Alaska-style fund that could distribute the industry's investment returns directly to Americans, though the plan remains preliminary and would likely require congressional approval. Reality check: The numbers are staggering. So are the assumptions about future wealth, billionaire follow-through and the public's willingness to trust its benefactors. Bill Gates and Warren Buffett launched the Giving Pledge in 2010, a voluntary promise by billionaires — including Musk — to give away most of their fortunes. Gates built a philanthropic empire, only to become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories. Anthropic's ambitions depend on extraordinary growth projections — its own employees envision 17% GDP growth in 2030 — while Musk has a history of making spectacular promises that fail to materialize. Anthropic's roots in effective altruism , a philosophy deeply distrusted by the Trump administration and its allies, also raise a more fundamental question: Who gets to define the public good? Between the lines: No industry requirements or consensus exist on how best to redistribute their expected wealth. But Trump Accounts — which allow families, businesses and individuals to invest in tax-advantaged funds for children — are emerging as a favorite vehicle for free-market AI leaders. Billionaire investor Brad Gerstner, a driving force behind the program, is championing a vision of broad-based ownership in which ordinary Americans share directly in the economic upside of the AI revolution. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in July pledged roughly $320 million in company shares to 2 million children through Trump Accounts — a potential blueprint for distributing an even larger slice of Musk's fortune. What to watch: The Trump administration hasn't fully relinquished its regulatory authority, potentially complicating the emerging experiment in AI self-governance. After Anthropic disclosed that its AI had submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police and improperly interacted with government websites, the White House declared that AI companies must report security incidents and remedy any harm. "This notification and remediation process is not optional," Trump's Super Intelligence Force warned — a striking assertion of federal authority just weeks after the president blessed a voluntary system of industry oversight. Axios' Zachary Basu and Bradley Olson contributed reporting.

events.title: Why Democrats are pushing their donors to care more about state legislative races
events.summary: The News YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — John Boccieri’s tour through northeast Ohio politics is a microcosm of the Democratic Party’s decline, especially in state legislatures. In 2008, Boccieri left his seat in the Ohio state Senate to flip a Republican-held House seat. He lost it in the 2010 GOP wave, which gave the party control over redistricting and put his old district out of reach. Democrats appointed him to a safe state House seat in 2015, though he left it to run for state Senate in 2018. But he lost that race, and went back to work as a pilot. This year, Boccieri decided to try again for a seat in the state house. He bet that Republicans’ winning streak couldn’t survive a second Trump midterm, with Vivek Ramaswamy leading their Ohio ticket. “The seat that I’m running in is still gerrymandered,” he told Semafor last week. “But we need someone who’s going to help Amy Acton, when she’s the governor, to push back on unregulated, unchecked data centers, and make sure that the state house corruption ends.” Boccieri now exemplifies a new trend in Democratic politics: In the final weeks before the midterms, the party is trying to convince its donors that a “blue wave” could spread even farther — if their money isn’t all spent on a handful of House and Senate races. “Democrats are always in this spot of this ‘coulda, woulda, shoulda’ with state legislatures,” said Leslie Martes, the CEO of Forward Majority, a nonprofit that spends on Democratic state legislative campaigns. The group has warned donors that Republicans are still ahead in both parties’ top target races at the state level. “There’s this idea that these top-of-the-ticket candidates are going to lift the whole ticket, but that’s not the case,” Martes explained. “I worked in North Carolina in 2008, when Barack Obama was winning the state, and we didn’t pick up a single seat in Raleigh. There’s a lot of work to increase the name ID of our candidates at the state legislative level.” The fight to control state legislatures intensified last year, after President Donald Trump urged Republicans to draw new congressional maps in the states they control that eliminate as many Democratic House seats as possible. Strategists in both parties said that this redistricting scramble has changed how donors are being approached for state legislative races — rarely the first places where the largest political funders send their cash. Mason Di Palma, a spokesman for the Republican State Leadership Committee, said that his group began warning donors that Democrats could force their own gerrymanders if they swept state-level races in 2026. In practice, that meant that if Democrats could expand their control in Minnesota, capture Wisconsin’s Assembly, and flip Pennsylvania’s state Senate, they would gain the power to delete GOP districts in each state. “If Dems get trifectas, what will stop them from redrawing maps?” said Di Palma. “Your dollar goes further in state legislative races.” Both parties have stepped up their recruiting for downballot races, with Democrats benefiting from an overall confidence that they’d make gains in the midterms. In Wisconsin they spotted a chance for their first trifecta since 2010 thanks to new maps; in Pennsylvania, the popularity of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro was already helping them inch toward Senate control. Know More Redistricting is reshaping the political outlook in many states, with the possibilities for partisan control divided into three categories. First, there are states where neither party thinks that they can break the governing trifecta: Republicans are at no risk in Arkansas, Tennessee, or Indiana; Democrats are not worried about losing either the governor’s office or the state legislature in New York, Illinois, and California. The dead zone includes places where state legislative elections are held in off-years: Louisiana, Mississippi, New Jersey, and Virginia. The next crop of states with marquee legislative fights this cycle feature one party that’s trying to break a governing trifecta, or at least end a supermajority that makes it easier for the party in power to force new maps through. This group includes Nebraska, where Republicans in the “unicam” have been a vote away from eliminating the presidential electoral vote for Omaha’s 2nd Congressional District. Ohio, where Democrats don’t think they can flip the state legislature, is also in this batch — it could still make Acton governor and elect enough legislators to sustain her vetoes. “I’m very excited that we may break the supermajority in this election,” Acton told Semafor last week. Finally, there are states where one party could win a trifecta, sometimes in places where they’d have the ability to draw new maps in 2027. Wisconsin and Pennsylvania top that list for Democrats. It also includes Arizona, where the party is a few seats away from control — and where Republicans have said they’d use a trifecta of their own to revisit the state’s redistricting commission. The total money heading into state legislative campaigns pales in comparison to what Republicans have spent to hold Texas’ Senate seat. But the States Project — which, like Forward Majority, was created to help Democrats win more legislatures — announced a $100 million haul last month; the RSLC is looking at spending “north of $52 million” on its targets. In key states, Democrats say that they remain outgunned; in Wisconsin, local GOP donors have helped swing-seat Republicans in the Assembly spend $11.3 million, compared with $7.6 million for Democrats. “The right wing has been at this for more than 50 years,” said Mandara Meyers, the States Project’s executive director. “They have entrenched advantages and GOP megadonors are still pouring millions into individual races.” David’s view The story of modern state legislature battles is a Republican breakthrough in 2010, followed by 16 years of Democrats trying to claw back whatever they could. They started with lawsuits and ballot measures; in Michigan, Virginia, and Colorado, they created less partisan redistricting processes that kept both states competitive, not slanted toward one party. Trump’s national redistricting push quickly changed their strategy, and the threat of new maps every two years helped both parties raise more money for 2026. Forward Majority’s ask for a final $2-5 million to avoid being outspent came after Republican donors to the party’s other PACs funded the key GOP state legislative campaigns. There’s table talk about whether Trump’s low approval ratings can hurt his party as much as Obama hurt his party’s in 2010. The spending picture is completely different now: Democratic donors pledged never to neglect state-level races again, and Republican donors never stopped investing in them. Democrats are still not sure whether they can break through in the sorts of non-urban, non-suburban areas where Republicans have been drawing maps for 10 years, confident that these voters are permanently realigned. events.title: Empathy divides Americans by religion, with white evangelicals standing apart
events.summary: Data: PRRI, 2026 American Values Survey ; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios White evangelical Protestants are the only major religious group in which a majority says empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth, according to a new survey . Why it matters : The survey lands amid a quiet civil war within American Christianity over who deserves empathy. Conservatives ranging from evangelical pastors to Elon Musk have framed empathy as a vulnerability in debates over immigration , racial justice and LGBTQ+ rights . In a February 2025 interview with Joe Rogan, Musk called empathy "the fundamental weakness of Western civilization," while acknowledging its potential good and warning against its weaponization. By the numbers: The annual American Values Survey from the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) released Tuesday found that 42% of white evangelical Protestants agreed that empathy is a foundational moral value that helps build a healthy society. Separately, 54% agreed that empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth. In every other religious group, PRRI found that at least 66% agreed with the foundational-value statement, including 73% of white mainline Protestants and Hispanic Catholics. Empathy's foundational value was endorsed by 83% of religiously unaffiliated Americans, 80% of respondents grouped under other non-Christian religions, 77% of Jewish Americans and 65% of Latter-day Saints. The intrigue: The survey found a 30-point partisan gap: 84% of Democrats agreed with the foundational-value statement, compared with 54% of Republicans. Independents were at 70%. White evangelicals stand out among religious groups, but PRRI reports religious and partisan results separately. The survey doesn't establish how much white evangelicals contribute to the Republican-Democratic gap. Zoom in: The divide also tracks with PRRI's Christian nationalism measure. Among people PRRI classifies as Christian nationalism adherents, 38% agreed that empathy is foundational, compared with 94% of rejecters. PRRI classifies respondents as Christian nationalist adherents or sympathizers based on support for a U.S. government and laws grounded in Christianity and the view that Christians should exercise dominion over society. Six in 10 adherents agreed that empathy can become dangerous, compared with 6% of rejecters. What they're saying: "As Christian nationalist leaders attack the sentiment of empathy, a disturbing 'empathy gap' has opened, separating Republicans and white evangelicals from most other Americans," PRRI President and Founder Robert P. Jones said in a statement. Jones said the findings raise questions about the moral foundations that let people from different backgrounds share a democracy. Methodology: PRRI conducted the American Values Survey online Aug. 20–Sept. 7, 2026, among 5,200 adults in Ipsos' KnowledgePanel and 339 additional adults recruited through opt-in panels to increase sample sizes in smaller states. The survey covered adults ages 18 and older in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. The margin of sampling error is ±1.6 percentage points at the 95% confidence level for results based on the entire sample.

events.title: Republicans see shrinking boost from redistricting
events.summary: House Republicans are quietly scaling back hopes for the 10-seat boost they sought from redistricting nationwide, amid a souring political climate and polls showing a collapse in GOP support among Latino voters in Texas and Florida . Why it matters: On their down days, Republicans privately worry that the great redistricting war of 2026 will net them only one seat nationwide, according to top GOP strategists. Zoom out: At the beginning of the cycle, Republicans viewed redistricting like an umbrella in a storm: It could keep their House majority dry in a light drizzle — but in a political hurricane, it wouldn't be enough. They're not second-guessing the redistricting strategy, even as they wince at the price tag. According to AdImpact, Republicans have spent $133 million on TV ads trying to win in 15 redrawn districts that were supposed to be easy pickings. Still, they no longer talk seriously about redistricting saving their House majority, as they did a year ago — before the Iran war helped boost inflation and sink President Trump's approval ratings. By the numbers: Early this summer, Republicans believed they had created 16 more GOP-friendly seats: five in Texas , four in Florida , two in Ohio and one each in Alabama , Louisiana , Missouri , North Carolina and Tennessee . But since then, courts tossed a Missouri map and the political environment has darkened, with Democrats holding an 8-percentage-point lead in new Washington Post-ABC polling . GOP support has eroded particularly among Latino voters , raising Republican fears of losing seats their mapmakers counted on after Trump nearly won the Hispanic vote outright in 2024. "Texas, I'd be surprised if we got all five," Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios this month. "Florida, I'd be shocked if we got all four." The other side: Then factor in California , where Gov. Gavin Newsom, eager to show his party he was willing to fight back, engineered a new map with four more solidly Democratic seats — and one slightly more competitive seat. Democrats are supremely confident they can win all five — and their main super PAC has already stopped super PAC spending in one. Zoom in: So, two weeks before the Nov. 3 election, Republicans are squinting at the map and expecting to win 7 to 12 of the 15 remaining seats they redistricted. The breakdown: GOP strategists privately think Republicans can still win 2 to 4 of the 5 seats that were redrawn in Texas, and 2 (maybe 3) of the 4 new seats in Florida. They could go 0 for 2 in the redrawn seats in Ohio. The revamped seat in North Carolina is a jump ball. They're banking on winning all three new seats in Tennessee, Alabama and Louisiana. Under their most pessimistic calculations, Republicans worry their mid-cycle redistricting wave could yield just 7 new seats in red states. But then factor in Newsom's countermove in California, which put Democrats in a strong position to flip 5 seats. And in Utah, a judge forced the state to redraw its districts, obliterating a GOP-friendly seat — and creating a Democratic-leaning one in the Salt Lake City area. So as it stands now, a worst-case scenario for the GOP's final score after all that redistricting: Republicans gain 7 seats and Democrats gain 6. A year of nationwide redistricting to net one Republican seat. The details: Republicans are confident about three pickups in Southern states, where the Supreme Court's Voting Rights Act decision allowed GOP legislatures to redraw maps. They have already conceded one redrawn seat in Ohio as part of their midterm triage . Then there's Texas. Republicans are truly confident about just two of the five seats they redrew: The 9th District in the Houston area and the 32nd District in the Dallas area. The main Republican House super PAC has pulled out of Texas' 28th District in South Texas, essentially conceding the seat held by Rep. Henry Cuellar (D). It was rejiggered from a district that Trump won by 7.3 points in 2024 to one he would have won by 10.4 points. In Texas' 34th District , which touches the Rio Grande Valley and was similarly redrawn to include more Republicans, parties are spending roughly $18 million on TV ads. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez had a small lead over Republican Eric Flores in the latest NYT/Sienna poll . And in Texas' 35th District in Central Texas, which went from one that Kamala Harris won by 33.7 points to one that Trump would have won by 10.4 points, both parties have spent close to $6 million, according to AdImpact. It's too close to call. The bottom line: In a true blue wave, Republicans could lose seats Trump won by double digits. But in that scenario, Republicans would be unlikely to blame their losses on redistricting. They'd point the finger at Trump.

events.title: Three returning Democratic committee leaders still behind on dues
events.summary: Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., is one of three House Democrats who have yet to pay their DCCC dues in full despite plans to return to top committee jobs next year, according to a draft of the DCCC’s September dues report seen by Semafor. The document, which is not final, only reflects dues paid through last month; Waters has paid $450,000 in dues to date, or about two-thirds of her goal, rather than the report’s $200,000, a person familiar told Semafor, which will be reflected in the DCCC’s October dues report. Other committee ranking members lagging on the goal, according to the September draft: The top Democrats on the House Administration and Ethics committees — Reps. Joe Morelle of New York and Mark Desaulnier of California, respectively. Outgoing ranking members Angie Craig of Minnesota and Nydia Velázquez of New York are also behind, though retiring members and frontliners generally don’t pay dues in full. A person familiar with DeSaulnier’s thinking said he always paid his dues in full and intends to continue to do so. House Democrats are considering rules changes to mandate dues payments to serve on committees like Appropriations and Financial Services. The clashes over dues are a perennial issue among House Democrats that has animated previous challenges to gavels, but they’ve taken on increased importance as Democrats try to flip the House. And with House races becoming more expensive, some in the party think the dues issue will resonate with the caucus. Virginia Rep. Bobby Scott, the top Education and Workforce Committee Democrat who is facing a competitive race, has paid his dues in full.

events.title: The budget deficit swells, while the cost of debt rises
events.summary: Data: Office of Management and Budget via Fred , U.S. Treasury; Note: 2026 GDP estimated using extrapolated Q3 growth via CFRB; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The U.S. budget deficit is ballooning, reaching $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures. Why it matters: That's the largest deficit since 2021, when the U.S. was climbing out of the pandemic recession. The deficit is being driven in part by the cost of servicing the nation's enormous debt at a time when interest rates are rising due, in part, to the inflationary impact of the Iran war. By the numbers: The federal government paid out $1.052 trillion in net interest on its outstanding debt — all those Treasury notes and bonds we keep writing about — for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, according to the Treasury data. That's more than what was spent on defense, and was the country's third-biggest outlay after Social Security ($1.67 trillion) and Medicare ($1.07 trillion). Stunning stat: Federal net interest costs in 2026 are estimated at 3.3% of GDP, which would be a record high, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Between the lines: This is the price tag for years of borrowing at much higher interest rates — a sort of new normal since inflation started rising in 2021. Rising interest costs add to the deficit, driving still more borrowing and putting additional pressure on the federal budget. The intrigue: The last time interest costs approached these levels was when President George H.W. Bush was in office. At the time, the administration negotiated a bipartisan deficit reduction package that raised taxes, breaking President Bush's infamous "Read my lips, no new taxes" pledge and arguably led to him losing re-election. Still, in the 1990s, the Clinton administration and Congress worked to balance the budget through tax increases and spending cuts. What to watch: There's little appetite for that kind of work from either party, but the so-called bond vigilantes might still press for it.

events.title: Israelis lose faith in elections ahead of vote
events.summary: The US isn’t the only country struggling with a slice of the electorate that lacks confidence in its domestic elections. Ahead of an Oct. 27 vote that will decide Israel’s future leadership, Israelis’ confidence in their elections sits at an eight-year low, according to new Gallup polling that found 56% have faith in the integrity of the vote. That’s down from a high of 71% in 2023, following the Oct. 7 attacks by Hamas. There’s a huge confidence chasm between those who approve of the country’s leadership under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and those who don’t — just 37% of the latter have faith in the vote. President Donald Trump has endorsed Netanyahu in his reelection bid (though his vice president, notably, has not ), but fewer Israelis are pleased with him: Sixty-two percent of Israelis now say they currently approve of US leadership, down 14 points from last year. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Anthropic’s leaked AI bill sparks backlash
events.summary: The News The debate around the contours of an acceptable federal AI safety bill shifted again after a draft of a proposal Anthropic has been pitching to lawmakers on Capitol Hill leaked late last week. Anthropic, long seen as the safety-promoting frontier lab, found itself on the defensive, with one of its top lobbyists posting about tweaks it plans to make to the draft that more accurately reflect the dizzying pace of AI progress and the company’s stance on pre-empting state laws. That draft bill is a legislative version of an AI safety framework the company has been pitching for months, a company spokesperson told Semafor. However, AI safety advocates are arguing it doesn’t go nearly far enough, unfairly pre-empts state laws, and accepts too much possible risk. OpenAI quickly saw an opportunity to distinguish itself from its rival, with Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane writing in a post Monday implicitly directed at Anthropic: “Policy decisions must ultimately be made through our democratic processes with our elected officials leading. … No one company (including OpenAI) should write the rules alone for a technology with such profound implications for our economy, society and national security.” Ashley’s view Over the past few years, Anthropic has embraced regulation in a way that other AI companies haven’t. As the frightening possibilities of its advanced AI have emerged — and as its fight with the US government has brewed — the company has started to seek regulation through methods that have promoted heated debate within the federal government (like pitching the terms that would allow officials to block the release of certain models). OpenAI has generally been a savvier, subtler Washington player, wanting to be seen as ready to endorse compromise federal AI bills written by lawmakers, as it pursues a strategy across the states of encouraging similar frameworks it finds acceptable.
